IVOTICE IS lIIREIII7 'GIVEN, that the next -LI GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for tte County of Chester will be held at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSPORD. in the said County, on MONDAY. the 6th day of April next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in ,the Forenoon.

The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hnnelreds of Bucklow. Macclesfield. and Northwich, forming the Khuts- ford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford Districtroust be in attend- ance at the Court House. Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 6th day of April next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester on THURSDAY, the 9th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury. Nantwich. and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Pettrjury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Che;ter at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 9th day of April next. at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace. Chester, 16th March, 1891.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

IT has been, observed that wherever there is a redundancy of shirt collar, there is usually a defici- eacy of brain. A MAN carrying a looking-glass said to a news- boy: "Come here and look into this glass and you will see a monkey." "How did you find that out ?" retorted the boy. , A NEGRO contentedly laid his head on a large stone jar for a pillow, and replied to one who inquired if it was not rather hard: "Not at all, sah, for I hab stuffed it with hay." A SHALLOW-BRAINED and talkative young man began to expatiate on his fonds:less for calves' brains, at dinner, when a witty lady shut him up, by exclaim- ing: "Oh 1 you cannibal 1" "ISN'T your son rather young to join the army?" said a recruiting sergeant to an old lady whe brought a boy of fourteen to him to enlist. "Why, no," she replied: "you see, I want him to join the infantry.' IticH CITY LADY (who has just moved into her newly-bought country villa, to the cervant)— " Now, Nannette, run out to the barn and tell the hens to lay the eggs for breakfast, and be quick about it."

A GOOD old deacon who was president of the county agricultural society, referred to the arrange- ments made for contests of speed between horses for purses at the county fair, as an enterprizing feature of the occasion.

• WHY HE HIIRBIED.—" Hallo, George 1 What's your hurry ? " George—" Just heard that a friend of mine was married this morning, and I want to get there in time to congratulate him before the honeymoon is over. I know the girl he's married."

"114vE won ever seen me with more on board than I could carry ? " asked a moderate drinker of a total abstinence friend, who smilingly replied: "No, my dear fellow; but I have seen you when I thought it would have been better if you'd gone twice for your load 1" A YOUNG mother travelling with her infant child, wtc.te the following letter to her husband at home: el We are all doing first-rate and enjoy- ing ourselves very much. We are in excellent health. The baby can crawl about on all-fours. Hoping that the same can be said of you, I remain," etc.

SCENE IN A COURT ROOM.—Clerk of the Court— " Prisoner at the bar, are you guilty or not guilty 7 " Prisoner—" Not guilty." The Judge—" Who is your counsel ?" Prisoner—" I have none. lam unable to employ a lawyer." Judge—" Mr. Boggs. I appoint you to defend this man." Prisoner— (looking at his lawyer)—" Never mind, Judge. I'll plead guilty." "WHAT a lovely face Mrs. Augur has in repose —perfectly beautiful 1 Don't you think so 7 " said an enthusiastic young man to a grave old gentleman, who replied: "I can't say; I never saw her face in repose. "Indeed 1" exclaimed the young man; "then you are not intimately acquainted with the lady?" " N-n-o—l'm her husband," said the grave old gentleman. A MAN who had a very jealous wife escorted a young lady home one evening, and as he was taking leave, she turned her lovely orbs full upon him, and said: "I'm so grateful for your kindness 1" " Don't mention it, I beg of you 1" he ejaculated, gallantly. The unsophisticated maiden, thinking of his jealous wife, misunderstood the motive of his remark, and answered quickly, in a reassuring tone: "Oh, I certainly won't, as long as I live, if you don't wish ine to 1"

A CONCEITED medical student, who was in the habit of pretending humility, called on a member of the faculty, and said: "Doctor, being on the point of leaving college, I come to express my thanks to you ftir the great pains you have taken with me. All I know I owe to you." "Oh," said the doctor, "such trifles are not worth mentioning."

"How high is_ the thermometer ?" asked a ltsi- ness man who stopped in front of Hudnut's drug store the other morning. "Jes' as high as 'twas yest'd'y," replied a newsboy, as he meandered toward the corner ;." they haint changed the nail she hangs on since it was first put up." A MAGISTRATE in Memphis, Tenn., said to a venerable negro who had been convicted of an offence: "It's tetrdollars fine, or thirty days in gaol; you can take your choice." "What did you say, sah ? " asked the old man. "I said it's ten dollars or thirty days in gaol, and that you can take your choice." "Yes, sah. Ts k you sah. You may gib me de ten dollars, sah, e you please," said the old man, as he eagerly held out his hand for the money. WHAT HE SAID.—" Children, how many of your parents say grace?" asked a Sunday-school teacher. "Please mum, what's them 7 " asked an overgrown girl in a last year's hat. "Why, Maggie," exclaimed the teacher, "is it possible you don't know what grace is? Doesn't your father say something before you begin to eat?" "Oh 1" responded the girl, with a glow of intelligence. "Yes, mum, he does; he always says: Don't make pigs of yourselves; that's all the butter there is in the house."

A POMPOUS man, with a very red nose, recently gave the newsboys and bootblacks a "talk" at their lodging-house. He asked them a great many foolish questions, and the boys got restive. Finally he asked: "What is a bouquet ?" "A bunck of flowers," answered some of the boys. "And now," he said, with an air of great importance, "tell me what a nosegay is." "It's a nose covered with rum blossoms, like yours I" yelled one of the older boys, and the lecturer sat down amid a chorus of laughter and hi-yis. THE last time that Daniel Webster visited the State of Maine there was a great excitement on the sub- ject of temperance. As soon as Webster got into his room at the hotel be ordered a bottle of brandy. The landlord went up to his room to explain that the Maine law was just then so strictly enforced that he dare not bring a bottle of brandy into the house. "The fact is, Mr. Webster," he said, "if I should bring a bottle of brandy into the hotel, there would be a search-warrant out for me in no time, and the constable wouldn't hesitate to come right into your room to serve the warrant." To this the "godlike Daniel" responded in the most impressive manner: " Sir, you bring the brandy here, and l'll soon put it where no search-warrant can find it I" A HYpRANT up town having burst, flooded the neighbourhood, and the water running into the cellar of a poulterer, drowned out the hens which he kept there. The poulterer went to the office of the Board of Public Works, where he found a dandyish-looking clerk in attendance, to whom he made a complaint, urging an immediate attention to the matter, as his hens had no place but the cellar in which to stay, and the water frightened them. "Hens 1" exclaimed the clerk, peering through his eyeglass. "Hens afraid of water! Why in thunder don't you keep ducks ?" A DOSE FOR A DOCTOR.—The Hon. Sunset Cox was once visiting a physician, in a thriving Ohio village, which boasted of the largest cemetery in that region. After dinner, while the coffee was being handed round, the host requested the witty Congressman to enrich his album with one of his humourous improvisations. "Certainly," replied Cox, with a smile; and, drawing out his pencil, he wrote, under the eyes of his entertainer, the follow- ing lines: "Since Dr. -- came to this town, To cure disease; casual and hereditary, The hospital has been pulled down—" "You flatterer I" here exclaimed the doctor, mightily pleased; but the Congressman went on: "And they have made a larger cemetery." TOO SHARP rOR HER.—As a sharp old New Yorker recently stepped from a railroad train in Chicago, a handsome young lady skipped up to him. threw her arms rapturously about his neck, and kissed him many times, saying: "Oh, papa, lam so glad you have come l" The old gentleman threw both arms around her and held her firmly to his breast. Soon she looked up int(l his face, and horror stood in her eye. " Oh, my! you're not my papa!" she said, tryne to free herself from his -embrace. "Yes, I. am, insisted the old gentleman, 'holding her tightly; ".. u are my long-lost daughter, and I am goir.g to !roe:, :ou right in my arms till I get a policeman." When the officer came, and found the old gentlemol:'s diamond pin in the girl's hand, he said: " new trick here." "Is it 7" -queried the cid gentl,rnan. " Well, it's several weeks old in New York.'

SOME young men who were bantering a good- natured fat man, said to,him : g` If all flesh is grass, you must toi a 10..4d of hay." "Well," he responded, A‘ I rather 'suspect I am, from the way the asses like to nibble at me.

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., has returned 'from America a decided anti-Parnellite, and he will take an opportunity of explaining his position at a meeting of his constituents at Liverpool next week. .

Among the subscribers to the Bradlaugh portrait fund at the National Liberal Club • are two clergy- men ,of the Estab:ished Church—Canon Wilberforce and Canon 11. C. Shuttleworth a peer, and a considerable number of M.P.'s.

Mr. Gladstone was the most cheerful figure at last week's Levee. He was attired in the very com- fortable uniform of an Elder Brother of the Trinity 'House, and seemed as nimble as if he were ready to lead off a hornpipe on any given cue. It was generally remarked in the Throne-room that Mr. Gladstone looked as if he were only half the age of Lord Salisbury.

The first proceedings against the Rev.J. Bell-Cox, of Liverpool, have not been initiated by the Church Association, but by the original promoter of the suit, Dr. James Hakes, who is bent on driving mat- ters to an extremity. The Church Association, however, are in thorough sympathy with him, and, but that their hands are wore than full, would probably be ready to assist him.

Not less than forty-eight members, pretty equally divided between the Liberal and Conservative benches of the House of Commons. have given notice to nanve the rejection of the Inflammable Liquids Bill. This unfortunate measure of the Home Sec- retary has achieved the position of being the most determinealy opposed Bill of any introduced in this Parliament. It beats the Wheel and Van Tax Bill.

"I don't seem to succeed even in dying," said Prince Napoleon the other day, who after lingering for two weeks has passed beyond the reach of pain. He attracted more attention in dying than he did when alive. His death almost made him popular. He showed more strength of will and heroism on his death-bed than he had ever done in active life.

Before leaving Winchester to return to London Mr. Justice StephEn entertained the barristers on circuit at dinner. In the course of the evening he ad( reseed to them a brief speech, in which he re- ferred to Lord Coleridge's interview with him, and said that till the Lord Chief Justice spoke be had not the slightest conception that his conduct on the bench had been made the subject of public comment.

Sir M. Hicks-Beach has riven permission to the Cobden Club to publish, as. a Cobden Club leaflet, and has corrected and amended for that purpose, a portion ot the speech which he recently delivered at the dinner of the London Chamber of Com- merce. In that speech he spoke out boldly in favour of the policy of Free Trade and against a commercial union with the colonies based on reci- procity.

Prince Napoleon refused to pardon his son Victor for disputing his right to the leadership of the Bonapartist party. The Empress Eugenie in her turn would not be friends with the Prince, even on his deathbed. She has never forgiven him for his hostility to her during the Empire. When the Emperor offered the Prince a place in the Imperial Cabinet, he declined with the remark, "I won't join a Ministry which contains a petticoat."

An instance of the obstructive attitude of the Post Office towards new ideas from any quarter is to be seen in its refusal to allow stamps to be "crossed," for the purpose of rendering them un- negotiable at post offices, and so checking pilfering. In India the Post Office has long permitted this pro- cess. The pen is just drawn down the middle of the stamp, after which The Post Office, though it passes the stamp for postal purposes, will not give cash for it.

The delegation sent over to America by Mr: Par- nell, and blessed by him in his bombastic manifesto the other day, has had a flat reception so far. His own meeting at Galway on Sunday was a poor one, though every endeavour was made to whip up an audience; and notwithstanding the special trains run for the purpose, not more than a thousand peo- ple were present. On the other hand, Mr. Davitt and Mr. Ilealy adaressed at Newry one of the finest meetings which have been held in the North of Jreland. The attempt to run Parnellism against i Home Rule s certainly not succeeding.

A striking illustration of the need of electoral reform, pithily conveyed in the phrase "one man one vote, is found in the report of the Home Coun- ties Division of the N.L.P. The executive committee of that vigorous organisation say :—" In the county of Middlesex there are more than sixteen thousand property voters, of whom half do not reside in the constituency in which they vote. The property owners form approximately one-fifth of the whole electorate of the county?' This is a sample of the state of things which Joseph and his brethren assisted the Tory Government to perpetuate.

Whatever causes may prevent the realisation of Sir Edward Watkins's Channel Tunnel project, it seems clear from Professor Boyd Dawkins's - state- ments,that they will net be difficulties of a physical kind. "Very like hard cheese" is this distin- guished geologist's description of the grey chalk through which the tunnel would have to be cut. Moreover, we are assured that notwithstanding "faults "there would be no danger of water rush- ing in and wrecking the works. As to the atmos- phere—well, 'it would, in Professor Dawkins's opinion, be very much purer than that of most drawing rooms. '

By the arrangement come to with the Govern- ment the Duke of St.,Albans is to receive in com- mutation, at nineteen years' purchase, of £965 in respect to the office of Master Surveyor and Keeper of the Hawks, the sum of £18,335; and the Marquis of Downsbire, as representative of the original grantee of the office of Constable of the Fort of Hillsborough, county Down, twenty-five years' pile- chase of £54 3s. 4d., or £1,35435. 4d. These noble- men cannot claim to have been unfairly treated by a State which does not always recognise the right of the officers and soldiers who have fought for it to a satisfactory pension. "To him that bath, shall be given."

Herr Ludwig Windthorst, whose death was announced on Saturday, and who was erstwhile one of the bitterest opponents of Prince Bismarck, was a strange contrast in appearance to the German Chancellor. The one, a burly giant in stature, with a big low voice and heavy tread, always arrayed in his uniform of a cavalry general with boots and spurs complete; the other, a little old dwarf,almost hunchbacked, with a singularly ugly yet clever face, watery eyes that were bidden behind a huge pair of blue spectacles, a monstrous and almost toothless mouth, from which issued a thin, piping, wooden kind of voice, and clean-shaven cheeks, in every fold and wrinkle of ,which there seemed to lurk a' sarcasm or an irony in store for the Chan- cellor.

div.head: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
div.p: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
By F. R. R.
HAVE THE MANX HOME RULE?

The English newspapers have .contained many references of late to a constitutional crisis in the Isle of Man. "Our crisis," says the "Manx Sun," "is still going on. So far we may con- gratulate ourselves that the price of wheat and other things has been unaffected by it." A few explanatory words will enable your readers to un- derstand both the crisis and the question of Manx Home Rule which is involved in it.

A short time ago, a company was formed for the manufacture of an explosive substance called " bellite," and purchased land in the neighbourhood of Ramsey, on the coast, whereon to erect their premises. They had chosen this island as the scene of their operations because no Act is in force here regulating the manufacture of explosives, and they hoped therefore to be able to produce bellite unhampered by the costly safeguards required by the English law. It seems, however, that the permission of the Tynwald Court (i.e., the Keys, Council, and Governor) to carry on the manu- facture of explosives must first be secured, and the Bellite Company sought it accordingly. The lower Rouse, the Keys, were in favour of granting such permission, but when the matter reached the Coun- cil and the Governor its reception was very different. The Governor consulted Colonel Majendie as to the requirements of the English law in the manufac- ture of explosives, and, thus armed, he induced the Upper House, or Council, to support him in amend- ing the Bill as passed by the Keys, giving him power to require such safeguards of the Bellite Company as would secure their operatives from injury. The Company declared it would not pay them to manufacture on those terms, and that rather than obey they would abandon their works. Thereupon a series of interviews between Council and Keys began. The Keys, as representing the people, are anxious to encourage the starting of industries in the Island, which hitherto has depended solely on its natural products and its visiting trade for the sustenance of its people. They claim that the ques- tion at issue is one that solely concerns the Aianx themselves, and that they are prepared to take the responsibility involved in having their own way. They have given way so far as to ask the Governor to incorporate his regulations in the Bill, and have offered to re-consider the bill in that form; but up to the present the Governor has declined to do so. Asked what course he should take if the Keys finally refused to reject the Bellite Company's Bill, the Governor replied that he should ask the Home Secretary to pass a short bill through the House of Commons, enforcing the English Explosives Act in the Isle of Man ; that is, in other words, compelling the Manx to do what they have declared they will not do, but, in the opinion of the Governor, ought to do.

At first sight the Governor's action seems right. The people ought to be protected against themselves. But it must be remembered that bellite is a patent article, manufactured solely by the company in question, and its character is quite unknown to the world of chemists. The makers, who alone are in a position to give a valid opinion, declare that it is not a dangerous explosive like dynamite or gun- powder; that it cannot be exploded by concussion, friction, or beat, but only by a detonating cap, and that such safeguards as the Governor requires are absolutely needless. So much for the crisis. But I will give your readers a few other facts hear- ing on the quesion of Manx Home Rule, which will surprise those who have credited the Isle of Man with the enjoyment of pure self-government. To begin with, the power and influence of the Governor are so great that the Keys, although they possess the right to assemble themselves for busi- ness, seldom do so until summoned by the Governor. There is no constitutional necessity for any periodi- cal meeting; only urgent business or a summons as stated calls them together. There are no political parties to prick on the lazy steed, and there is no responsible Government to give an account of its stewardship. The reins are almost always in the hands of the Governor, and much ' depends on his character as a., statesman in the promotion of legislative measures. 'Hitherto, at all events within recent years, the island has been happy in its Governors; Governor Loch's memory is still fragrant, and Governor Walpole is on the whole a popular and successful ruler. Then there is the Council, or Upper House, com- posed, as I have told your readers, of high insular officials, the paid servants of the country, and in no way responsible to the people for their acts. They can veto the measures of the Keys, and in many ways hinder and harass their work. And again, the franchise, especially in the sheadings, is very restrictive, considering the low rentals which pre- vail here. The . voting qualification is, in the towns, a £4 tenancy, and in the country an £8 occupancy, a state of things comparable only (the poverty of the Manx workingman being re- membered) to that prevailing in England before the passing of the first Reform Bill. A further quali- fication ot the Manx claim to Home Rule exists in the fact that the full Tynwald Court, whose consent to all measures is necessary, cannot meet without being called by the Governor, and then it can only transact such business as it has been called, together to consider. The Keys may assemble theinselves, may pass bills that may urgently demand imme- diate action, but until the whole Court is summoned, and passes the measures of the Keys with the sanc- tion of the Governor, they cannot become law. And not even then! Before any Act of Tynwald can be- come law it must be submitted to the Queen and secure her sanction, and must be proclaimed from Tynwald Hill! Further, the Keys have no control over the Customs, and even public bodies like the lia.rhour Board are practically independent of them. They have, it is true, as in England, the sole right as representing the people to initiate legislation in- volving the expenditure of public money, but even that power is overridden by the Governor's veto: Lastly, "it is a common thing for the English Government to require the Manx Legislature to adopt laws analogous to those in force in England, and, if reluctance is shown, pressure is brought to bear on the authorities to enforce their adoption." I conclude with a quotation from a lode! authority which puts the case quite truthfully as far as I have been able to judge, after the most careful en- quiries from friends here whose knowledge is in disputable (including a member of the Keys) : "The Isle of Man has freqoently of late been held up to the rest of the Empire as an example of the success of what is called 'Home Rule.' A careful examination of the working of its ancient constitu- tion, as it is at present administered, can only lead to the conclus on that it is in no respect an ex- ample of Parliamentary Government, but that it is rather an example of a constitution perverted and used as a cover for the strongest and most unmi- tigated case of personal rule known in the British Empire."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1891. MR. G-LADSTONE AT HASTISGS. PEACIVAL GORDON;
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1891. MR. G-LADSTONE AT HASTISGS. PEACIVAL GORDON;

There was a remarkable demonstration at Charing Cross Station, on Tuesday forencion on the departure of Mr. Gladstone to fulfil his engagement to speak at Hast- ings. A large crowd gathered, many weaaring sham- rocks in observance of St. Patrick's Day. Mr. Gladstone was warmly cheered as he drove up. /Mr. Causton, M.P., presented an address from the Liberal and Radical or- ganisations of the metropolis to Mr, Gladstone, who briefly expressed his thanks, to the disappointment of the crowd, who had expected a speech. He gave no address. The cheers were renewed as the train left at 12.15. The only stoppage in the route was at Tunbridge Wells, where the right hon. gentleman, replying to an address, declared that the Home Rule which the Liberal party would propose for Ireland would command the confidence of Ireland, would be compatible with English honour, ptomote English interests, and would bring happiness and contentment to the sister isles. He also insisted on the abso!ute secrecy of the ballot. The right lhon. gentleman having concluded his remarks, the order to resume the journey was at once given, and the train moved off. Arrived at Hastings, Mr. and Mrs. Glad- stone drove in a barouche drawn by two borses, driven by a postilion, and escorted by mountedpolice. Through- out. the route, despite the rough weather, was crowded with sightseers. The procession was greeted with en- thusiastic cheers.. Luncheon was served at the Hastings Railway Station, after which Mr. Gladstone drove to the theatre...

MASS MEETING IN THE THEATRE. The mass meeting was held in the Gaiety Theatre, which has accommodation for about 1,500 persons. The time fixed was a quarter past three,but by half-past one the entrances to the various parts of the house were thronged with persons awaiting the opening of the doors, and there was great pressure on the barriers which were fixed at the front, and placed in charge of members of the borough police. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, accom- panied by Lord Brassey, entered at twenty-five minutes past three. The entire audience rose, the ovation lasting several minutes. Lord Brassey took the chair, and in opening the proceedings, said that to introduce Mr. Gladstone to that great and imposing meeting was idle and unnecessary. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone's name was hourly on every lip. He was loved as no other leader had been loved by his followers. (Cheers.) To sum up .his career, he (Lord Brassey-) might say that his efforts had been devoted to the cause of freedom, and that his sympathies had ever been shown to the feeble and oppressed. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone, who on rising, was received with pro- longed and enthusiastic cheers said that the Foreign Office had had to deal with many knotty ques- tions but ,speaking generally there had been little in Lord Salisbury's foreign policy to which they as Liberals ought to object. As to the finance of the coun- try, however.he complained that the power of the House of Commons to control the expenditure of the country from year to year was being encroached upon by an in- sidious method, and that the country was being treated to fictitious surpluses of revenue over expenditure. Upon the Irish question he declared that rather than place the constitutional leadership in the hands of Mr. Parnell the Liberal party were ready to face defeat, exclusion, and political misfortune. They were never more determined upon prosecuting their march as a united host towards the attainment of the great objects they had in view. Having spoken upon questims remaining to be dealt with,he said they would prosecute their great enterprise because it was in that way that they would assist the union of classes, the dominion of law, the stability of the Throne, and the welfare of all. _

Describing the speech, a special correspondent says: —Mr. Gladstone was in good voice—clearly heard in the remotest corners of the building. He was in excellent spirits. The gay humour of his description of Tory finance sent his audience into roars of laughter. " Ships are changing." said he, as "incessantly as ladies' bon- nets." There were as many fashions in one as in the other. Yet the Tory Government had committed the country for seven years to a hard-and-fast line of naval "What would you think of the lady who ordered seven years' supply of bonnets rigidly adapted to the present pattern." A large, and not the least striking, portion of Mr. Gladstone's great speeeh was a. merciless exposure of the dangers and' the unconstitu- tional trickeries of the finance of the Tory Government. Secrecy and the destruction of the control of the House of Commons were, said Mr. Gladstone,the characteristics of the ministerial finance—secrecy and sham surpluses. On this great topic Mr. Gladstone's ringing periods were a clear, unescapable challenge to Lord Salisbury's Government. There was a storm of applause when Mr. Gladstone,with one of his most vigorous and characteris- tic gestures, declared that he considered" the waste of five millions a lesser evil than the concealment of one." The same effect was produced when it showed how the" Public Endowment Bill," even if it had been defensible, N%-a.s based upon- a fictitious sur- plus. He turned Mr. Goschen's finance inside out. Loud applause greeted him when he declared that the Home Rule of the future would be, in essentials, the Home Rule of the past ; and that the Liberals of England, Scotland, and Wales would refuse to recognise as the leader of the Irish people the man (Mr. Parnell) whom the great majority of his followers had deposed. Then, in his youthfully buoyant, good-natured, but unsparing manner, he made sport of the" Unionists "—downright- sport—aud he enjoyed it to the full. " Oh," said he, "I should be delighted if the Tories gave the Irish Home Rule. The Tories gave Catholic emancipation. ,The Tory party lives by its defeats. (Laughter). It comes up like Punch in the show, in spite of all the knocks that fall on its head!' "But "—and here Mr. Gladstone dropped his voice, he paused—" what has Ireland to ex- pect from that ill-starred abortion of a party called " buthere he stopped again, and looked round About him leisurely, as if he were trying to think out the name. It came at last, in a deep-toned, slow, deliberate, humor- ously contemptuous—" Liberal Unionists." His brief, clear, candid, dispassionate sketch of Liberal relation- ships with the Irish party was listened to with profound, admiring attention. From beginning to end of Mr. Gladstone's speech there was not a harsh or ungenerous expression. But the address was about:the most formid- able indictment that even Mr. Gladstone ever uttered against the party of privilege and reaction. He gave Lord Salisbury credit for his foreign policy; but the rest of his address was a notice to quit. That the speech must exercise an immense effect in Southern England was evidently the opinion of all who heard it.
THE WORLD'S FAIR AND BITNYAN'S
COTTAGE.

A gentleman resident in Bedford recently received a letter from an old Bedfordian who is now practising as a physician in Chicago, asking him to arrange for the purchase of Bunyan's Cottage at Elstow, for trans- ference to the World's Fair at Chicago. This, however. is impossible, but the gentlemau who received the letter, has recommended that models of the cottage and Elstow Church should be made for the Fair, and probably this will be done.

div.head: ALLEGED DOUBLE NafIUADL
div.p: ALLEGED DOUBLE NafIUADL

At the Manchester Police Court, on Tuesday, a young man named Walter Frederick Chadwick, was charged with being concerned in the murders of Mrs. Samuels, at Kentish Town, in 1887, and his aunt Mrs. Lucy Clark, in Marylebone, in 1888, robbery being the motive in both cases. Louisa Davies, a dressmaker, who had been living with the prisoner, was examined, and said that Chadwick told her nine months ago and repea' edly since that three of them went to rob Mrs. Samuels's house, and when she appeared he knocked her down. As to the alleged murder of his aunt, prisoner told witness he had not killed her, but he had a good idea who had. On the application of a Scotland-yard inspector, the accused was remanded.
AN INCE CURATE'S BREACH OF PROMISE.

On Tuesday morning, in the Sheriff's Courtroom, St. George's Hall, before Mr. Lewis Williams and a sheriff's jury, the case of Oldham v. Whitfield was brought before the court with the object of assessing damages in favour of the plaintiff against the defendant. Mr. Pickford (instructed by Messrs. Wilson, Dean, and M‘Master) was counsel for the plaintiff, and the defendant was repre- sented by Mr. Gully, Q.C., The plaintiff, Esther Old- ham, is headmistress of the Ince Central Infants' School, and the defendant is the Rev. John George James Whit- field, 8.A., one of the curates of Ince Parish Church, near Wigan. Mr. Pickford informed the court, after the jury had been sworn, that they should not have to trouble the jury except to return a verdict of £l5O by the consent of the parties. The jury returned a verdict accordingly, and the proceedings closed.

div.head: COLLISION AT SEA AND LOSS OF 22
div.p: COLLISION AT SEA AND LOSS OF 22
LiVES.

A disastrous collision took place on Friday night between a ship and a steamer' resulting in the sinking of the latter and the loss of 22 lives. The English ship British Peer (Captain Dakin), 1,428 tons, with linseed, from Calcutta, via.' Trinidad, to London, when about 120 miles south-west of Scilly, collided with the steamer , Roxburg Castle, of Newcastle, about nine p.m. on the 13th inst. So severe was the collision that the Roxburgh Castle immediately sank, taking down with her 22 out of a crew of 24 all told. Her captain, named Tyrer, of Brixham, and one seaman, named Whitelow, were res- cued, and landed at Falmouth on Monday morning. The Britisirkeer received very great damage by the collision, and when about 90 miles south-west of the Wolf Rock she was taken in tow by the steamer Morglay, and brought to the entrance of Falmouth harbour, where a local tug took her into port.

div.head: OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT. • By SYLVANUS COBB.
div.p: OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT. • By SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER 111. FAREWELL TO ANOTHER-AN AMBITSCADN.

The dead of Talavera had been buried; the woundecl cared fur; and the armistice was at an end. On the third morning after the battle, the English having moved back as far as the Lesser Benito, a consultation of surgeons was holden upon the case of Sergeant John Coverly. His wound was in an alarming condition. Gangrene had set in, and its spread promised to be rapid. There could be but one conclusion on the part of an intelligent and experienced physician: If life were desired, the leg =lust come off at the hip joint; and this decision was made known to him.

The veteran heard without a quiver. "If you don't amputate I shall surely die ?" he said, interrogatively. "you certainly will; and that, too, speedily." "And if you perform the operation—what then ?"
"Why," returned the surgeon-in-chief, hesitat- ingly,—" we should in that case feel that we had done what ive could."

"Answer me plainly. I am not afraid of the truth. Is there—can you see—a possibility of recovery after my leg is taken off?" "Honestly, Sergeant, we cannot. I may as well tell you at once: There is a slight scratch on your shoulder—" a " Zounds !" broke in the old man. "It burns and throbs as though it tvas an angry wound." "And yet," added the surgeon, "it was only a scratch in the beginning; and now gangrene is there. The removal of the leg would not purify your blood." "Very well," said Coverly, without hesitation. " I now know that I must (lie; and I know that such a death is likely to be painless. So, good sits, I will not suffer needless torture; and, wheri this old body is laid away it shall be intact. Make me as easy as you can, and accept my deepest gratitude; for I well know that you would save we if saving were possible." That was on the morning of Monday, the last day of July. Before noon Sergeants Coverly and Crawford, together with others of the regiment, were placed in an ambulance, aaul started on the road towards the western frontier; for Sir Arthur had determined to reach the Portuguese boundary before reorganizing his forces. A day aug. a half on the road, and on Tuesday evening they stopped near the village of Almaraz, where they camped for the night. Percival had hardly slept since the death of his father. It was care of his grandfather, however, that had kept him wakeful. But on this Tuesday evening the old man was so easy, and so entirely free from pain, that the boy gave himself freely up to the drowsy influence and slept soundly. But while the boy slept Toot Crawford kept watch. Despite the heat and the climatic miasma, Tom was mending rapidly. His general health was well nigh perfect, only his lameness tying him to the ambulance.

Towards midnight the 'keen watcher detected a marked change in old Jack's breathing. The respirations were becoming shorter and shorter, and more faint. There was no sign of labour, nor of pain, but only a gradual sinking of every vital function. From the roof of the ambulance • was suspended a lighted lantern, by the fitful gleams of which Tom could see his friend's face, that it was pale and sunken, but calm and placid, with something like a smile resting upon the strongly. marked features. He spoke, and the closed eyes slowly opened. _ _

" !—Tom !—O! I've had a dream so sweet and blessod that lam sorry I ever awoke. I think I saw Robert and Bessie,—and the other Bessie— my own—the first Bessie's mother." He spoke in gasps, and not above a whisper. "Say, dear old Jack," said Tom, after a pause, "how do you feel? Out with it. Let me know the truth." The old man seemed startled. His sense of extreme ease, and his beautiful dream, had served to make him happy, and he had not looked beyond. But his eyes were opened now to the truth. He could feet that, the end was near at hand; and so he told his companion. "0, dear Tom, I am glad you woke me up, for I do not think I should ever have opened my eyes again had you not spoken. Yes, I feelit here,"— and he laid his hand over his heart—"and I feel my breathing failing. I must turn the charge over to you now, if ever. The boy is asleep?" " a log." "I am glad. Poor boy ! how faithfully he has nursed me. 0, Tom! you will be good to Percival! You will keep the faith to the end ?" "I will, dear Jack. From this time I pledge my every energy, of both mind and body, to the little hero's good, and I will give my life, if need be. I think I shall be spared to take care of him."

"I know you will be, Tom. I feel it in my bones. And now to the work. Here is the packet. You know what it contains, and—" The failing man' asshe spoke, had sought to take the packet from his bosom; but he had not the strength, and his faithful comrade came to his assistance. Tom found the papers, and having made sure that the envelope was intact, he trans- ferred the parcel to the inside pocket of his own vest, where he said ha would sew it in on the first opportunity. Once more lie assured old Jack that he perfectly 'understood the nature andbmission of the papers, and bade him believe that all would be well with his grandson. After this the old man seemed inclined to drop off to sleep again. He was too weak to speak, save in a low whisper; and it was with an effort that he could lift a -hand. Tom marked the signs, and awoke Percival. _ _ _
_ " Percy ! I think you my bid your grandpa farewell. flush ! Not a word of sorrow. He will fall asleep without an atom of pain. Let him sleep happily,"

With wonderful self-control the boy moved to his grandfather's side, and lifted the frosted head to his bosom, holding him iu tender embrace. The old hussar looked into the boyish face, and sweetly smiled. Au earnest look followed, and presently, with much emotion, he whispered : "My blessed boy !—my best beloved !—your old grandfather is going; but, 0! I hope it is to a better and happier world ; and, when years have passed, you will follow. Percival, I charge you, so live, if you can, that when your final hour shall come, you can bid adieu to this lower life without one vain regret. Be honest; be truthful; be loyal and true • be bold and fearless in the way of right; and be afraid only of wrong and error. In short, dear boy, study the teachings of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Cluist ; and keep the faith, as thy mother taught thee. And the boy, unable to keep back the flooding tears, kissed the seamed and furrowed brow of his grandsire, and, from the fulness of his heart, gave the promise. Again the old man smiled; and with that smil6 lighting up the sunken features he fell asleep. On the following morning Col. Maxwell sought the abbot of an old monastery, near at hand, and obtained permission to inter the body of the dead hussar in consecrated ground. No questions were asked concerning the religious faith of the deceased. The pious old monk knew that the Englishman had lost his life in doing battle against the Vandals who had ruthlessly robbed so many of their art-stored convents, and he gave the requested sepulture with- out objection. And, as Sergeant John Coverly had been the oldest non-commissioned officer in the regiment, the full troop turned out in repect to his memory, and a volley was fired over his grave, On'tbe day following that on which the mortal remains of Sergeant Coverly had been interred two more men died in that same ambulance: so that, when it set forth on the next day's march, it contained only three men besides our hero, and the driver—all three of them sergeants. Percival had been permitted to ride because he had no horse, and because there had been plenty of room. On a drizzly, disagreeable afternoon,—it was the day following the death of the two sergeants,— while Percival sat with the driver, admiring the grandeur of the Sierras de San Benito, which had been in sight since morning, Col. Maxwell rode up, his horse being led by an orderly, and bade the driver pull up. His wounded foot was badly swollen, and pained him so that he could not hold it io the stirrup. In fact, he could not bear the hanging of the foot from the saddle.
" Well, Sergeant," he said, addressing Crawford, who was the ranking man within, "1 think you will have to make room for me. This foot of mine won't let me keep the saddle."

"There's plenty of room, Colonel, if you can put up with our company." "No more or that, Tom. Comrades in distress should be comrAdes indeed. I must come in on an equality; and if you would make me comfortably

at- home you must maae yourselves the same. our surgeon tells me that this is the easiest riding ambulance in the division, and that he is carrying by far the lightest load." And after he had entered, and his orderly had placed at his disposal two or three soft cushicins, he explained to his companions that the ambulance which they now occupied had been originally built for the field and stall of Lancaster's Division, and its springs had been fashioned by the earl's own design. "After Lancaster's retirement," he continued, "the silken trappings and soft ottomans became faded and worn and tattered, and it was turned over to the line, while a new, and a larger, and more elaborately ornamented vehicle was built and furnished in its place. But they did not think to make use of the old foundation, and that was where they made their mistake." "That solves the mystery," said Crawford. "We have been wondering at the marvellous case of the ambulance ever since we occupied it. Some of us have been in ambulances before, but this, as compared with others we had known, was as a child's cradle compared with a harrow." For a little time the three sergeants felt that their social comfort would be sadly interfered with by the presence of his lordship, but within half an hour he had placed them completely at their case, and before the day was done they were enjoying his society immensely. He told them stories of his own campaigns—told in a free and easy manner, just as he would have told them at his club—and he proved himself as good a listener as he was speaker, for he led them to tell of their own adven- tures, and he plainly signified that he enjoyed them.

Maxwell's command was a part of the rear guard of the retreating column, and on the night follow- ing his entrance into the ambulance he encamped in a little hamlet called St. Martin, close under the shadows of the towering Sierras. The colonel found comfortable lodgings for the night in the dwelling of one of the principal men of the place, and on the following morning, as he arose from the breakfast-table, he was informed by his host that there was a sick man in the house who wished very•much to speak with him—an Englishman, the host said, who had been travelling througit the country, and who had been taken sick on the mountains.

Col. Maxwell followed his entertainer to a well- furnished chamber, where he found the man in question sitting up in his bed. The sound of approaching footsteps had evidently called him to that posture. "Harry Maxwell! Thank Heaven for the sight of your honest face !" At first the colonel did not recognise the wan, pale face, though it was familiar. "What! Don't you know me ?" And the smile accompanying these words revealed him. It was Sir Philip Trenchard, a baronet of Somer- set, of Maxwell's own age; a classmate at Oxford, a companion of the same club, and a dear friend always. It was tho first time they had met for several years, and Sir Philip had been very, very eager to see his old friend since he had known of his presence in the place. Maxwell summoned an orderly, aid told him to send to him the adjutant of the regiment, who had quartered beneath that same roof during the night. Ere long the adjutant made his appearance, and having introduced him to Sir Philip Trenehard, and briefly explained the circumstances of the meeting, he ordered as follows:

"You w,ill form the troop as it was formed yesterday, and march promptly at the sound of the bugle. Let everything move except Wilson's ambulance and its occupants, and you may tell them to wait for me. I shall not remain long, and yet I cannot tear myself away just yet. W shun has good horses, and we shall not be a great while in overtaking you. You understand ?" The adjutant repeated the order, and having been assured thftt he had it correct, he took his leave.

And then Maxwell turned to his old friend, and in a brief space they were deep in the stories of other days. Outside waited Jack Wilson with his ambulance. At six o'clock the column was armed, and at half- past six the bugle sounded for the forward move- ment.

An hour passed, and the rear of the retiring army had been long out of sight, when Wilson asked Percival if he would not run in and see if the colonel realised how time was passing. "Tell him too," the driver added, "that I have seen men skulking in the hamlet whose appearance Ido not like. Bless his good heart! he don't know bow he is tarrying." . . .

The boy, himself iinxrons, did not hesitate. He went in, and made his way to the baronet's chamber, and shortly thereafter Maxwell came hurrying down. He confessed that he had for- gotten himself entirely; and yet he had a good excuse. Sir Philip l'renchard was an educated physician, and he had been examining his wounded foot; and, moreover, he had given directions for proper treatment and speedy cure. "We are not more than an hour behind," he said.

"A good hour and a half, sir," corrected the driver. "Well, well, we will soon overcome that. Take advantage of smooth stretches of road, Wilson, and hurry on. By the way—the boy says you have seen several skulkers whose looks you did not like. What is it ? "

"That was all there was of it, sir. Two or three evil-looking fellows, half an hour ago, were skulking atoun4 the huts on the opposite side of the way, and I fancied they had their eyes on our ambulance."
"And you have not seen them since ?" " No, sir."

• "Very well. If they mean mischief, we can give them a warm reecption. Luckily we are well sup- plied with arms. lam sorry I stopped so long, but regrets will not avail. Let us' move on, and look to our arms as we .go." The colonel and the boy took their seats in the ambulance, and the driver whipped up. In a chest forward, with various hospital stores, were six carbines, a species of short musket adapted to cavalry, and a dozen heavy pistols, together with plenty of ammunition. These were all taken out, and loaded, even Tom Crawford, despite his wounded arm, being la ble to help in the work.

At the distance of little more than a mile from the hamlet the road bent abruptly around a bo!d spur of the mountain range, and here the way was rough and uneven, so that the driver was force 4 to drive with the utmost care. The turn had been made, and in the far distance ahead Wilson fancied that he could detect the dust of the moving armyl but his attention was very soon called in another direction. He had withdrawn his gaze from the distant cloud, and was guiding his horses over a pass where the rocks were laige and dangerous, when the animals suddenly stopped, and shied from the road. He looked up, and saw four men directly in the path, while others seemed to be emerging from the thick wildwood on the mountain side. They were ugly looking fellows, full-bearded and tawny, and habited in the garbs of Spanish bandits. Our driver's first impulse upon beholding the intruders was to apply the whip. The rascals saw the move- ment, and two of them leaped to the horses' heads, and grasped the rings of the bits, whereupon the startled animals reared, and then swiftly baoked away, and in their awkward plunging they turned so sharply to the right that the rear part of the ambulance was driven into the thick brushwood. This hospital waggon was arranged with its door of entrance in the rear, while along on the aid ce were small square openings, protected by cluvas flaps, or curtains, for ventilation. The boy Perci- val occupied the seat nearest the place of entrance, and when he found the rear half of the vehicle plunged into the tangled wood he quietly opened the door and slipped out, sinking at once upon his hands and knees, and crawling swiftly away under close cover. He had one of the heavy pistols in his hand, besides his own smaller pistols—a brace of them—in his pockets.

At the first alarm Maxwell had sprung to his feet, and raised the curtain nearest to him, and he saw four •men emerging from the wood close at hand, he knew, furthermore that others had approached in front. "To arms !" he cried. "Let us be prepared, but do not fire until I give the order. If there—"

His speech was cut short by the sudden backing of the ambulance, which movement threw hioi violently against the side, but without bodily injury. By the time he had picked himself up the voice of the driver was beard. He spoke through an opening at the end of his seat.
"You had better not fire," he said. "We are surrounded by bandits—a full score of them— armed to the teeth."

As soon as the vehicle came to a standstill, the colonel took another look and saw that Wilson had not exaggerated. He had thought of fighting, but if the miscreants meant only to rob them it would be poor policy to invite their fire. He looked around upon his companions and saw only three besides himself, and one of those could not hold a musket to his shoulder, though he. might fire a

pistol. There was Sergeant Tom Urawtorn, stout, brave and true, whose wounded arm might fail • with a carbine, but who might be depended upon to do good work with the pistol. Then there was Serge.mt Malcolm Dunbar, stalwart and gallant, able to handle arms, though weak to stand. Next came Sergeant Felix O'Grady, a genial, true-hearted son of the Emerald Isle, as brave as the bravest and true as steel His would was in the hip, his arms being well and strong. But where was the boy, Percival? Who had seen him ? "'loin, where is he? He sat near you when I saw bim last."

Tom was startled. He remembered, now that his attention was called to it, that the boy had opened the door and he must have jumped out. "Unless," he added, " the sudden jolt as vve brought up in the bushee threw him out." " Of one thing we may be sure, yer honour," said O'Grady, "the little darlitf never ran away through fear." "No," added Maxwell; "fear would not have led him to leap plump into the fire. But—hold I What now 1"

At this point the two men at the horses' heads had succeeded in bringing the ambulance back into the road, where it had been quickly surrounded; and as the colonel spoke his last words the door in the rear was pulled Open and a burly, black - bearded bandit appeared at the entrance with half a dozen more of the same character behind him. _
"Tow," said Maxwell, in a hoarse, hurried whisper, "we are indeed surrounded. It would be madness to olkr battle."
" It would be suicide, my lord; but we'll stand by you, let what will come." "Hark I Let us hear what the rascal has to say." (7o be continued).

IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. PROMOTION IN THE NAVY.—AttentiOn was called by Lord SUDELEY to the block of promotion in the rank of lieutenants in the royal navy. The noble lord contended that if promotion was so slow the service would suffer, as parents would not send their sons into the navy. After a few remarks by Lord NORTHBROOK and others, the subject dropped. 'THE SEIZURE OF A. BRITISH STEAMER.—Lord SALISBURY, replying to the Earl of Kimberly, said he had received no information other than that published in the news- Papers, with reference to the seizure of a British steamer by the Portuguese. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. • The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was ordered to issue for the election of a member to fill the vacancy in North Sligo caused by the death of Mr. M'Donald. WOMEN AND THE LABOUR COMMISSION.—Mr. W. H. SMITH informed Mr. 'Bryce it was not advisable that women should serve on the Labour Commission. Fe- Male witnesses, however, could give evidence. PAUPER CHILDREN AND CANADA.—Mr. RITCHIE, in answer to Mr. S. Smith, said the number of pauper children sent to Canada during last year was 375; and in 1887, the year preceding the modification of the rules laid down by the Local Government Board, the number Was 166. ENGLAND AND PORTUGAL—Sir J. FERGUSSON, replying to several questions, said the British steamer the Countess Of Carnarvon had been seized on the Limpopo river by the Portuguese,<M a charge of smuggling, and if de- tained on that ground only legal proceellings would be taken. The importation of arms And ammunition into Mozambique was prohibited. MR. STOREY AND THE SILKSWORTII AFFAIR.—Mr. STOREY drew attention to the recent prosecution instituted by him as to matters arising out of the evictions at Silks- worth. He said he had failed to sustain the charge owing to the bench being packed by his political oppon- ents and was proceeding with his remark when he was called to order by the Speaker for endeavouring to re-try the case. MORNING SITTINGS.—Mr. W. H. Smini, in ,moving a resolution in favour of having morning sittings on Tues- days and Fridays, said he did not believe he was demand- ing anything Which the circumstances did not justify. If the proposal was sanctioned, the Irish Land Bill would be taken on the• Thursday after the Easter holidays, but the Budget would not be taken for some days later.—Mr. LABOUCHERE protested against the time of the House being taken in this way.—Mr. GLADSTONE said an express declaration ought to have been given that supply would be put forward at an early date, and hoped there would be no attempt to avoid making a House at _nine o'clock on Fridays. The motion was carried without a division. • SUPPLY.—IRISH VOTE.—The House having gone into Committee of Supply, a vote of £150,000 for the Royal , Irish Constabulary police force hind was agreed to, as was also one of £3.915 for superannuation allowances. ,On the vote of £3,917,003 for diverse Civil Services, Mr. tiAlsoucHEßE moved its reduction by £lOO, part of the salary of the Foreign Secretary, as a protest agaiast British action in the Soudan. A long discussion took Place on the subject, and the motion was ultimately "egatived without a division. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord ChanBellor took his seat on the woolsack at I ilalf;Past five o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Duke of Richmond, the Earl of . Relmore, the Earl of Camperdown, Lord Belper, and . Lord Houghton were appointed members of the Commit- Oil Railway Rates and Charges. The Sale of Goods ' Bill was read a second time, its object being to bring into a single code the law as to the sale of goods. The Tithe Rent Charge Recovery Bill was read a third time, Lord lirabourne protesting strongly that it would inflict the maximum of injustice. The Technical Instruction Bill Was also read a third time. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past six o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. Thjg was the first regular morning sitting of the House this session, the Speaker taking the chair at two o'clock. RAiLWAy Bims.—The Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail- .way Bill was read a second time, after Mr. WHITLEY had Intunated that the clause enabling the company to erect an hotel on their land would be withdrawn. The Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire (Extension to Lon- don) Bill was read a second time, after considerable discussion, and subject to an instruction as to whether the site of the proposed terminus is the best in the interests of the people of London. QUESTIONS.—Mr. RAIKES, in replying to several ques- tions, said he had given directions for the establishment of a service which, he believed, would meet such public demands as exist for the more rapid transmission of !Ingle letters. Sir JAMES FERGUSSON, replying to Mr. iorton, Said that no answer has yet been received from IN_ ewfoundland regardiri e the request from her Majesty's Government to appoint' a delegate on the Board of Arbitration in reference to the Fisheries dispute. GAMBLING, &c.—Mr. MermEws informed Sir G. Camp- bell that fresh legislation was not contemplated for the suppression of gambling at races. Mr. SMITH promised to state the terms of reference to the Labour Commission in a few days. The Custody of Children Bill was read a second time, as was also the Savings Bank Bill. At the evening sitting, a motion directed against gambling was negatived by 70 to 47; and the House was counted out at twenty minutes past eleven. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.
_ The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve, but a House was not made until twenty-five minutes Past twelve. LOCAL OPTION FOR WALES.

Mr. B. ROWLANDS moved the second reading of the Liquor Traffic Local Veto (Wales) Bill. He said if it Was legitimate to make this question the subject of ex- Periment there could be no place where so satisfactory an experiment could be made or where the people so ardently desired that it bliould be tried. Lord CARNAR- TRENT moved the rejection of the bill. He said the inevit- able result of the measure must be the fostering and bol- !tering up of so-called clubs—of private drinking estab- ,lehments, which were so frightful and fruitful a source Of drunkenness, immorality, and crime. Mr. J. MeLEAN !ecended the amendment, saying he opposed the bill /rem the point of view of common sense. Mr. OSBORNE MoRoAN said that 90 per cent. of the Welsh people r ere in favour of the bill. Mr. MATTHEWS said that 'Or himself he could not vote for the bill. The nleasure was unjust to those engaged in the trade and to the moderate drinker, and it would be im- Possible and impracticable in the larger towns of the aountry. If they were to apply such a law to Lon- no, he should be sorry to be responsible for the Peace and order of the capital, and there were many Other large towns where it would be an act of insanity to tttempt to prevent all sale of intoxicating liquor.—Mr. ,_dourr MORLEY supported the principle of the bill, though 'le objected to some of the details. He did not think it Would be safe to enforce prohibition with less than the LIIPPort of two-thirds or Three-fourths of the total num- "" of Persons entitled to vote. It was because he was - Persuaded that the temperance cause could only be effec- tually promoted by such a measure as the present that he should vote for the bill. On a division the second reading was carried by a majority of six, the numbers '-'ing—for the bill, 185; against, 179. Mixens' BILL.—The second reading of the, Miners' Right Hours Bill was moved by Mr. ABRAHAM (Rhondda), but the time for adjournment having arrived debate was Postponed till thp 15th April. MiscELLAicEous.—The Army (Annual) Bill and the Public Bodies (Provisional Orders) Bill were read a third time. The Registration of Electors (Acceleration) Bill Was withrdawn.—Mr. Jackson brought in a bill, which Was read the first time, to atnend certain provisions of the law with respect to money charged on or payable out of the consolidated fund and with respect to public ac- counts. The House adjourned at a quarter to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THErvpilv. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four o'clock. The Consolidated Fund Bill and the Army (Annual) Bill Were read a first time. THE BORROWING (INFANTS) AND OTHER BILLS.—OH the Itotion of Lord Herschel], the Borrowing (Infants) Bill W„as read a second time. The report of amendments to 1.0.0 Clergy (Immorality) Bill was received, and the Tech- Veal Instruction Bill passed through committee.—Earl :litowNLow, replying to tbe Earl of Dundonald, promised 'hat the Government would give every consideration to a'nY practical suggestion for the employment of retired B,oldiers and sailors ashore.—Lord KtrerrsFonn called at- ,ention to the Newfoundland papers laid before Podia- Inent, and asked their lordships to read for the first time 1,1.' bill which was intended to simplify the position as be- f'reen the French and the Newfoundlanders. After some • rnarks from Lord Kimberley and Lord Salisbury, the ""I was read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minntes to eight. . HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. I,.'4„oEsTiobis &c.—The Great Northern Railway (New „I",e) Bill was read a third time. Mr. ML'rrxEws, in to Mr. Cobb, undertook to procure a return of the nrnber of persons in prison for contempt of court on the of January last. Mr. STANHOPE informed Mr. Frit- rukard Morgan that the expediency of forming a batta- :n of Volunteers for Merionethshire was again under his fAration. Mr. RAMPS explained the additional ,acilities which the Post Office intended to give for the ▪ ansmission of messages for short distances. Mr. 'resecußic, informed Sir H. Roscoe that a public-spirited igeentleman had offered £BO.OOO to build a British Art Gal- on a site at South Kensington. Sir J. FERGUSSON 11_11_ormed Mr. Campbell Bannerman that he had no know- ,rge as to how the report of the Colonisation Committee prematurely furnished to the "Times." BILL.—The House considered the Lords' ,rzi.endinents to the Tithe Rent Charge Recovery Bill, and WILLIAM 'HARCOURT complained of the way in which :_u_e l:ndments had been introduced. Several amendments Z_ e dealt with. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE moved an amend- to provide that the section should not apply to cases "wriere contracts for tenancy were entered into before the
passing of the Act. Sir M. flicKs-BEAcK could not accept the amendment. On a division the amendment was re- jected by 167 to 106. At twelve o'clock the debate stood adjourned till next day.

div.head: EXPLOSION IN THI4I SOUDAN.
div.p: EXPLOSION IN THI4I SOUDAN.

100 DERVISHES KILLED. Intelligence reached Cairo on Monday stating that a month ago an explosion occurred at the arsenal at Om- durman, Khartoum, by which 100 dervishes were killed and a quantity wf ammunition destroyed.
THE BACCARAT SCANDAL

Messrs. Lewis and Lewis deny that there is any truth in the statement that an apology will be tendered by the defendants in the action brought by Sir William Gordon- Cufhming arising out of the baccarat incident at Tranby Croft. NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERIES.

A Paris telegram im Monday says the arbitrators chosen by the Governments of England and France in the Newfoundland fishery dispute are the following : M. Martens,Professor of International Law at St. Peters- burgh University; M. Rivier, Swiss Consul-General at Brussels and President of the Instittte of International Law ; and M. Gran, a former Judge of the Supreme Court in Norway.
MR. PARNELL AND HIS DELEGATES.

NEW YORK, March 16.—The opinion is expressed in many quarters that the visit of the Irish delegates will prove a failure. The Press generally condempt3 Mr. Parnell's manifesto, and advises the people not to sup- port the mission. The newspapers in the West, who have hitherto been favourable to Mr. Parnell, lay that the delegates may pass round the hat, but that they will return empty-handed. •
THE TELEPHONE BETWEEN LONDON
AND PARIS.

Penis, TIIESDAY.—The first official trial was made this afternoon of the newly-established telephonic communi- cation between Paris and London. The experiment was completely successful, the voices of telephonists at the London end being distinctly audible. M. Amiot, Inspec- tor General of Telegraphs accompanied by his assistant, M. Thomas, went specially to London to be present at the telephoning of the first messeage.

div.head: DEATH OF PRINCE JEROME NAPOLEOX..
div.p: DEATH OF PRINCE JEROME NAPOLEOX..
Rumn, TIIESDAY.—Prince Jerome Napoleon expired at half-past seven o'clock this morning.
THE PRINCE'S MEMOIRS

A Paris telegram says that portions of Prince Napo- leon's memoirs' written by himself, are said to be about to be prepared for publication by his intimate friend M. Masson. They extend from the period of the Prince's early childhood to the date of the promulgation in France of the laws of exile, and embrace the whole of Prince Napoleon's political career. They have not yet come intokthe possession of M. Masson, but are certainly to be published.

div.head: DEATH OF ANOTHER BONAPARTE
div.p: DEATH OF ANOTHER BONAPARTE
A telegram from Ajaccio states that Princess Marianne Bonaparte. granddaughter of Prince Lucien, brother of Napoleon the First, died here yesterday of nephritis in her eighty-first year.
__.o._. THE BLACKBURN ABDUCTION CASE.
CONFLICTING DECISIONS A WRIT REFUSED.

The case in which a lady living at Clitberoe was forcibly carried off to Blackburn by her hushand on the Bth inst. was before 14r. Justice Cave and Mr. Justice Jeune in the Queen's Bench Division on Monday, on an application for a writ of habeas corpus directed against Mr. Jackson to bring up his wife before their lordships in order that she mighiybe set free. In support of the appli- cation affidavits were presented sworn by the two sisters of Mrs. Jackson, who asserted that the wife was kept a close prisoner by her husband, that she was in great dis- tress, and that she had.begged.to be allowed to return to Clitheroe. Their Lordships, after pointing out that the husband was entitled to the custody a his wife, and that the latter had been disobeying an order of the Court which had been granted to Mr. Jackson for the resti- tution of conjugal rights, dismissed the application. They "could not see a rag of cruelty "in the case.

A WRIT GRANTED BY THE COURT OF APPEAL. In the Court of Appeal, on Tuesday (consisting of the Lord Chancellor, the Master`of the Rolls, and Lord Jus- tice Fry). Mr. Finlay, Q.C.' applied for a writ of habeas corpus directing Mr.E. H. Jackson' of Blackburn, to bring up his wife, now compulsorily detained in a private house at Blackburn, with whom she had refused to live, although he had obtained an order for the re- stitution of conjugal. rights. The application had been made on Monday in the Divisional Court, and refused. The Lord Chancellor doubted whether there was an ap- peal in such a case. Mr. Finlay contended that there was. He would state the facts of the case, and the court could tnefi decide whether it had power. The learned counsel then submitted his case, after which the Lord Chancellor said the court would hear the question of jurisdiction argued on another day, but the order of the court now was that a writ of habeas corpus wasto go, to be returnable at that court on Thursday morning. The Lord Chancellor added that the writ would apply to all persons concerned in the detention of Mrs. Jackson. The decision in the appeal in the abduction case has greatly increased the excitement in Clitheroe. The rela- tives of Mrs. Jackson allege that they have a very strong case. On Tuesday night they had an opportunity ot com- municating with Mrs. Jackson ,and she expressed her de- light at the result of the appeal.
MR. AND MRS. JACKSON IN COURT. ' THE WIFE SET FREE.

There was a crowded attendance of the public and Bar at the Court of Appeal, on Thursday, to hear the argu- ments on the writ of habeas corpus directed against Mr. E. H. Jackson, of Blackburn, ordering him to bring up his wife. Mrs. Jackson was present, and occupied a seat in the well of the court. She did not seem 'discomposed by the proceedings. Lady Esher and Lady Halsbury occupied seats on the bench. Mr. Henn Collins opened the argument against the jurisdiction of the Court of Ap- pleal. The Lord Chancellor decided that there was right of appeal. Mr. Collins then argued against the writ of habeas corpus, and submitted that Mr. Jackson had the right to take possession of his wife with so much force as was necessary. The Lord Chancellor remarked there was insult as well as force in this case towards the lady. The Matter of the Rolls referred to the fact stated in the affidavit that the lawyer's young clerk seized the lady by the shoulders and pulled her into the carriage on her back, leaving her legs outside, and the Lord Chancellor added: Some gentlemen with more sense of decorum,put her legs in. I-am not at all sure that the insult offered to the lady in seizing her in such a way ought not to be taken into consideration. The affidavits show too, that, when she got to the house at Blackburn. she refused to eat,for fear of being drugged, and her bonnet was thrown into the fire. Mr. Finlay argued the lady's case,and their Lordships then invited Mrs. Jackson into their private room to question her.

JUDGMENT. The Court found that Mrs. Jackson had not been in- duced to refuse continuance in her husband's house, and should uot be compelled to remain there by force. The Lord Chancellor was very severe on some of the argu- ments adopted on behalf of the husband's case. The authorities cited were, he said, tainted with the absolute dominion of the husband over the wife. The Master of the Rolls said the propositions put forward meant that the wife was reduced to be an abject slave of her hus- band, and His Lordship referred in sarcastic terms to the arguments adduced with reference to the.. clitTerence between confinement and imprisonment. He laid it down than an English husband had no more right over the person of his wife than he had over the person of any other woman. A person in court was so carried sway by his feelings during the remarks of the Master of the Rolls and the Lord Chancellor that he audibly took exception to some of them, and at length was ejected by an usher. The seizure, continued Lord Esher, was under circumstances of extreme insult, and as between husband and wife it was brutal. Lord Justice Fry having concurred in some- what milder language, Mrs. Jackson was free to leave the court with her friends who had so successfully moved the High Court of Justice to interfere on her behalf. Ap- -1 Parently the idea was entertained that Mr. Jackson would not be quite willing to deliver up his wife, and Lord Halsbury intimated that any attempt on his part to recapture the lady would be treated as a gross con- tempt of court and would be treated accordingly, and Mrs. Jackson carefully guided by a posse of officials,was conveyed through the justices' private entrance,and sub- sequently left the Law Courts by a side entrance, accom- panied by her solicitor. ,Before the proceedings closed, Mr. Forbes Lankester asked for costs.—The Lord Chancellor did not think the court had power to give costs. Anyhow no costs wculd b 3 giVen•
