div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1891.

r The plaintiff depollid to the circumstances which occurred on January 20th.—The defendant told her to leave, and she would not. He took hold of her shoulder, and said if she wanted a technical assault she had It. He then put his hand again on her shoulder, and said. " If you are a lady you will leave." She then handed him a written protest, and left the schoolroom. A large crowd had followed the defendant into the room. _ _

Cross-examined: She anticipated that there would be • forcible ejectment, and had prepared her written protest. The witness's attention was called to entries in her log- book, where Mr:Proud had in October, 1889, signed as manager. She said she mentioned the matter to the vicar, who said he did not know what right he had to do it. Mr. Proud had also intialled the daily registers. She had heard Mr. Woollacott had brought four actions. When she was summoned to the meeting of the com- mittee she refused to go or show her agreement. She did so on the advice of the vicar. To reach her room the defendant and the others would have to come through another room,but she could not say whether they had to break open any doors. When she reached the school at eight o'clock in the morning thp door was unlocked to her by Mr. Woolla.cott. She supposed the National Union of Teachers, of which she was a member, would pay the costs of the action.—Mr. Gully: She rather hopes that your clients will. (Laughter.)—The plaintiff added that• she had been taking the advice of the Teachers' Union, and they took up the matter. She took away the school registers,and refused to give them up. She did so under advice, but on being sued in the County Court she gave them up. The Rev. GEORGE ALLTow, vicar of St. Barnabas', for the lastseven yew, said he was chairman of the school committee. Miss Parsons conducted herself satisfac- torily until the time she was ejected. At the meeting in May, 1889, Mr. Proud was nominated as treasurer, but the motion was not put to the meeting. Mr. Allton had not resigned at that date. He had objected to Mr. Pilk- •ington front the first, and had no notice of the meeting at which he was elected. Neither Mr. Proud' nor Mr. Pilkington had paid any subscription until November 1889.—Cross-examined: Witness was recognised as cor- respondent to the Education Department, and had acted up to the present examination. He did not know that Mr. Pilkington was now the acting correspondent. The department had withheld the grant for the past year. His son was 20 years of age when he was first appointed on the committee: His son did not pay any subscription until after the present dispute. Mr. Pierpoint did not pay any subscription. As to the October meeting he did ,not know that Mr. Parr left a notice at his house. As far as he knew the minutes in the book produced had not been altered.—At this point the court rose.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS DISPUTE.
div.p: THE ST. BARNABAS DISPUTE.
ACTIONS FOR ASSAULT AT LIVERPOOL
ASSIZES.

On Tuesday afternoon at the' Nisi Prius Court, at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Lawrance and a special jury, there was commenced the hear- ing of a case in which Miss Mary Eliza Parsons, of Winsford, lately head mistress of St. Barnabas' Schools,Warrington, sued John Tomlinson, solicitor, of Preston, for damages for an assault committed upon her, on the 20th of January last, whilst she was acting its head mistress of the school. An ac- tion was also brought by Mr. Woolacott, late head master of the schools, against Mr. Pilkington, for assault upon him on the same date. The assaults had been committed by the defendants in the exer- cise of a right claimed by them as managers of the school, to eject them from the premises, in accor- dance with a resolution of the Committee of Management. Mr. Gully, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. P. H. White (instructed by Messrs. Jenkins and Uns- worth, of Warrington), appeared for the prosecu- tion,:and Mr. Bigham, Q.C., and Mr. H. A. Macuab (instructed by Mr. Tomlison), for the defence in both cases. • Mr. Gully, in opening the case of Miss Parsons, said the action was brought substantially to test whether the defendant had a right to eject her from the school; and the question would turn on whether she and the master had ceased to hold their positions, and become trespassers on the premises. While she was mistress at the school a dispute arose between the members of the committee who managed the school, and certain members had taken upon them- selves to dismiss her. There was no suggestion of mis- conduct against her. St. Barnabas' Schools were estab- lished under the trust deed dated October 10th, 1885, and the management was entrusted to a committee of management, consisting of the minister for the time being, the two churchwardens, and two other persons who should be subscribers of not less than two guineas per annum. The first committee consisted of the Rev. G. Allton, Messrs. Smith and Parr, and A. G. Allton, the vicar's son. The plaintiff was appointed mistress in September, 1887, the agreement being that she was to receive the infant school fees and half the Government grant, three months' notice tq terminate the agreement to be given on either side. In February, 1889, Mr. Woollacott was appointed schoollnaster. In the same year there was a vacancy in the treasurership of the schools, by the retirement of Mr. Holmes, and on May 23rd a meeting was held when it was agreed that Mr. R. Proud should be treasurer. The minute on the matter contained the words, " A. G. Allton retired; no busi- ness." It seemed that Mr. Proud now claimed that he was not only elected treasurer, but a member of the committee, in the place of Mr. Allton; but it would be shown that Mr. Allton, jun., had not resigned. On June 1 following, another meeting was held, when it was re- solved that Mr. Proud be appointed manager as well as treasurer, " in place of A. G. Allton, on the receipt of his resignation." It would be shown that Mr. Proud had only been elected treasurer. On October 11th, there was a meeting of the school building committee, at which Messrs. Smith, Parr, Proud, and Pilkington were present. They resolved themselves into a management com- mittee without giving notice to the vicar or to Mr. Allton and they proceeded to elect Mr. Pilkington as a member of the committee. The vicar afterwards called the usual quarterly meeting, at which he objected to Mr. Proud taking any part in the business. The meeting was at a standstill, and nothing was done. No more meetings were called by the vicar, but on Nov. 26 Messrs. Smith and Parr called a meeting which was also attended by Messrs. Proud and Pilkington, and they resolved to remove the vicar from the office of correspondent or medium of communication between the Committee and the Education Erepartment. It was also proposed by Mr. Proud, seconded by Mr. Smith, and carried, that the plaintiff and the master pay into the bank at the entabf each week all the school fees, and hand to the treasurer a statement as to the income for the month and the expenditure for the same period. The Committee were not entitled to call upon the plain- tiff to hand over the school fees at the end of each week, and she refused to obey the resolution. On December 13 the same four gentlemen met again and passed a reso- lution that the master and mistress have one month's notice to terminate the existing arrangement. Now ac- cording to the agreement they ought to have had three months notice. Finally, OA January 18, 1890, a resolu- tion was passed that the salary due having been ten- dered, and the plaintiff and the master having refused to quit the school and give up the school property, Mr. Tomlinson, solicitor, be employed to take such legal pro- ceedings as were necessary to compel them to do so. On January 20, Messrs. Smith, Proud, and Pilkington, accompanied by Mr. Tomlinson,proceeded to the school, and the defendant placed his hand on her shoulder and asked her to leave. She told him she would not put him to the trouble of putting her out, and she left. A more vivacious scene occurred when Mr. Woollacott was turned out. Mr. Gully added that if the plaintiff had been a trespasser in the school at that time the Commit- tee of management would have had the right to turn her out, but individual managers would not have that right. A schoolmaster or mistress was not in the position of a, mere servant, and they could not be removed for miscon- duct *ithout the giving to them of proper notice calling their attention to the alleged misconduct, and giving them an opportunity of explaining. They could only be removed upon adequate evidence. He contended that Messrs. Proud an 4 Pilkington had no right to act, as they were not subscribers in the year of their. election.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The hearing was resumed on Wednesday morning, when Mr. Gully put in the trust deeds of the schools and closed the case for the plaintiff. Mr. Bingham for the defence maintained that Mr. Proud was properly appointed manager of the school. Prior to May 23rd, 1889/the vicar, who was at logger- heads with the committee, told Mr. Proud that he wished him to be made a member of the Management Committee. Mr. A. G. Allton, the vicar's son, was simply a schoolboy at the time and a nominee of the vicar ; and he never aV- tended any meeting except when his father whnted him to record his vote. On June Ist Mr. Proud's election was confirmed, and he had afterwards signed the school log- book and registers as treasurer and manager. There would, of course, be a contest as to what took place at the various meetings. The vicar's letter in answer to a proposition to elect Mr. Pilkington, stating "unless my son will resign there is no vacancy," showed conclusively that in the vicar's estimation Mr. Proud was a duly elected manager. When Mr. Pierpoint died in June, 1889, there was undoubtedly a vacancy, and the meeting of the 11th Oct. was held. Though summon,ed in the usual way, the vicar did not choose to come back from Blackpool to attend the meeting, nor did his son turn up. Subsequently the committee endeavoured to get some information about the teaching staff from the vicar, but without success. On the 20th November the vicar con- vened a meeting, brought his son with him, and pro- duced a minute-book, from which the defendant believed a leaf had been torn out, and an entry re-written to the effect that "Mr. Proud be appointed manager as well as treasurer in the place of Mr. A. G. Allton on receipt of his resignation." Upon this the vicar argued that his son had not resigned. and that Mr. Proud was not a member, though on the other side it was e.ontended, that the son had resigned and that Mr. Proud was duly elected. Afterwards the committee requested Miss Par- sons to pay the school fees into the bank,, not know- ing at • that time that she was entitled to retain them, as information had been refused. Miss Parsons, was A...)eatedly asked to furnish accohnts of the money received, but she declined to do so, or to attend before the committee. On the 18th December a month's notice of dismissal was given to the master and mistress, and on the 2nd January they were in- formed by letter that the committee intended to carry out that notice. When the managers and defendant went to the school they found the door locked ; some one had to get over the wall, and the door had to be broken open. As to the legality of the proceeding he contended that the committee or any body of gentlemen who em- ployed a teacher in this way under these circumstances could, at any moment, with or without cause, put an end to the employment, though probably an action for wrongful dismissal might lie. If the lady was actually refusing to recognise or obey the reasonable orders of the committee they had the right, not only to require her to go, but to require her to go without paying her at all. As to the question of paying subscriptions, he pointed out that MI% A. G. Allton never paid any until after this dispute arose, and Mr. Pierpoint had never paid any, while Mr. Proud and Mr. Pilkington did pay their sub- scriptions.

- WITNESS said they should have been. At the meeting in November, witness objected to young Mr. Allton's presence, as he had resigned, and the Vicar said he had not. Witness objected to the minute as read, and asked the Vicar to produce the original minute, and he said he had written it on a slip of paper. He fumbled about among his books, and then said he had lost it. By Mr. GULLY: Witness had never seen minutes sketched on a piece of paper to be copied into the book afterwards, but he had not been used to meetings. The minute read on the Ist June was not the minute that 'appeared in the book on May 23rd. The Vicar wrote it in the book then, not on a piece of paper. Witness was a party to the resolution of December 13th, that the schoolmaster and schoolmistress and assistant have one month's notice to terminate existing arrangements. He understood that by arrangements were meant those as to payments into the bank and nothing else. He never agreed to the discharge of Mr. Woolacott or Miss Parsons, until they refused to come to terms. He told Mr. Woola- cott that he never agreed to Mr. Brown being put in his place. The witness in further cross-examination created much laughter by saying that the motion for Mr. Brown's appointment was carried unanimously, (as stated in the book), because there was a majority. He did tell Mrs. Looker that he was no party to Woolacott's dismissal. What he said was true at the time. (Laughter.)
Mr GULLY: It has not become untrue since.

WITNESS proceeded: It was over a fortnight or three weeks before he had told her that, that he said to her he wanted to look at the dictipnary to find out what the meaning of " arrangements "-was. Mr. GULLY: You have cleared your mind on the sub- ject now, I suppose. What do you understand arrange- ments to mean now? WITNESS (hesitating) : It means to make fresh ar- rangements. (Great laughter.) We are not supposed to live by dead men.
The JUDGE : You are not what ? WITNESS: We are not supposed to live by dead men's rules. WITNESS proceeding: He did not tell Mrs. Looker he would not consent to Woolacott's dismissal.

By Mr. Biouem : lam Vicar's churchwarden. Mr. GULLY: They had to choose between him and Mr. Smith, you know. (Laughter.) WrrNEss, in answer to Mr. Bigharn, said he objected at some meetings, to Mr. Woolacott's dismissal. R. PRoup said he was one of the managers of Messrs. Crosfield's soap manufactory at Warrington. He had been a member of the Building Committee for St. Barnabas', almost from the first. He had been trea- surer of the building fund. He remembered the vicar asking him before the meeting of May 23rd, if he would be his churchwarden. Witness said he would not be churchwarden for anyone. R. P. SMITH, churchwarden, and one of the school managers, said at the meeting of the Management Com- mittee on May 23rd, 1889, he and Mr. Parr (his co-war- den), and the Vicar being the only persons present, witness proposed, and Mr. Parr seconded that Mr. Proud be elected one of the managers of the school, and treasurer, and the proposition was carried, the Vicar voting for it. Nothing was said about young Mr. Allton. On June Ist there wasamother meet- ing of the Committee at which the Vicar, himself, Mr. Pierpoint, Mr. Parr and Mr. Proud were present. The minute of the previous meeting appointing Mr. Proud manager was read. The Vicar opposed the minute on the ground that his son had not resigned. At this point the witness betrayed a decided inclination to go back to the May meeting, in spite of the Counsel's en- deavours to keep him to the June meeting. On his say- ing to the Judge: I want to explain it your lordship will allow me. • The Judge replied: I should like to get away from the meeting of May if we ever live so long as to get back to the June meeting. (Laughter.) Ile more Mr. Bigham asks you about the June meeting the more you go back to the meeting of May. Mr. Glitzy: He wants to go back to April. The JUDGE : (to the witness) : Do you want to go , lback to April. 'I am afraid it is April the first. (Laughter.) Try to answer Mr. Bigham. When he asks a question he has good reason for asking it. Examination resurried : Witness said the Vicar at the June meeting, read the minute of the pre- vious meeting in this way; that Mr. Proud had been elected as manager and treasurer upon receipt of the resignation of Mr. A. G. Allton. The words as to the resignation had been added by the Vicar, and witness objected to the minute as read,on the ground that Mr. A. G. Anton had resigned previously. Witness's recollec- tion was not that the minute read :—" Proposed by Mr. Smith, seconded by Mr. Parr that Mr. Proud be appointed treasurer, A. G. Allton retired. No business." On their objecting to the minute as read by the Vicar he drew his pen through the qualifying words. At the succeeding meeting in November the minyte was again read, and objection was taken to it by witness and Mr. Parr, who on the Vicar saying that his son had not resigned, and would not, replied that he had and his rrslgnation had been accepted. The Vicar was asked to read the minute he had put his pen partly through, and he then said ha had written the minute on a slip of paper, not in the book. Mr. Allton jun., was present, and said he would not resign. By Mr. GULLY: Witness saw the Vicar on the Ist of June draw his pen through words on a leaf the size of one in the minute book, and it appeared to be in the book. MIL PARR corroborated the previous witness, and stated that on June Ist, the Vicar said his son would give place to Mr. Proud. Mr. Pierpoint objected to the minute as read by the Vicar at the meeting on that date, and at Mr. Pierpoint's request, the Vicar drew his pen through the conditions about the receipt of his son's resignation. Mr. BINGHAM : These words are not scored out. • _

The Vicar, Mr. Smith, Mr. Parr, Mr. Pilkington' and to witness's surprise Mr. Allton, jun., attended. Witness objected to him as not a manager, remarking that he could not be one as he had not paid his subscription. The Vicar was asked to read the minute for June Ist. He did so and it read that witness had been appointed treasurer and manager " upon receipt of Mr. A. G. Allton's resignation." ' Mr. Parr objected to the condition as to Mr. Allton as not in the original minute,and asked the Vicar to show him the page of the book where it had been altered. The Vicar was confused, and on being pressed said he had written it out on a slip of paper and mislaid it. Mr. GULLY read a letter from Mr. Proud to Miss Parsons dated May 25th, 1889, in which ha informed her of his "having been proposed as treasurer ". Counsel asked witness why he used the expression " proposed "and did not mention his being appointed manager, having been elected both. WITNESS: I don't know that there is anything par- ticular in that. Mr. GULLY: You had not made up your mind even then whether you would be treasurer. WITNESS said it was perhaps on account of being new to the business. In further examination a letter was read by Mr. Gully fr3m witness to the vicar, stating that he had presented the copy of the minute appointing him treasurer to the bank, and pointing out a certain formal alteration waS desired by the bank to put it in order. The witness explained as to this that he accepted the description of him as treasurer, because the bank had tO do with him only as treasurer. Thewitness in answer to Mr. Gully, said he did not look at the minute book on the 23rd of May, because the vicar was always very careful that they should not do so. Pressed on this point witness said he did not say the vicar prevented them, but he always had the book in his possession, and they had a lot of nuisance over a building committee minute. Mr. GULLY: He was chairman of the meeting and had custody of the book. Mr. PILKINGTON gave generally corroborative testi- mony as to what occurred at the meeting in November. JOHN WALKER, bookbinder, was examined asan expert to deterntne the point of whether a page had been removed from the minute book, and on examination of it said a page had been taken out, but not the page immediately preceding that containing the minute of June Ist, alleged to have been altered. The counsel then had a consultation, and Mr. BIGHAM said he had arranged with Mr. Gully that the defendant should consent to a verdict against him for 40s. and costs, and that the same verdict should also be given in the action Woolacott v. Pilkington. It was to be understood that Mr. Proud arid Mr. Pilkington did not claim to act on this committee, unless, of course, they were properly elected in future. It was also his duty to say that, having heard the evidence of the last witness, the imputations, which undoubtedly were made upon the Rev. Mr. Allton, ought to be withdrawn and apologised for. On behalf of his client he might say that they thought there had been some tampering with the entries, but it was obvious they must have been mis- taken, and that what they saw was a draft minute pre- pared by the vicar before he entered it in the book. He (Mr. Bighatn) trusted there would be an end to the liti- gation that had taken place, and that if there were any claims by the plaintiff or Mr. Woollacott in respect of salary or anything else they would be settled without further litigation. Mr. GULLY said no doubt the result was that his client had a claim for wrongful dismissal, not a very large amount, but he might say that his client would not press it unreasonably, and would give eVery opportunity to make a reasonable payment. His LORDSHIP said the defendants were very fortunate in having fallen into the hands of Mr. Bighana, who had done everything that a gentleman should do.—The jury then returned a verdict for the plaintiff for 40s. and costs. —ln the case of Woolacott v. Pilkington, judgment for the plaintiff for 40s. and costs was agreed to.

SUICIDE IN A POLICE CELL AT ASHTON. A sensational discovery was made in a police cell at Ashton-in- Makerfield, near Newton-le-Willows, on Saturday evening. During the day a labourer named John Barker, residing at Stubs haw Cross,was arrested under a warrant on a charge ot unlawfully assaulting a married woman named Jane Byrne. On Saturday evening, at nine o'clock, he was found to have committed suicide by hanging himself with a muffler.

On Tuesday morning an inquest was held at the King's Arms Hotel, before Mr. Brighouse, county coroner. Police Constable Morson, testified to the arrest of the deceased en Saturday, upon the charge above referred to. —Sergeant Williams also deposed to receiving the pri- soner, and seeing him searched, after which on being put into the cell, he asked that he might be allowed his scarf, as he suffered much from quinsey. Having known the prisoner well for six years,lie could say that he had never seen him without a heavy scarf or shawl round his neck, because of the complaint.—Police Constable Dixon spoke to visiting him during the afternoon andevenini.r., and he last saw him plive at eight o'clock. On revisiting the cell about nine o'clock he saw the deceased in a reclin- ing position by the wall,and on exaMining him found him suspended by his scarf from the heating apparatus pipes. Dr. Hannah testified to being called to see the deceased soon after nine o'clock. He endeavoured to restore ani- mation, but failed.—A son of the deceased also gave evi- dence as to his father suffering from quinsev, and to his being Sometimes stramyein his manner,but aid not think he was inclined to insanity. It transpired that he had threatened to drown himself on Saturday morning before being arrested, but was prevented from doing so. After hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of " Suizide during a fit of temporary insanity."

IRELAND.

• LNTI-PARNELLITES AT NEWRY. Mr. Davitt and Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P. visited Newry, on Sunday, and had a Cordial reception M.P., an immense gathering of the people of the district, whd passed reso- lutions against Mr. Parnell and in support of the re- cently established National Federation. Mr. Davitt, in the course of a loner speech, denied that, as represented by, Mr. Parnell, the majority of the Irish party were seceders. Mr. Parnell was now taking an interest in the working-men of Ireland after neither saying nor d..ing anything for them during eight years. Mr. Healy also spoke. MR. PARNELL AT GALWAY. Mr. Parnell left Dublin on Saturday evening for Gal- way, where he addressed a meetink of his supporters on Sunday. At Athlone, where the hon. member staved on Saturday night,he was received by an enthusiastic crowd. In an address delivered from the window of his hotel he repeated his assertion that he had been faithful in his service to the cause of Ireland. No opposition was mani- fested at the Gal vc ay meeting on Sunday, at which Mr. Parnell gave utterance to many hard words respecting the action of English Liberals aud of the majority of the Irish Parliamentary party. Mr. Parnell, speaking at Cork, on Tuesday, defended the attitude he had maintained, and prophesied victory fdr his side in the struggle. He strongly denounced the interference of English politicians, and characterised as I dishonest and traitorous the conduct of some of the Irish I members.

MR. PARNELL'S CHALLENGE ACCEPTED. Mr. Maurice Healy, M.P., has declared himself ready to accept the challenge thr3wn down by Mr. Parnell on Tuesday, 1.. y resigning his seat in order to seek re-elec- tion for Cork, it Mr. Parnell does the same. In a letter to Mr. Parnell, Mr. Ilealy expresses the hope that Mr. Parnell will not repeat the tactics of Committee-room 15 and Boulogne, and seek by any new stratagem to avoid a promise voluntarily made. ANOTHER SHOOTING OUTRAGE. Armed men raided the house of a farmer named McKee, at Kilmorna, Clare, on Wednesday, and fired shots through the window, one narrowly missing the head of McKee's daughter. Another daughter ran shrieking from the house, and the ruffians fired after her, and also at a man named Hegarty, who was approaching the h Nise.

"THE Life of WILLIAM GREGSON, A Sturdy Temrerance Advocate," will be read Reformer. with interest by all classes of readers, but especially by the friends and suppor- ters of the temperance cause. It has been written by Mr. J. G. SHAW, of Blackburn, to whom Mr. GREGSON narrated the chief incidents in his career not long before his death; and it possesses there- fore something of the charm of autobiography, with the advantage of such comment and com- mendation as could not be made by a person who was writing of himself. Mr. SHAW has done his work well; he has had an admirable subject, and he has made good use of his material. The volume is one of about 300 pages; it is adorned with an excellent portrait of Mr. GREGSON, and it has been well printed by the publishers Messrs. J. G. and J. TouLaiiN, Blackburn. The story of the develop- ment and adventures of the sturdy reformer was well worth telling; it is as fascinating as a novel, with the added feeling that it is a true story, and that it preaches in every line that, as Busais has it—
The rank is but the guinea's stamp— The man's the gowd for a' that.

WILLIAM GREGSON was composed of the stuff of which heroes are made, for he was never known to shrink from toil, or sacrifice, or danger, when one or other was demanded in the cause of truth. He was born at Ribchester, of humble parents, and, when a young man, he worked in a cotton factory as a weaver. But before he was twenty he saw the need of advocating " total abstinence" in prefer- ence to "moderation," and his first speech was made in supporting this view. Working at Low Moor, near Clitheroe, he sometimes tramped a score of miles in the few hours in each week which he had at his disposal to advocate the temperance cause. The first post which he occupied as a paid missionary was at BlacKburn, and he accepted it although the Society could only offer him 15s. per week ! What this sacrifice meant may be in some degree realised when it is stated that the oppor- tunity was also given him of becoming an over- looker in a cotton mill at 358. per week. From Blackburn Mr, GREGSON went to Brigh- ton; and was afterwards stationed at Hull, York, and other places before he became one of the per- manent agents of the British Temperance League. During all these early years he was content to labour for a bare subsistence, for his heart was in his work, and his courage was unfailing. Ho had a genius for the sort of speech which goes straight ! home, as thousands in this district can testify; while his good-humour, and combativeness enabled him in a hundred struggles to come off victorious. And they were struggles in those days! It was a common thing forty years ago for the publicans to hire men to break up, temperance meetings; to distribute beer at outdoor gatherings; and not unfrequently re- sort to actual violence. But these: men met their match in WILLIAM GREGSON. Whenever a glass of beer was offered him—as was somet;mes done in derision—he made it a rule to accept, de- livering his lecture. as best he could, glass in hand. He always finished by pouring the stuff into the street,or roadway,and putting the glass in his pocket as a trophy of the contest. A man of his tempera- ment and pugnacity in fighting the battle of free speech sometimes ,got in the law courts, but he seems in almost every instance to have proved victor in the long run. The poet JOHN CRITCHLEY PRINCE was arillongst those who signed the pledge at his solicitation, and one result was that noble poem known as "The Angel of Temperance. Dr. TEMPLE, Bishop of London, took the pledge at a meeting which the temperance advocate addressed; and another convert was Mr. William BRADLAUGH, brother of the late Mr. C. DRADLAI7OII, M.P. Mr. GREGSON was known and esteemed in almost every town in England, for, until he resigned his post, in 1887, as an agent of the League, he was constantly . employed in travelling and speaking. He did not cease work then, although warned to do so, but was ever ready, until his death in December last, to address either temperance or political meetings in Bleckburn and the neighbourhood. It is a matter almost, of course, to say that Mr. GREGSON. was a Liberal, although he was brought up as a Churchman, his father being sexton at Ribches- ter Parish Church. A vigorous, earnest, active mind, such as his, is ever alive to weak points in the existing order of things; and as he saw defects he was eager in seeking to remedy them. For many years he occupied the position of Town Councillor of Blackburn: and when be died—" with harness on his back "—his opponents were as warm as his friends in tLstifying to his ability, integrity, and high character. He was never rich as the world counts riches; but few men were so rich in the consciousness of a good w°rk well done; and he had that in his later years which, as Shakespere tells us, should ien accompa ds. age—honotir, obedience, love and troops of frny old

Mr. Gladstone LORD RANDOLPH OHURCHILL at made a statement which was as Hastings. frank as it was true when he said of Mr. GLADSTONE that, with increasing age, there was increasing brightness, and the speech at Hastings, on Tuesday, confirms the statement. It is a masterly exposition of the present political situation—of the weakness of Toryism and of the strength of Liberalism; and it would be a service. to the nation if it were reprinted and sent broad- cast throughout the country. The admission that there is no objection to be taken to the conduct of foreign affairs lends force to criticism of misman- agement in other matters; fol. when Jingoism was the dominant feature of Tory foreign policy, the leader of the Liberal party was unceasing in denun- ciation of it. What, by-the-by, has become of the Jingo? Is he to be classed as extinct, like the , Fair Trgsder, the Dodo, and the Megatherium ? Reverting to matters up to date, the taxpayer will do well to ponder over Mr. GLADSTONE'S exposure ' of the stupidity of the Government in committing the country to a seven-years' plan of spending Ten Millions of money on ship-building at a time when, as Sir THOMAS FARRER remarks, "there is almost as much fashion in ships of war as in ladies' bonnets." The pressing need in this matter is to turn the Tories out as soon as possible, and get back, under a Liberal Government, to the sound rule of letting Parliament provide year by year for the defence of the nation. Another and not less weighty reason for a change is that the Tories, with their usual way of muddling finance, have, while professing to show a surplus of over three millions, been spending over four millions more on the army and navy than were provided for in the taxation of the year, the rest being a "concealed contraction of public debt." But it is concealed no longer; Mr. GLADSTONE has poured a flood of light upon this dark transaction, and Tory finance stands, as heretofore, condemned. Refer- ring to the Irish question, the Liberal leader treated Mr. PARNELL with more consideration than he deserves; but he did not fail to give a flat contradiction to the impudent statement that the deposed chief had, in the past, opposed the claims of labour candidates at the bidding of Liberal leaders. "If the Liberal leaders," Mr. GLADSTONE added, "have taken any part, and they have taken a part with regard to labour candidates, it has been the desire from the bottom of their hearts to Promote by the use of every legitimate means at their command an increase in the number of repre- sentatives of labour who now sit in the House of Commons." After the complete change of front on this question—a change obviously resorted to in sheer desperation —nobody in this country is likely to be misled by Mr. PARNELL. It is not alone the revelations of the Divorce Court,—it is the shameless betrayal of confidence for the basest of all purposes—that has caused the demoralised Chief to fall, "like Lucifer, never to hope again." tut Mr. PARNELL is not Ireland; and it is for Irishmen to let it be seen that the aspirations of a nation are not to be thwarted by the selfishness and guilt of a single individual. Let them be true to themselves, and England will be true to the cause of Home Rule. That is the moral of Mr. GLA.DSTONE'S speech; and it is a moral which finds a place in the heart of every man who is worthy of the name of Liberal.

The WHAT is known in Warrington as School Ds pute the St. Barnabas School dispute, . is like the moon, in that it has in"Y phases. A judge and jury were occupied during two days this week at the Liverpool Assizes, in determining whether an assault had been committed in the dismissal of the school- -master and schoolmistress. The real issue was, 'whether two of the school managers, who were party to the dismissal, had been duly elected and had authority to act. There seems to have been some misunderstanding about the minutes, and it was suggested that they had been tampered with by the Vicar, the Rev. G. ALLTON, to Salt his pur- pose. But this allegation could not be sustained, and was, therefore, withdrawn. The result was a verdict for the plaintiffs, by consent, for 408. and Costs. Whether other proceedings for wrongful dis- missal, &c., will follow, remains to be seen. It is to be hoped that,as suggested in court, pending issues Will be amicably settled. If, as would appear, Messrs. PROUD and PILKINGTON were not in law, 'entitled to act as managers, they could not, we Presume,be proceeded against for wrongful dismis- sal as managers. But both they .and Messrs. SMITH and PARR are deserving of every sympathy, seeing that they obviously acte4 in good faith and had no personal ends to serve. So far as tke plaintiffs are • eeneerned, they are fortunate in being backed by the National Union of Teachers. There can be no (3bjection to this; but why should not the defend- i .4nts be helped in fighting what they have regarded '4B a public battle? We should be glad to hear of ,a subscription being opened on their behalf. The \rlear, as it seems to us, is the least deserving of a :Word of sympathy, for if he had shown ordinary 'tact and good feeling there would have been less 'Qf that disaffection which has brought St. arnabas, both in church and school matters, so 'frequently before the public. The latest t extra- ordinary act is the closing of the day school, since the verdict was given. This is done on the authority of the Vicar, and his churchwarden, Qtid of his son—who is in Africa. But why should .tbe Children be made a party to the dispute? Why •should their education be neglected because the llev. GEORGE ALLTON cannot agree with his sch-,01- 1111anagers-? These are questions which the parents 'are asking,but there is not much likelihood of their 'getting a satisfactory reply.

According to the published returns, the total sum raised by the Salvation Army by Self Denial Week is £30,577 18s. 3d. This is something to boast of; it indicates an underlying reality of some kind—call it what you will.

There is Local Option as to licenses in Canada, Queensland, Newfoundland, &c. How is it that thr,. mother country is so much behind her offspring in this matter? Let temperance re- formers see to it that they question every candi- date on this subject; and that they do not vote for anyone who utters an uncertain sound.

There is one distinct sign of progress. On Wed- nesday, a Local Option Bill for Wales passed the second reading. There have been plenty of resolu- tions in favour of the local veto, but this is the first time a bill has successfully passed the ordeal of a second reading. The Home Secretary did his level best to strangle the measure; but he failed; the bill was carried by the narrow majority of six.

The Welsh people residing in Warrington have set themselves the task of providing a Welsh church, which is to cost £6OO. They will succeed, for they never fail when they set out to accomplish an object of this kind. They deserve every help because they are showing how they can help them- selves. There was a concert in aid of the scheme, on Monday evening, which was very successful.

Carlyle who was the subject of a lecture at War- rington Training College, on Tuesday, had a good many hard things to say about very many people; but here is a hard thing which Kinglake, the historian had to say about the Chelsea sage : " Carlyle talks like Jeremiah ; but so far from being a prophet he is a had Scotch joker," adding, "I believe he knows himself to be a windbag." And yet when we read Carlyle, we cannot but say—" A greater than Kinglake is here."

There has been an unreasoning run on the Savings Bank of Blackburn, in consequence of the County Court judge having ruled, in reference to a deposit (which somebody sought to attach)that he could do nothing, as the Bank was neither a partnership nor a company. Such a decision ought to have had the effect—if any at all—of assuring the depositors that their money was safer at the Savings Bank than anywhere else. But men are like cattle when they are panic-stricken; they do not reason—they rush wildly on.

Co-operation as applied to butter-making in Ire- land is succeeding. According to a statement made by one of the hon. secs. of the Irish Industrial League, there are at present 15 dairy factories in the Limerick district, and the improvement in quality and output of butter is such that " each cow is worth from : Os. to 40s. more to its owner than before." As there are about 100,000 cows in the neighbourhood, this means increased value to the tune of £150,000. Very good; "the resources of ivilisatiou are net yet exhausted,"

Great is the Yankee in fertility of resource. How to lessen the number of criminals, paupers, and the victims of hereditary disease is one of the problems of the age. Dr. Pomeroy, of Boston, has a way of his own. He would intercept the streams of crime and corruption which are now constantly pouring into society, by transporting the unfit ones to islands of the sea, each sex by itself, or by other and more safe means." This is a drastic remedy—too drastic for this generation. He had better out with it, and let us know what. are " the other and more sure means."

Mr. Parnell has been issuing a manifesto to Irishmen in America, as if he had not made it sufficiently manifest that h 5 is no longer to be trusted as a leader of Irishmen. He must think his countrymen are only one remove from the lun- atic asylum if he really believes they will swallow such rubbish as this :—" It becomes my task td restore this unity and reconstruct our movement, lopping off all unsound materials, taking effectual precautions against the admission in future into our army of any weak, treacherous, or self-seeking elements." After this, " Satan rebuking sin" isn't in it; he must pass the cake to Mr. Parnell.

The Rev. C. A. Berry, of Wolverhampton, is being offered £l,OOO a year to go to Brixton Independ- ent chapel. This is certainly a pretty loud "call." The " Star " says if he accepts, " he will be a great acquisition to the ranks of Radical ministers in London. Mr. Berry is a thoroughgoing progres- sist in everything, and a sturdy advocate of social and political reform. Mr. Berry has received many calls, but the Wolverhampton people don't like to let him go. He might have been Ward Beecher's successor. At present he may choose between the secretaryship of the Congregational Union, for which he has been nominated, and the pastorate of Brixton Chapel."

We give, in another column, extracts from the annual report,just issued, of the Medical Officer of Health for Warrington. It is, as usual, a pains- taking and suggestive document. It cannot be regarded as .satisfactory that the death-rate for the past year—which is 22.68 perl,ooo—is F 27 higher than the average of the past ten years. Until recently there has been a tendency to decrease in the death-rate, and we may be sure that " this effect defective comes by cause." Dr. Gornall repeats various suggestions which he has ' made, and in view of the increase in the death-rate his suggestions ought to receive the immediate and careful atteßtion of the Sanitary Committee and of the Paving and Sewerage Committee.

"The glorious uncertainty of the law "was sure- ly never better exemplified than in the application for a writ of" Habeas Corpus" arising out of the Blackburn abduction case, on Monday. The appli- cation was dismissed as something scarcely to be thought of, Mr. Justice Cave and Mr. Justice Jeune being emphatic in the expression of opini, that no case was made out for bringing Mrs. J a,ek- son into court. Next day the applicants go to the Appeal Court, and the decision is not only re- versed, but the writ is made to apply to "all con- cerned in detaining Mrs. Jackson. The complete- ness and suddenness ,of the reversal present the solemn old fogies of the law in a comical light. The old song still holds good— If 6,t first you don't succeed,

The "Daily Telegraph" takes Mr. Gladstone to task for "denouncing the tyranny of the Tory majority, which will not let the navy be starved; and then inveighing against Mr. Parnell and his siapporters for not instantly yielding to the majority in the Irish wing." As to this pointless point, he must be a very poor reasonm who cannot see that the" Telegraph" has floundered into a fall- acy of the most glaring kind. The difference—and it is.all the difference in the werld—botween the t'wo is that Mr. Gladstone does yield to the majority. He 'may denounce the conduct of the Tory majority in the House of Commons, but he doEsn't set up a Parliament of his own. Let Mr. Parnell content himself with denouncing the Irish majority, but at the same time yielding to it, and the cases will then be parallel, andireland will be at peace.

Caste is as real a thing in India as a simoom, or a famine. A Sessions judge and jury at Moor- shalabad have been occupied for 34 days it' dp- termining whether the son of a wealthy Jain had been defamed by the charge that be had bro'ken caste, along with two co-religionists, by taking European food along with Europeans. The young men were treated as outcasts on their return froii2. England ; and there can be no question as to the gravity of the charge—from the point of view of the Jain community, which is so antique that it counted itself" very superior" when the anceini, Briton painted his body and paddled his own canoe. The jury gave a verdict for the defendant, on the ground that the libel, assuming it to be a libel, was justified, that is to say, the charge of breaking caste was proved to be true in substance and in fact. After this, young Nahatta and his friends might as well come to England for good— and go the whole hog.

THE VALUE OP PROPERTY AT EAULESTOWN. .

At the New Market Inn, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Thomas Sutton, auctioneer, Warring- ton, offered for sale, before a large gathering of pro- perty owners and others, several lots of property. Lot 1 consisted of two shops, and a dwelling-house, Nos. 6, and 8, Bridge-st. Earlestown, in the occupa- tion of Mr. Jos. Burchall. Lot 2, dwelling-house and shop, Nos. 10, and 12, Bridge-st., Earlestcwn, in he occupation of Mr. Thos. Nevitt. Lot 3, dwelling- . house and shop, No. 14, Bridge-st., Earlestown, in tha occupation of Mr. Thomas Nevitt. The three lots were offered as a whole, the first bid being £1,200, rising to £1,330, at which price they were withdrawn. They were then offered septuately, lot I, bringing out a bid of £3OO. This being the only offer, it was withdrawn. There was no offer for the other two lots. Lot 4 comprised six cottages, situate at Collins Green, in the occupation of Messrs. McCawley, Mullhearn, Mills, and others. The highest bid was £3O each, at which price they were withdrawn. Another lot of four cottages situate in Legh-st., Nos. 74,76, 78, and 80. was offered, the first bid for these being £250, but the reserve being £4OO, the property was withdrawn. _ _ . CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WINWICK. The annual meeting of members of the IVinwick polling district (Newton Division Conservative Association) was held in the schoolroom, on Mon- day evening. Mr. Reginald Owen, sen., presided,, and was supported by the Ri.N. J. Carson, Messrs. J. Swinton, J. Kerfoot, W. Carson, Peter Longton, G. Brimelow, S. Thotnason, W. Holbrook (registration agent and secretary. Newton), and Thomas Fielding, of the National Union of Conservative Associations, London. There was a good attendance. A letter of apology for non-attendance was read from Mr. George Comber. On the motion of Mr. E. C. Cooper, Mr. George Comber was unanimously re-elected chairman of the polling district. Mr. Knowles moved that Mr. Reginald Owen, :wit. (Croft), be re- elected vice-chairman. The proposition was agreed to. The Chairman moved, and it was carried, that Mr. E. C. Cooper (Winwick) he re-elected district secretary and treasurer. Mr. J. Kerfoot moved that ' Messrs. Joseph Swinton (Arbury ) and Peter Long- ton (Winwick) be elected delegates to the Council. This was passed. Mr. R. Clark moved that the old Committee be re-elected, with power to add to their number. The motion was carried. The Rev. James Carson proposed, and Mr. S. Thomason seconded, "That this meeting expresses its unabated confid- ence in the Unionist Government, and begs to thank our member, Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., for his able representation of the Newton Division." Mr. Thomas Fielding, who supported the resolution, gave an address. EASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES.—J. a. W. DEATH OF AIR. HENRY LINAKER, OF

all times were void of narrowness and bigotry. By the people of Aston he will be remembered as the chief agent in getting that township freed from the unjust church- rate, an act which reflects the highest credit upon his character. Both in private and public life Mr. Linaker earned the respect and admiration of his fellow men ; and his demise, although he had attained the allotted span of man, will leave a void that can scarcely be filled. He had spent a life of ceaseless activity, and he died in harness, with all the honours of a long and useful life thick upon him.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

One of the most prominent public men in the Runcorn district has passed away in the person of Mr. Henry Linaker, of the firm of Messrs. Linaker and Sons, estate agents, Union-st., Frodsham. For some months past Mr. Linaker had been in declin- ing health, and had only been able to partly carry out his multifarious duties. A few weeks ago, whilst attending an arbitration case at Bridge- water 1-louse, Runcorn, he caught a cold, and This acting upon an enfeebled constitution, again pros- trated him, and he succumbed at six o'clock on Monday evening. He was in his 70th year. Mr. Linaker comes of an old Lancashire family and was born at Meals Hall, Clturchtown, near Southport. For some generations the Linakers have been agents for the Hesketh estate, Churchtown and young Linaker was articled as an estate agent. and surveyor in the Fleetwood Estate Office. Shortly after he had served his apprenticeship, in the year 1844, Mr. Linaker came into Cheshire, to undertake the appointment of agent to SirArthurAqon,G.C.B., of Aston Hall. He also for 47 , years, up to the time his death, held the agency of the Aston Grange estate. But his well known busi- ness capacity, and strict integrity gained him business outside the county of Chester, and he held agencies in the counties of Herefordshire. Lincoln- shire, Warwickshire, and Worcestershire. His services too were requisitioned by the agricultural community in transactions too numerous to be specified, and the office of Linaker and Sons had a most enviable reputation. On the nomination of Sir John Whittaker Ellis Bart., he was elected a fellow of the institute of Surveyors. As to Mr. Linaker's private life, it eKtends over a period of no less than forty years. From an early.period of his residence at Frodshanf.he was a member of the Board of Guardians, and his colleagues expressed their confidence in him by elevating to the post of vice-chairman, during the chair- manship of Lord Cross. The clerkship becoming vacant in 1863, Mr. Linaker resigned his seat on the Board and applied for the vacancy, to which he was appointed. As a matter of course,he also became the Clerk to the Rural Sanitary Authority on its formation in 1875 and to the Assessment Committee, and in this threefold capacity he had served the ratepayers faithfully and well for the past ' thirty years. His business capacity, sterling ability, and ' clear judgment enabled him to grapple with the most difficult problems, and his technical knowledge was of the greatest benefit to the Union in the valuation of the new and the re-valuation of old property of various kinds. His labours for the Union in connection with the construction of the Ship Canal must be fresh in the memory of our readers, and it is safe to assert that the ratepayers have obtained concessions and privileges from the Ship Canal Company, mainly through the knowledge and exertions of the deceased gentleman. On the form- ation of the Daresbury Highway Board, 28 years ago, he became clerk to that body, an appointment he also re- tained up to his death. In politics the deceased gentleman took no part. Though in religion he was a churchman, his views at

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The mortal remains of the deceased gentleman were interred in their last resting place in the burial ground attached to Aston Church, on Thursday afternoon. The funeral cortege which consisted of a number of Coaches and private carriages, left Frodsham at two o'clock, and was met, before reaching Aston, by gentlemen from all parts of the county. There were representatives of all the public bodies with whichthe deceased had been con- nected, farmers for many miles around, the tenantry of the Aston estate, and many friends and acquaintances. Heading the mournful procession was the hearse, ac- companied by the 'soarers, Messrs. G. Gleave, H.Smith, S. Dutton, S. Withinshaw, R. Gleave, James Smith, J. Spender, seitior, W. Spruce, Wardle, A. Priestner, Thomas Hewitt, ,R Wade, S. Horton, J. Priestner, W. Wilkinson, J. Withinshaw, M. Sumner, H. Rowbottom, T. T. Johnson, H. Wright, W. Garnett, Thos. Rigby, J. Weir, W. Lowe, J. Acton, S. Stormont, J. Lowe, James Mc Waters, W. Lowe, T. Ainsworth, J. Tomlinson, J. Potts, J. Ashton (Chairman of the Board of Guardians), W. Whitlow, W. IL Wass, W. Mellor, S. Taylor, J. Collin, IV. Billington, Lea, John Roberts, J. L. Jones, R. Tickle' G. Ward, W. Howard, Thomas Riley, W. R. De Prez, JamesFarrington, T. Andrews, A. Bate, A. Hutchinson, J. Dutton, Dr. Steele J.P., G. L. %Vigg J.P., and others. The coffin, which was made of oak grown on the Aston Estate, and fitted with handsome brass furniture, was carried into the chancel of the church at the request of Mr. Talbot, and the service for the burial of the dead was read by the Rev, H, B. Blogg, vicar of Overton, and the Rev. E. Marsden, vicar of Aston. The church was crowded to excess, and a large number, who wished to pay their last respects to the dead, were unable to gain admittance. The service at the grave side was performed by Mr. Blogg and Mr. Marsden, assisted by the Rev. W. Fielden, curate. The coffin was hidden beneath beauti- ful wreaths inscribed "The sorrowing widow and children." "In memoriam from Emma" Mr. A. H. Talbot, Mrs. Talbot, Mrs. Algernon Talbot.
