div.head: BRICKLA. YER KILLED AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A BRICKLA. YER KILLED AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening, George Weedall, foreman bricklayer, was killed whilst working in a sewer at Heath-road, Runcorn. Weedall was at the bot- tom of the sewer, and his labourer, a youth, James Wright, was about to lower a dozen bricks to him, when one slipped from the loop in which they were placed, and struck deceased on the back of the head. He died early on Thursday morning. He leaves a widow and a large family. The inquest was held yesterday, by Mr. J. E. Worslev.—Mary Jane Weedall,eldest daughter, identified the body, arid said her father was 38 years of age.—James Wright described how he had fitted the bricks in the loop of the rope. lie could not explain how it was a brick had fallen out. He thought he had put them in tight.—Mr. Fred Wilson, contractor, said the bricks were placed in a double sling. It was the uni- versal custom to lower bricks in this way.—The Coroner said it appeared to him to be a very dangerous mode,but the jury could not say there had been any negligence. He advised the jury to add a presentment to their ver- dict, recontmending the contractor to consider whether he could not find some other and safer means of lower- ing bricks to men engaged in such work.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
THE ELIJAH.

Runcorn Volunteer hall was crowded on Tuesday evening by an audience gathered to listen to the performance of Mendelssolin's " Elijah " by the members of the Runcorn Musical Society: There was a chorus of about 120 voices, a powerful or- chestra, and the following principals :—Madame Conway, Miss Emilie Lloyd, Miss Clara Taylor, Miss Janet Pierpoint, Mr. Henry Guy, Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, Mr. J. Morrison. and Mr. Frank Whitworth. The ora- torio abounds with good things, and it is gratifying to be able to record that the choir accomplished their work in a manner thatcalled forth unbounded praise; and the applause was loud and frequent. Small blemishes here and there may be overlooked in the general excellency of the•perforinance,which was a credit to the conductor, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, and to all concerned.. The orchestra was a most capable one, and added much to the enjoyment of the company by the skiiful manner in which the accompaniments were played. Madame Con- way, a soprano of good tone and power, was highly successful, and Miss Lloyd sang with much expression, her sweet contralto voice being heard to great advantage and she was encored for " 0 rest in the Lord." Miss Taylor and Miss Pierpoint took Dart in several concerted pieces with credit. A tenor with a good clear voice, Mr. Guy scarcely did justice to the music, being somewhat lacking in expression. Mr. Pierpoint's vocalisation was noticeable for dramatic power and breadth of expression, and he certainly never surpassed his efforts of• Tuesday night. He was several times 'enthusiastically encored. Mr. Morrison and Mr. Whitworth ably took part in the double quartette. Mr. F. Duncanson was the leader of the band and Mr. W. J. Thomas was the organist.
HORRIBLE DEATH OF A CHEMICAL LABOURER AT WIDNES.

A labourer named Thomas DeWyre, known to his fellow workmen as Thompson, met with an awful death at Messrs. Muspratt's Works, on Sunday afternoon. DeWyre had been employed at the works for about two months, the scene of this opera- tions being the magnesium shed. About four o'clock on the day named he borrowed a wheel-barrow from a fireman named Charles Fenny. and almost imme- diately afterwards the screams of a person in great pain were heard, and Fenny found that DeWyre had fell into the well of boiling water. Fenny was unable to pull the man out by his own unaided efforts and he called P.C. Thompson to his aid and together they pulled him out. He was then quite dead. The inquest on the body was held at the Norton Arms Hotel, Lugsdale-road,on Tuesday morn- ing by Mr.W. T. Husband,the deputy coroner. Mr. Rich- mond, H.M. inspector of factories was present, and the firm were represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles and Mr. Fledley the manager. Superintendent Noblett watched the proceedings for the police.—Sarah Ann Jones, of 37, Alforde-st., identified the body and said the deceased had lodged at her house for a month. He was 30 years of age.—Martin Malony, foreman at the works, said he knew the deemed as "Thompson." He worked in the magnesium shed. On Sunday afternoon at 4 p.m., witness was at the side of a well of boi'ing water used for boiling down muriate of potash. The water was five or six inches deep and was very hot. The de- ceased was in the well ; he was quite dead. The deceased must have fallen through a hole at the top. There was a lid to the hole, but when the liquor was boiling the lid was removed, in order to let the steam out. The deceased had no business there. He had seen the de- ceased alive at 11.30 a.m. ; he was then quite sober. The well was almost level with the ground. The deceased's place of work was 100 yards away. The volume of steam w.ts so very thick that it was impossible to see through it. The hole was 2ft. 6in. wide.—Charles Fenny 14, Gladstone-street, fireman, said he saw the deceased at 4 o'clock, and he was then sober so far as he s-tw. He asked witness to lend him a barrow and he did sa. Five minutes after deceased had wheeled the barrow away, Donoghue told him there was a man in the well, and he at once shut off the steam. He then seized de- ceased's hand and pulled Him up but the skin peeled off his hand and he fell back into the boiling water. He shouted for P.C. Thompson, who was near, and together they pulled the deceased up. He was quite dead. He

rbelieved the man had fallen in.—P.C. Thompson gave evidence of a confirmatory character, and said there was no fence round the well to prevent a person walking in. There was 3ft. 3in. of water in thewell at the time. In his opinion the deceased had walked through the steam and fallen into the well.—The jury, who had inspected the scene of the accident, returned a verdict of acciden- tal death, but added a presentiment to the effect that the well ought to be fenced off.
WIDNES COUNTY COURT.
A sitting of this court was held yesterday, but there were no cases of public interest disposed of.

ST. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE, RIINCOHN. A magic lantern entertainment was given on Tuesday evening, illustrative of the life of Christ and other sub- jects. Mr. W. Iloxworth was the exhibitor, and Mr. William Cooper explained the views.
WIDNES CYCLE CLUB.
Mr. James Kiddie lessee of the Widnes Alexandra Theatre, has promised to give a championship medal for competition by the memners. Four other medals will also be competed for during the season.
ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES FARMER.

While driving on his farm in North Wales, Mr. William Longton, farmer of Widnes, was thrown from his trap and sustained injuries, which happilyare not of a serious character. The horse took fright from some unknown cause.
Sr. PATRICK'S DAY AT RUNCORN.

In celebration of St. Patrick's Day, the members of the St. Edward's League of the Cross, held a concert in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Tuesday evening. Songs were given by Mr. Clegg, Mr. Newton, Miss Hague and Miss Comerford, and a magic lantern exhibition of views of Irelaad was given by Mr. T. Bowyer, the views being described b-y Mr. Moulton.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. The adjourned debate on "The Direct Veto Bill and the Electoral policy of the Alliance," was resumed at the weekly meeting, on Saturday evening. Mr. J. Jones opened the debate, which was conducted in animated fashioa, strong remarks being made with respect to the tied house system; and it was felt that if England were to become a sober nation, temperance reformora must tlke more vigorous action.

div.head: RUNCORN c.E.T.s
div.p: RUNCORN c.E.T.s

Under the auspices of the Runcorn branch of the C.E.T.S., a public meeting was held in the National School, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. J. E. Meredith. Mr. Clarke Aspinall delivered a speech, dealing with temperance topics, and he strongly urged the necessity for legislative action in regard to the drink traffic. An address was also delivered by Mr.W.Mundin, of the Ship Canal Mission. The usual votes of thanks were passed. EASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES.— J. 8: W. DUTTON'S, Sankey- st., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

His Honour Judge Ffoulkes hvld a sitting of this court on Tuesday. There were 72 original plaints, 2 adjourned plaints, and 7 judgment summonses.—John Dutton, farmer, Woodhouses, Frodsham, sued for £8 damage done to his grass by cattle belonging to the defendant. Mr. J. Burton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. E. W. Humphreys for the defendant. The defendant had paid £1 into court in settlemement of the claim, but after hearing evidence, his honour gave judgment for the full amount with costs.

div.head: HALTON TOWNSHIP MEETING.
div.p: HALTON TOWNSHIP MEETING.

The annual township meeting for Halton was held on Thursday evening in the church schoolroom, the vicar presiding. The following were nominat?.d for overseers: —Messrs. Thomas Wright, Hugh Rowe, Joseph Astbury, John Baguley, John Lea, and Joseph Pritchard. Mr. John Lea was elected waywarden, and Messrs. Joseph Astbury and Wm. Nixon, burleymen. Mr. James Looker was re-elected ft member of the Burial Board and Peter Rollinson was elected in the place of Mr. John Barrow. Messrs. S. Saunders and S. Blair were appointed to audit the accounts of the Board. Mr. John Baguley was nominated as guardian. _ . .
EASTER SHOW OF 'NOVELTIES.—J. .3; W. DUTTON'S Sankey- St., Warrington.—Advt.
REV. FRANK BALLARD'S VISIT TO RUNCORN.

Those who are interested in till advance of social Christianity will be pleased to hear that the Rev. Frank Ballard M.A. B.S.C. F.G.S., F.R.M.S., will visit Runcorn and deliver his lecture on " Modern amusements; their use and abuse" in the Bethesda Lecture Hall on Monday evening. Mr. Ballard is now well-known as the author of many works which have drawn forth controversy,and at the last Wesleyan Couference, though he was assailed for his opinions by many of the older Methodist preachers, yet he thoroughly assured all of his zeal and earnestness for the welfare of the souls and the bodies of his fellow men. He wrote" Brief Reply" to Mr. A. G. Brown's "The Devil's Mission of Amusement," and had since written a work in five parts entitled " What are the Churches for ?" the last part of which, entitled " Christ's Utopia," has just been published and has met with the approval of all broad-minded Christian people.
DEATH OF MR W. B. GIBSON, OF FRODSHAM.

Mr. William lia,nton Gibson, of Overton, Frodsham. died on Monday last, at the advanced age of 82 years. 60 years ago Mr. Gibson established a business as iron- monger in Bridge-st., and a few years later opened the Premises now occupied by Messrs. Handley and Beck. He also formed the business at Frodsham now carried on by Mr. J. W. Rothwell, one of his apprentices. In pro- cess of time Mr. Gibson took intopartnership Mr. James Handley, J.P., and an additional business was opened, and shortly- afterwards Mr. Gibson retired, since residing at Frodsham. He was a man of the strictest integrity, and of a most charitable disposition,and he will be much missed by the poor people of the neighbourh•lod. In re- ligion hewas a Presbyterian, and although he did not take an active part in politics he was an ardent Liberal. For some years he was a member of Runcorn Board of Commissioners,and he was a director of the Runcorn Gas Company up to the time of his death. His remains were yesterday interred at Overton Parish Church by the side of his wife who pre-deceased him by a few years. He leaves three daughters to mourn his Ws. EASTVR SHOW OF NOVELTIES.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey- et.. Warrington.--Advt. FUNERAL OF MR. JOSEPIT WILLIAVS OF RUNCORN._

The mortal remains of Mr. Joseph Williams,of Brindley Cottage, Irwell-lane, whose death was recorded last week, were interred at the Public Cemetery on Saturday after- nocn. Many blinds were lowered in token of the respect In which the deceased gentleman was held. Preced- 1 ing the hearse were Dr. Robinson, Messrs. James Dobson. S. Ra.venscroft, R. Norman, B. Kniveton, S. Pope, B. Orosby, and S. Coventry. In the first carriage were the Rev. H. Burson. Me..srq. J. Reynolds, W.. Kay, Faulkner, and Henry Faulker ; 2nd carriage, Messrs. S. Taylor, George Dutton. J. Lamb, Joseph Williams (nephew) 3rd carriage, Messrs. F. A. Lake, Arthur Rilev,W. Williamson, Arnold Unsworth, and the Rev. W. Ken-drew. The coffin, on which was inscribed "Joseph Williams, died March 11th, 1891, aged 75 years:" was borne to its last resting place by Messrs. J. W. Woodland John Lunt, T. Molyneaux, and S. Hignett. The burial service was read by the Revs.H. Burson and W. Kendrew. Floral tributes were sent by relatives and friends; and Miss Connie Williams, the deceased's only grandchild, placed a basket of beautiful flowers on the coffin. Mr. T. Caygill carried out the funeral arrangements BASSINETTER.—J .S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-at., Warr ington. —Add .
WIDNES WESLEY CIRCUIT.

The quarterly meeting of this circuit was held in Lacey-st. schools on Monday. The local preachers met about three O'clock, when Mr W. Chettoe took his fare- well of the brethen prior to his departure far London. Mr. T Dodd underwent a successful examination and W2S admitted to full plan.—The members of the meeting and friends were entertained to a substantial and well served tea by Mr. and Mrs.. J. Williamson, of Halebank. Therp were about one hundred prPsent. The business meetit* commenced at seven o'clock, the Rev. T. Law presiding. The senior stewart submitted the financial statement for tha quarter, showing .a small balance in hand. The numerical statement, submitted by the Chairman, recorded 627 members and 167 juvenile members. On the motion of the stewards the Rev. G. S. Meek was thanked for past services, and invited to remain a third year. The stewards reported that since the last meeting they had invited the Rev. W. M. Kidman, of Stockton- on-Tees, to succeed Mr. Law next September, and he had acccpted the invitation, and submitted their action to the meeting for its approval. The Rev. G. S. Meek reported about 2,300 children in the various Sunday schools of the circuit, 1,300 being members of the various Rands of Hope. The annual report of the " Magazine" Committee, which was read by the trea- surer, Mr. G. Davies, showed that the publication had paid its way.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present—Rev. Father Clarke, Major Waring, Messrs. R. 11. Davies, and S. Quinn.
INCREASE OF WAGES.
The General Purposes Committee submitted a recom- mendation that the salary of Caretaker Parsons be In- creased from 275. 6d. to 303. per week. Carried.
DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing February there were 168 applications for school fees which were recommended to be paid in 143 cases. Forty parents were summoned before the magistrates for con- travention of the Education Act ; 39 were fined and one boy was sent to an Industrial School. The committee recommended that on the completion of three years' ser- vice, the salary of the Attendance Officer, R. Grant, be increased according to the scale of the Board.—These minutes were adopted. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT: THE BOARD IN AN UNDIGNIFIED

POSITION. The School Management Committee recommended that the tender' of Messrs. Philip, Son, and Nephew, of Castle- at., Liverpool, for the supply of articles required by the, committee for the next twelve months be accepted. The Committee reported that they had let the West Bank Infants' and Girls' play ground to a Tennis Club, from six to nine o'clock each evening for the sum ,of 2s. 6d. per week, and fixed the re- numeration of the caretaker for attending to the same, at 4s. per week. They had also allowed the free use of a room at the Simms Cross Schools on Tuesday evemings, from half-past eight to nine o'clock, to Mr. Showan and Mr. Belford, for rehearsals for a proposed concert in aid of purchasing a musical instrument for the senior departments of Simms Cross Schools.—The Chair- man, referring to the last minute, said it was rather singular they could not have a musical instrument with- out having an entertainment.—The Clerk said the instru- ment was intended for the boys' and girls' department. They had not got an instrument with which to teach music, and the Inspector grumbled each time he came.— Father Clarke: To whom will the instrument belong ? The Clerk: If they get one it will be given to the School Board.—Major Waring: It is not quite dignified.—The Chairman: I don't think it is, Mr. Waring.—The Chair- man: Have the teachers made any application for a musical instrument ?—The Clerk replied that they. had, ' and it was decided that so many instruments should be ' bought, but these departments did not get one.—The Chairman said it was a most undignified thing to appeal to charity in this way.—Eventually the minute was re- ferred back to the Committee. The other recommenda- tions were pissed.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported receipts amounting to £177 us. 6d., and recommended for payment accounts amounting to £729 9s. 3d.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C.
BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. "I

That there will not be a contest at the forthcom- ing Local Board election at Widnes, the rival rate- payers' association having agreed to the re-election of the retiring members. That the Government inquiry into the applica- tion for a charter of incorporation takes place on Wednesday next, and there can only be one result as the application is unopposed. That there is a rumour on foot that the United Alkali Company intend to close several of their works at Widnes, and it is a fact that the works of Messrs. Hay, Gordon and Co., are now at a stand- still. That the election of Guardians at Runcorn pro- mises to be of more than usual interest. The retiring members, with the exception of Mr. Grice. who unfortunately is suffering from ill- health,will without doubt be nominated and Mr. D. IL Jones will again seek to represent the rate- puyers. That the temperance party of the town have also decided to run a candidate, and their choice has fallen upon Mr. Thomas Lee, grocer and baker. That the news of the death of Mr. 11. Linaker of Frodsham, was received with regret throughout the entire County of Cheshire. That he was a man of the strictest integrity, and of great intellectual vigour, and in the multifarious offices which he filled the duties were always car- ried out in a manner that left room for no improve- ment; and his death leaves a void that cannot easily be filled.

PENKETII. LECTURE ON "SELF-KNOWLEDGE." On Wednesday evening, in connection with the Mutual Improvement Association, a lecture on " Self Knowledge," was given by the Rev. T. Roes. There was a good attendance, and the meeting was presided over by Mr. J. Watson. The lecturer com- menced by giving a definition of the word know- ledge, and then proceeded to describe the many different things we ought to know in connection with ourselves. The lecture VT as most interesting, and at its conclusion a discussion followed, in which the Chairman and Messrs. Jones, Budden, Snoddv, Peers, and White took part. The meeting con- cluded after unanimously according a vote of thanks , to Mr. Ross. TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT.

Last evening week a tea party of the employes of the PenkethTanning Company Limited, followed by an entertainment, was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. The tea was generously provided by the directors of the Tanning Company. The tea, which was prepared by the wives of the workmen, was on the tables at 6 o'clock. About 250 persons sat down to it, and justice was done to all the good things provided. After tea an entertainment, con- tributed by the workmen, was given. The chair was worthily occupied by Mr. C. E. Parker, and he was supported on the platform by Messrs. J. Dodds, W. J. Wigfield, and R. H. Posnett. The programme was of a most interesting and varied character. The meeting was opened by a pianoforte solo by Miss Coates, followed by a clarionet solo" For-get-. me-not," by Mr. H. J . Jones. Songs were given by Messrs. A. Appleton, L. Smith, F. Goulden, J. F. Budden, T. Eames, H. S. Jones, H. Hampson. and J. Townley. A very interesting reading was also given by Mr. J. Dodds. The second part of the programme consisted of a magic lan- tern exhibition by Mr. R. Garnett. The lantern slides had been produced from negatives taken by Mr. Garnett last summer in die Western Islands of Scotland. An address was given by the Chairman, (Mr. C. E. Parker) in which reference was made to the recreative scheme which the Tanning Company have in hand for the benefit. of their workmen, full details of which, have already appeared in our i columns. The baths, &c., are n'c.ourse of construc- tion. A short address was also given by Mr. Dodds. The evening was most pleasantly spent through- out.
THE ALLEGED FRAUDULENT BANK-
RUPTCY AT ST. H.E.LENS.

On Tuesday, at the Liverpool Winter Assizes, before Mr. Justice Day, John Edmundson the younger was indicted for having committed various offences under the debtots' act, 1869, at St. Helens, and also with having committed perjury. Mr. M'Keand and Mr. Parry were for the prosecution, and Mr. Segar and Mr. Horridge defended. Mr. ArKeand, in opening the case, said the charges against the prisoner,were that on a certain date previous to Sep- tember 30th, when he was adjudged bankrupt, he did not fully and truly discover to James William Lamb, the trustee appointed under his bankruptcy, all his property —that was to say, his boots,shoes,and fixtures—how and to whom he disposed of that property, and on what consideration, and when he disposed of certain boots and shoes ; that he did not deliverer up to his trustee the same boots and shoes; that within four months of his becom- ing a bankrupt he fraudulently removed a certain por- tion of the boots and shoes; and, with intent to defraud his creditors, disposed of :ertain boots and shoes other- wise than in the ordinary way of his trade. After a lengthy hearing the prisoner was found guilty, sentence being deferred.

div.head: SENTENCE.
div.p: THE SENTENCE.
On Thursday morning Edmundson was brought up to receive sentence. Mr. Justice Day said the case was a very bad one indeed, and he sentenced the prisoner to twelve calendar months' imprisonment.

A London morning contemporary says it is confidently expected that Lord Hartington will accept the chairman- ship of the Royal Commission on Labour. Captain Norton, of the Middlesex regiment. has been found dead in his bathroom with a pistol shot in his head, under circumstances pointing to suicide. The Queen, who was accompanied by the Empress Frederick and other members of thc Royal Family. on Wednesday, unveiled, at Eton College, a statue of her Majesty, which has been erected over the new schools'.
THE GLISSMAKERS' STRIKE AT
WARRINGTON.

The strike of employes of Messrs. Robinson,. Skinner, and Co., still continues, and there does not appear to be any signs of an immediate settlement of the dispute. Should the strike continue much longer it will probably result in a number of the firms' other workpeople being thrown out of employment. We are informed also that a number of men employed by Messrs. Bolton, glassmakers, Orford-lane, have sent in a demand for higher wages.

We have been supplied with the following state- ment which gives the masters' side of the case:— The dispute arose from the menobjecting to make common custard glass at the number according to catalogue, namely, 70 per move.' The men claimed it as a light custard, which 60 per 'move.' The em- ployers wished the matter to be referred to experts, but the men refused, although they knew the same i custards are reckoned at 75 at neighbouring works. IThe dispute would have remained in abeyance but the men passed a resolution that no custards of any kind should be made until they had succeeded in reducing the number. After waiting several weeks, it was thought better to test the matter fairly by ordering custard dishes to be made. The tesult was that all the men instantly left work, and to make matters worse, the Glassmakers Society demand that—though the men left without notice, and did not come to work the following week, though all was prepared for their doing so at very considerable cost—full wages should be paid for all the time they have absented themselves, amounting to something like £lOO. This is such an arbitrary proceeding, that no manufacturer would submit to it.,,
THE LATE MR. R. CItOZIER, ARTIST.

We take the following from " Manchester Faces and Places" :—This eminent former resident of Warrington, and Manchester painter, passed away on the 7th ult. in his 76th year, at his resi- dence, Sydney-st., Chorlton-on-Medlock. He was an ex-president of the Manchester Academy of Art, of which he was one of the founders, a prominent con- tributor to its most successful exhibitions, and throughout his successful artistic career, one of its most earnest and consistent promoters. Mr. Crozier was born at Blackburn, and was the son of Mr. Geo. Crozier, one of the leaders of a remarkable band of Lancashire working-men botanists. Even whilst a boy Robert evinced a passion for art, and in his early occupation as a coach painter, he met with the late Mr. William Bradley, the artist, who was a friend of the family. The success of the Peel Park Exhibition was the origin of the Manchester Academy of Art. Ten artists were elected to fund it, Mr. Crozier being one of their number. In 1861 he was elected liter- ary secretary of the society, treasurer in 1868, and president in 1878. His services, which extended over a long series of years, were given without fee or reward. It was only a mall before his death that he resigned that position, having held office for twelve years. Ile was a constant contributor to the exhibitions of the Academy since its foundation, and the results of his work were frequently seen in the displays connected with the Royal Exhibition before it was merged in the Art Gallery Com- mittee.

Of Crozier's apprentice days at Warrington, where the family then lived, Mr. Letherbrow contributes some interesting particulars. which strikingly pic- ture the stern period of probation through which Crozier passed, and the characters among whom he lived. The sth of May, 1828, was an era in the life of young Crozier, for on that day, at the age of twelve and a half years, he went as an apprentice to William Maskery, in ‘Vinwick-street, to learn the art and mystery of coach-painting. Chief among the curious characters with whom,as has been. said, Warrington abounded in days before railways, one of the most original and striking was young Crozier's master, Maskery. A tremendous Tory and thorough-going Church and King man, he was, for three successive years,,warden of the Parish Church. A. strong pillar and buttress of the Establishment, a scorner of Dissent (especially of the followers of Priestley), an upholder of rigid orthodoxy, he in- sisted, at confirmation time, on all his apprentices being properly grounded in the vital principle of religion, and confirmed by the Bishop of the diocese. At the same time he was a man who gave the reins to ungovernable rage, and who elevated blasphemy to the rank of a fine art. "In the Warrington workshops our apprentice gained a great deal of knowledge, both practical and theoretical, which was of the utmost service to 'him in after life. It enabled him amongst other things to see the technical method which had been employed in the painting of a picture, and, there- fore, the only way in which it could be cleaned and restored without injury. Three things are needed in picture restoration, namely, intuition, practical skill, and veneration, all of which he possessed in a high degree. He had become skilled, too, in. the mechanical arts connected with painting and drawing, and in the deft wielding of hammer and nails and all the tools of trade. He had learned to be neat, natty, expediti- ous, and, above all, orderly. But one of the most valuable results of such a training is that work be- comes an instinct, and unremitting labour the habit of life. On October 17th, 1836, the term of the indentures of seven years (plus one year and five months) came to an end. The sum of five shillings was expended in treating shopmates, in accordance with the time-honoured custom of loos- ing,' and, with another five in his pocket, the future President went down to the great deep (the river Mersey), took ship (th- Old Quay packet), and, with his possessions in one hand and his fare- -eighteen-pence—in the other voyaged to the great town of Manchester, whither his parents had preceded him.
MUSICAL TABLEAUX AT WYCr,IFFE HILL, WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening a zieries of musical tableaux were given in the Wycliffe Hall, by members of the Wycliffe Young People's Society, in the presence of a large and appreciative audience. The Rev. J. Yonge presided, and prefaced the entertainment with a somewhat lengthy speech, in the course of which lie explained that the songs by which the tableanx would be accompanied were selected from Baring Gould's "Songs of the West," and carried the mind back to very ancient times. Mr. Baring Gould had experienced great difficulty in getting these songs together, in consequence of neither the words nor the music of them having been printed, and of their having merely been handed down orally from father to son, some of them dating as far back as the time of Henry the 7th. Mr. Gould had, in collecting the songs, travelled through Devonshire and Cornwall, and had interviewed a great many of the oldest inhabitants there, and in one case penetrated into Dartmoor prison to get a -song from a man 89 years of age. The reason, the Chairman pointed out, in many cases, of the slngs not having been published was that they had been put down by Parliament. He claimed for Mr. Corney the credit of getting up the entertainment, and remarked that he had devoted much time to that end. Tho tableaux were as follows :—lntroduction: The Queen's Command. 1, Plymouth Hoe, The Sailor's Farewell. 2. The Peasant's Home. The Absent Sailor. 3. The Peasant's Home. The Sailor's Return. The singers were Messrs. E. Booth, G. H. Yonge, J. Knowles, W. Brown, W. Farrar, S. Jeffery, J. Podmore, W. 1 !Avis, A. Griffiths, and S. W. Jeffery, Mrs. S. W. Jeffery, Miss Hulme, Miss B. Rathbone, Miss Payton, Miss M. Payton and Miss M. Ball, Mr. W. H. Payton being the accompanist. The scenic effects were of a very plain description, as became the incidents pertaining to homely life of an ancient period. The songs were charmingly quaint in character, and notably may be mentioned "The thatched cottage," sung by Mr. J. Knowles who,with his long pipe and comfortable appearance. realistically typi- fied an old farmer of the more arcadian times represented. His song was heartily encored, as also was that of" The farmer's son," by Mr. W. Farrar ; "Parson Hogg," by Mr."Podmore ; " Thomasine Ennys," by Mr. G. H. Yonge; "The Miller and the Maid," by Miss B. Rathbone ; and " Widdicombe Fair," by Mr. A. Griffiths; "Upon a Sunday morning," was very prettily sung by Miss M. Ball, and deeerved an encore, though she did not obtain one. The character of" The old singing man," by Mr. S. W. Jeffery, was well sustained by that gentleman, who looked a truly venerable old" gaffer," his appear- ance suggesting an antiquity almost as remote as that of the old-world ditty he sang. The proceedings were con- cluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

The nomination Of candidates for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of Aston Manor, caused by the death of Mr. G. Kynoch, Conservative,took place on Tuesday, when Captain Grice Hutchinson,Conservative and Mr. Phipson Beale, Q.C., sladstonian Liberal, were nominated.

div.head: NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.

At the annual meeting of the Council of the National Liberal Federation, at Liverpool, on Wednesday, Mr. Schnadhorst referred to the temperance question, and said the time was approaching when it would be the duty of the Liberal party to degislate upon it. He re- garded the prospects of the Liberal party with the great- est confidence and hope. At the meeting of the Commit- tee in the afternoon resolutions were adopted in favour of Welsh disestablishment, one man one vote, registra- tion reform, and the fair representation on the Labour Commission of the industrial classes. Correspondence which had passed between Mr. Schnadhorst and Mr. Tims on labour representation was read. The latter asked whether the Federation would urge the voluntary with- drawal of fifty candidates in London and the country, so that the same number of seats might be contested by direct representatives of Trade Unions. Mr. Schnad- horst replied that the Federation was always anxious to accept labour candidates, but such an attempt as that suggested to interfere with the rights of constituencies would cause a storm of indignation, and make the suc- cess of any labour candidate an absolute impossibi- lity.
It is understood that Lord flartington has definitely accepted the chairmanship of the Royal Commission of Labeur.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday, James Wood, a youth, who described himself as a pain- ter's labourer, of Manchester, was charged with riding from Manchester to Warrington on the Cheshire Lines Railway, the previous night, by the train leaving Man- chester at 11 o'clock, without a ticket. The prisoner pleaded guilty, but stated that he was drunk and did not know what he was doing or where he was going. The ease having been proved by two railway officials, he 'vas ordered to pay 10s. and costs or go to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: ASSAULTS ON WIVES
div.p: ASSAULTS ON WIVES

At the Warrington Police Court. on Wednesday, John Edwards, a labourer, was charged with having assaulted his wife on the 16th inst. He pleaded guilty, and it was said that he had made twenty previous appearances at court. The defendant alleged that his wife bad been guilty of some very provoking habits towards him. The bench decided to impose a fine of ss. and costs, and ordered defendant to pay 55. a week towards the main- tenance of his wife and family.—A young man, named Matthew Hunt, was charged with. having been drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-st., and with assaulting his wife. He pleaded guilty. Councillor Dixon deposed to seeing the defendant give his wife two or three heavy blows in the street. Mrs. Hunt did not press the case, and said that it was her own blame because she wanted htr husband to go home. Defendant was fined ss. and costs, and was bound over to keep the peace for six :months.

CHARGE OF BEING ON ENCLOSED PREMISES FOR BAD PuRPOSES. At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, James Bamford, aged 15, was charged with being on enclosed premises behind Sir A. B. Walker's public-house in Golden Grove-st., for an unlawful purpose. The lad had been found in a recess in the wall, and refused to give any account of himself, but when brought to the police station said he had been from home for several days. He had given the name of Taylor to the police sergeant and said he lived in Norman-st., and that he had nothing to eat at home. The prisoner and another boy had on a preyious night been sleeping in the recess where he was -found, and Alderman Harrison suggested that his only ,object in being there again might be to sleep there : but it was proved that to get to the place he would have to scale a wall seven feet high. The lad's mother was in court, and said he had a good home to go to. The case was adjourned till Wednesday.
STEALING AN OVERCOAT AND BOOTS.

Arthur and Elizabeth Longshaw, the former a green- grocer's assistant, were brought up on remand, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday, charged with stealing from the stall of Joseph Frisby, Market Place, on the 7th inst, two pairs of boots, value 175., also with stealing an overcoat, from a stall in the same place, belonging to John Morton, tailor and clothier, of Man- chester, for whose appearance the case had stood over from the previous day. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan had found the prisoners in bed drunk, at the lodging- house, in Hill-st., in which they lived, the female having her clothes on, and in their possession the boots and a pawn ticket for the coat. He subsequently discovered that she had got a 'woman named Harriet Dainteth to pledge the boots for her for 3s. ed., and also that they had had possession of the coat to which the pawn ticket related, and that the female prisoner had pawned it. The Sergeant's evidence was corroborated, and Mr. Mor- ton identified the coat. The prisoners were sent to jail for a month's hard labour each.

SHAMEFUL CRUELTY To A MARE. George Connolly, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a mare on the 12th inst., and Samuel Sutcliffe, was charged with aiding and abetting the offence. P.C. Wheatley deposed to seeing Connolly with a horse and cart in Sankey-st., oh the day in question. The horse fell down, and he assisted in getting it up, and examined it. It had an old wound and a new wound on the left shoulder,one of its hind legs was swollen,and the animal was bleeding at the side and the mouth. Inspector Bowen corroborated. He said the mare was plastered all over with fuller's earth, and the blood was coming through this from its -wounds. He never saw a horse in a worse state in his life. Inspector Wilson, agent for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said on the 14th inst. he examined the mare in its 'stable, and found it in a starving condi- tion. There was hardly a bit of flesh on its legs, and the mare fell in the stable through weakness. There was a large wound on its back nearly four inches long, and there were wounds on its sides, hip bones, and shoulders. Be never saw a horse in a worse state in Warrington.— Inspector Bowen stated that Sutcliffe was the real owner of the horse.—Connolly said be had advised Sutcliffe to make away with the mare on account of its condition, and to take it to Mr. Toole's, but he said he could get more elsewhere. Sutcliffe said he did go to see Mr. Toole, but he was not in.—The defendants were fined 255. and costs each; in default a month's hard labour.

The players presented an amusing sight after the first few minutes' play, and occasionally the game resorted to a burlesque of the Rugby code, much to the amusement of the Onlookers. Holmes at the last moment took the place of Jolley on the Warrington side, whilst the Rangers had their best team up.

Jackson started, Evans meeting the kick off with a reply which settled the oval at half-way. Apparently it seemed to be the wish of the players to disfigure them- selves at the earliest opportunity, and a series of scrim- mages at centre afforded the pack a capital chance of so distinguishing themselves. Much amusement was caused when Drury essayed to get clear, but he was literally rolleci in the mud. The home forwards worked the ball by degrees to the Warrington end, until a drop at goal by Chapman was met by Webster, a tall kick by the latter placing the game at the half-way. A further set of scrimmages added to the grotesque picture, and eventually a really smart dribble, considering the cir- cumstances, for the players seemed incapable of main- taining a footing, by Frank Turner, Holmes, and H. Ashton menaced the home defence, and this being aug- mented by Fair Turner, J. T. Bate, and Bandies, the play was on the Rangers' line. Ashton (Broughton) ran the oval out and punted to Boscow, who fielded the oval well, and still Warrrington were aggressive. Deakin dropped well ,but again the Warrington forwards asserted their superiority, and despite an effort by Jackson nnd Longworth, Turner and Berry made a rush through the opposing defence only to find Chapman passing to H. R. Ashton, who at once made off at top speed. The Ranger was, however, pressed, and a faulty pass was intercepted by Daniels, who looked a certain scorer, but preferring to pass, Donohue took up the movement and he finally threw to Webster, but the last essay was at fault; and of course the chance was lost. The Rangers' forwards again worked the oval out of danger, and another fine rush headed by Dillon and H. Ashton, again called upon Deakin, who got his charge away in clever style. War- rington had a spell of defending, and Jaclon almost scored, the i.sult of a fine dribble. However, the attack was but a mere flash-in-the-pan, for Webster, James Bate and Daniels kicking effectively, the oval was once more at the Ranger's quarters. A series of fine passes between James Bate, Evans and Daniels relieved the monotonous forward play, and-the latter waseventually knocked into touch a yard from the line. A similar movement was tried a moment later, with no better fate and Broughton again relieved. James Bate ran finely round the opposing halves, but 'the heavy state of the ground, coupled with the greasy state of the oval, spoiled a certain score. The home forwards revelled once more in the mud, and took play beyond the half way, but Evans. Webster, and the two Bates by individual es- says harassed the home defence, the Warrington centre making a bold bid, being pulled up on the verge of scor- ing. Play was again at the quarter flag, and the first half-hour ended with not a single point scored. After the usual breathing time, Frank Turnerrestarted, and the same monotonous play was witnessed. Interest in the game was at a low ebb, and only the occasional efforts of the visiting backs gave life to the proceedings. James Bate and Frank Turner got the oval away from the centre, but the homesters resorting to forward tactics, which undoubtedly paid on such a miserable ground took Play near the Warrington 25. Ashton (Broughton) essayed to drop a goal, but the two Bates, Webster, and Evans, showing combination in their play, soon had the oval back at the Rangers' end, where Bandies led a move- ment, play being ultimately taken to the line. Some sharp practice betwen the two Bates ended in J. T. Bate crossing the line, but the point failed to gain the assent of the official who has sanction of such matters, and a five yards scrimmage being formed the Rangers resorted to their old method of relieving, and a forward rush again saw play at neutral ground. Frank Turner and Berry got clear from a line out, and dribbling on to Deakin, play was under the home posts. The two Bates, Evans, and Daniels passed freely, the latter being held on one occasion on the line. Webster had now a tine chance from a pass by Evans, but he preferred to drop, the kick being charged. Berry, however, grounded, but still the point was not allowed. Play was of a give-and-take nature now, and some idea may be formed of the condi- tion of the players from the fact that when the contest was being waged on the popular side enquiries had to be made at the close as to special individual efforts, the players in question being unrecognizable. Each goal was threatened, and the game terminated in a draw, the score being : Warrington, 0-0-1; Broughton Rangers, nil. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back ;J. W. Evans, H. Webster, and W. Daniels, three-quarter backs ; James Bate, and J. T. Bate, half backs ; Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, H. Ashton, W. Berry, T. Donohue, W. Povey, W. Bandies, E. Dillon. and J. Holmes, forwards, Broughton Rangers: G. Deakin, back; F. R. Ashton, H. Chapman, and S. Medley, three-quarter backs; T. Wall and J. Drury, half-backs; J. Jackson, S. Osman, W. Storer, W. H. Longworth, A. R. Wheeler. F. Isherwood, 3. Fitton, A. Storer, and A. Chapman, forwards. Referee, Mr. la. Williamson.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bevrsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
WAURINGTON RANGERS v. WIDNES ATHLETIC.—These teams met on the ground of the former on SaturrlaY. Nothing was scored beyond minors, and the game ended in a draw—two minors each.

WARRINGTON STAR V. SILVERWELL RANGERS (WIGAN). —The above match was played on the Star ground, on Saturday. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors,seve- ral of the Star team gave them up, and returned home, and consequently six 2nd team men were played. Final score—Warrington Star, 3 tries, 6 minors ; Silverwell Rangers, 2 tries, 4 minors.

WIDNES V. TOTTINGTON.—Widnes journeyed to Tot- tington on Saturdaay afternoon, but no match took place owing to two matches having been arranged for the afternoon, viz., with Walkden "A " team at 2.30, and with Widnes at 4.30. The Walkden team did not arrive until after four o'clock, and the competition being for the South Lancashire Cup, the Tottins,,ton Committee decided to play the Walkden fixture. This resulted in the match with Widnes being cancelled._ '

I RUNCORN v. BIRKENHEAD PARK (A TEAMS).—Whilst the first team was engaged at Runcorn, on Saturday, the second string were contesting with the A team of the Park at Birkenhead. Runcorn kicked off. and Shaw, within a very short time from the start,registered a try, but no goal succeeded. The home team commenced to play with spirit, and forced two minors ; but the Run- cornians then put on pressure, and some fine passing resulted. A try was scored by Webb, but again the place at goal failed. May, later on, got over, and a goal re- sulted, and at the close of play Runcorn had succeeded in obtaining 2 goals, 3 tries, and 4 minors ; Birkenhead, 2 minors. WARRINGTON RANGERS v. WIDNES ATHLETIC.—These teams met on the ground of the former on Saturday, before a fair attendance. The home team losing the toss, Whitfield kicked off, the ball being well returned to centre, and after a series of exchange kicking between the opposing backs, the oval found a resting place in the visitors' quarters. Owing to the sloppy condition of the ground the game was confined to the forwards, the Rangers having the best of it, but could score noth- ing tangible, the greasy nature of the ball and strong defence of,the Athletics preventing certain scores. The game however, was well contested, the visitors almost notching a, goal from a free kick, a minor being the result. Both sides strove hard to obtain the Verdict, but nothing was scored beyond minors, and the game ended in a draw—two minors each.

WARRINGTON " A " V. BROUGHTON RINGERS "A."—This return fixture was decided on the Wilderspool when, despite the threatening state of the weather, a capital attendance had assembled. Shone for the Rangers commenced operations, and after Sampson's fine punt had driven his opponents back, a fast dribble by Buckley and Barnes found Warrington on the attack. The home forwards began to show their ability and agility, the outcome being that Lally passed wide to Heesom, who again menaced the visitors' citadel, a minor resulting. The drop out failed to bring the much- desired relief, for Lawless ran grandly, his final pass being poor, and another minor was registered. This sort of thing did not suit the Warringtonians, as after Jolley had put in a high punt, the same player passed finely to Potts, who scored an unmistakable try, which was enhanced by Sampson kicking a grand goal from touch. A determined rush by Nowell and Shaughnessy had the desired effect, which was considerably enhanced by Ratnford's grand run. A minute later Howard mulled the ball, and Barnes obtaining possession at midfield ran in a splendid try, which Sampson converted. In nowise ' disheartened, Broughton initiated an attack, dribbling to their antagonists' lines, where a free kick was awarded for an informality, the shot at goal being futile. Drop- ping out, the ball was soon fluttering about the visitors' "25," a free kick being further improved by Quinney, and Shone heading a rush into the home territory;where Sampson saved in the nick of nime. Buckley relieved by a run, and Jolley obtaining the leather ran and punted, and in again going for the ball was obstructed. A free kick being awarded, Sampson, to everyone's surnrise, landed a magnificent goal from centre, for which hOwas deservedly cheered, half time arriving with Warrington three goals to the good. With a fresh kick off, Thornley, Molyneux, Craghan, and Knowles were witnessed peg- ging away,only to find the oval sentflying back by Robin- son. Line outs and scrums were then the order of the day, but eventually Craghan, Lloyd, and Thornley drib- bled over the line, a minor again accruing. On resu- ming, Howard intercepting a pass, put in a fast sprint to the centre, and a long kick by Robinson looked ominous, but Sampson was quite safe. Another rush by Thornley, Buckley, and Teare was splendidly saved and nullified by Howard, but a lot of passing by the home backs repeatedly tested the Rangers' defence. Just as thevifii- tors were badly passed, Nuttall came away with a fine dribble, and then a really fine bit of passing by Heesom, Craghan, Lloyd. and Knowles ended in the latter romp- ing in from midfield, and Sampson kicked another goal. Directly after this a magnificient piece of play fairly roused the enthusiasm of the onlookers. It was started by Lawless passing to Lally, who got finely away, and threw to Thornley who repassed to Barnes, and another try was obtained—a really grand effort. Restarting the Rangers made a slight excursion to the Warrington end, Buckley, Isherwood, Molyneaux, and Teare causing a hasty retreat and a minor was registered. The homesters then pressed, some powerful kicking by Jolley being of immense service, and Potts ultimately getting the ball near centre, ran in a grand try, and Warrington retired winners by 4-2-5 to 0-0-1.

div.head: RUNCORN V. BIRKENHEAD PARK.
div.p: RUNCORN V. BIRKENHEAD PARK.

Played at Runcorn on Saturday before a large number of spectators. The home team suffered by the absence of Houghton, Faulkner, and Abrams. Wainwright, how- ever, consented to play,and Pendlebury went half back, Wainwright wing threequarter. During the first half "The Park" completely held the game in hand. A mull by Woods gave Smith a chance to score, which was taken full advantage of. With this success they played with great determination, and having put an extra back out, checked the passing amongst the home backs. After changing ends the Runcorn men threw a little more en- ergy into the game, and Hugh Hughes with judgment got the ball to Davies, who fairly galloped away over the Park line, and later this movement was adopted with the same suceess, though the goal kicking. was a failure. Dolan gave Crompton a chance. which he quickly took, and dodged over the line under the posts, and whilst being tackled by Tomlinson, stooped down and let go his hold of the ball a few inches from the ground. The Park appealed that he had not touched the ball down according to rule which the referee upheld—hard lines after so good an effort. Hampson next scored near the corner flag, the match concluding in a victory for Run- corn by three tries to one. In the forward ranks Broady, Gayter, and 0. Hughes were prominent individually, but concerted play was at a discount. On the Park side Tomlinson, full back, was extremely safe, and the Rev. Mr. White played with rare judgment; his saving and collaring prevented disaster to his side repeatedly. In the forwards Chadwick was head and shoulders above his colleagues, being ably assisted by Wood and T. W. Lockwo.d. .The whole pack played a hard, fast game, and mare than held their own in the pack and on the loose.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

The return match was played at Broughton on Satur- day, before a poor assemblage. What with the frost, rain, fog and sleet, the Rangers' ground presented a sorry sight. Not a single blade of grass was to be seen, and following the frost on Friday evening had come a downpower on Saturday morning. The surface was a lining of mud, whilst beneath it was as hard as adamant,

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTRALL.-RUGBY.

There are two ways of looking at the match that took place at Whalley Range on Saturday. Either the Glou- cestershire team have been overrated or the Lancashire fifteen had never previously shown the public of what they are capable. Rugby football in the West must be of a poor calibre if the men of Gloucester have rightly, earned the honours which entitled them to come to Man- chester and confront the elect of Lancashire. The game was not five minutes old before the great crowd of spec- tators could see that the colours of the home team were in no danger of beiug lowered by the strangers, and as the play progressed it only served to further emphasise the undoubted strength and skill of the Lancashire fif- teen. They surpassed all previous efforts, and wound up a brilliant season with a magnificent victory by four goals and two tries to nothing.

Lancashire went into a fray with tremendous energy, the forwards forming the packs without the slightest hesitation, and when the ball came into the loose it was a treat to see the way in which they dashed off with it at their toes. Whether in the scrimmages or in the open the Lancashire forwards more than held their own,doing better work than in any of the games this season, which is very high praise indeed. It was not to be expected that the Gloucester eight could cope with their nine oppo- nents, and the extra advantage they were supposed to have from the four three-quarter system was not made manifest. Indeed, in every department the Lancashire team were smarter, and fully established their right to the distinction of champion county. A total of 27 goals and 33 tries to six tries—or 114 points to six— in ten matches is a record which is probably without a parallel, and is not likely to be disturbed for many a year to come.

Gloucestershire were doubtless surprised by the splen- did form of their antagonists, and it is only fair to sup- pose that they were not seen at their best. A weak spot was that of full back, Hughes making mistakes that were readily turned to account by his active antagonists. Hooper, on the other hand, did some very smart things at three-quarters, his runs being about the best features of the afternoon, whilst Taylor also came out well. The half backs did not strike one as being over-smart, but they had a very hard task to face. The forwards never shirked their share of the work, but here again they had an uphill job.

No fault could be laid at the door of a single member of the triumphant team, everyone of whom rose to the occasion. Coop came through with immense credit, and further confirmed the widespread opinion that no better full back could be desired. Valentine had a good day. To score three tries was a grand performance, and he did much good work besides. M'Cutcheon was a trifle better than Gwynn, especially in tackling, but both did excellent service. Berry was quite at his best, the try he secured being a beauty ; and Cross gave entire satis- faction. The forwards of the county had done uncom- monly well in all the ten engagements, and if they can maintain their form until the Rest of England appear at Whalley Range we shall have a match worth seeing.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

The new scheme of the Association League is a big un- dertaking. Instead of the League being limited to a dozen clubs it is proposed to extend its operations to 36. these being told off into three divisions. The proposed change has been under careful consideration for some time and is very favourably received. If the scheme is adopted it will probably mean the absorption of the Alliance, and be expected to be particularly beneficial to many of the best of the Lancashire clubs. The great difficulty will be to manage the enlarged body to the satis- faction of all concerned.

The League tournament is rapidly approaching com- pletion. The cup will pass from the North End to Ever- ton, and it is not a little strange that both of these clubs should te beaten in their last engagement. Everton were taken down at Burnley, as were Preston a week ago,the latter making a poor fight indeed at Sunderland. Al- though Evecton will pose as champions of 1890-1. they do not come within a couple of points of their record of a year ago, whilst North End are six points behind. Notts, on the other hand, have made made splendid pro- gress. having ascended from the tenth to the third position.

div.head: TRE PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: TRE PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

A iueeting of the inhabitants of Warrington in support of the proposed new Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway was held in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and amongst those on the plat- form were Lord Hope and Mr. Nicholson, of Maccles- field, (directors.of the new Company), Mr. J. Baker, of Chesterfield, (one of the solicitors of the Com- pany), Aldermen Harrison and Sutton; Councillors H. Roberts, R. Heaton E. Greenall, Dr. Cannell, Muir, Hepherd, and lutchinson ; Messrs. W. D. Jeans, J. L. Whittle (town clerk), G. Woods, J. L. Tunstall, T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Dodds, and W. Diggle. There was not a large audience, and at the beginning of the meeting there was only a spare attendance. The Maxon' in his opening remarks, referred to the negotiations between the Warrington Corporation and , the directors of the new , Company. The Corporation I had simply wished to safeguard the interests of War- rington vrith regard to the public roads that were to be crossed, and the directors had met them in a kind manner and said they were perfectly prepared to grant the Cor- poration everything they asked if it were asked in reason. He believed they had now got such clauses inserted as would satisfy the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) He should just like to say that personally he believed that the in- troduction of another or even two or three more railways would be very welcome to the people of Warrington. There was every reason to believe that in future years Warrington would be a very large town, and if they wee to have facilities for getting goods into the town and carrying their manufactured articles out they could not have too Much railway accommodation. He was sure the people of Warrington would do all they possibly could to further the interests of this new railway. (Applause.) Mr. BAKER, solicitor to the railway company, then gave some particulars as to the scheme. He said that railway had been promoted in the first instance by gentlemen who were interested in the development of their estates, and who wished to find an outlet for their coal to the sea. The line has been laid out to com- mence at Warrington, and Warrington in fact was the largest town upon the route. They hoped it would be- come very much larger, and that eventually it would be one of the leading towns in the kingdom. (Hear, hear.) They hoped that 'barge quantities of coal would be brought from the Derbyshire coalfield to the docks at Warring- ton and thence exported, and not only coal but also a large traffic in merchandise. The railway crossed England to the east coast where they had power to construct another large dock at Sutton-on-Sea. Warrington would, therefore, be at one end of a large commercial high- way, and must consequently benefit very largely by the trade which would be centred at the end. Latchford, 1- which was now principally open grass land, would then probably be covered with buildings of a commercial character ; which meant employment to hundreds, and perhaps thousands, of people, a large addition to the residential population,and a great increase in the size and property of the town. • They hoped therefore and expected that Warrington would support that railway in every possible shape and form. The gentleman who had pushed the scheme to its present stage had borne the burden and heat of everything, and they now looked to some of those present to associate themselves with the promoters and assist them to obtain Parliamentary sanction for the line and also to carry it out. They certainly hoped that, whenthe proper time came, a very large amount of capi- tal would be taken up in Warrington and the district,and they should like to see some of the magnate's of Warring- ton come fon -ard and associate themselves finanlally with. the undertaking. Having mentioned that it was proposed to make a good passenger 'station near St. James's Church, Mr. Baker went on to describe the route through which the line would run to Sutton-on-Sea. At this last place power had been secured for making a harbour and it was considered to be the very best site on the east coast for the purpose. They expected to make a dock into which vessels could enter at all states of the tide. It was a place eminently suited for fishing, and already many of the fishing smack owners of Grimsby were looking forward to the construction of this dock and had promised to remove their business to SuttOn entirely. That would enable Warrington to receive a supply of fish which was brought into the harbour at Sutton. They hoped, in fact, to develop both Warring- ton and Sutton into two first-class ports, between which there would be a constant traffic of merchandise. (Ap- plause.) He concluded by mentioning that the neW railway would be 1601 miles in length. The MAYOR at this point read a telegram from Lord Manvers who regretted his inability to be present. Alderman HaunisoN proposed "That this meeting of the inhabitants of Warrington hereby testifies its approval of the proposed Lancashire, Derbyshire and I East Coast Railway and calls upon the inhabitants,manu- facturers and traders of Warrington to support the pro- moters by all means in their power." Having spoken in support of the resolution, he said the Corporation made demands recently for the enlargement of the area of the borough, and he might venture to express a hope that if the railway was successfully carried out and Warring- ton really did anything substantial towards its promo- tion, the gentlemen who constituted the backbone of the undertaking would not in the future offer any captious opposition to such a scheme if it were thought desirable to carry it out in. the future. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Mr. J. DODDS seconded the resolution moved by Alder- man Harrison. He was quite sure that Warrington; would give a practically unanimous support to that rail- way, and he thought there was every reason why the support should be given. (Applause.) Alderman Sumer also supported the resolution, • and remarked that if the town increased there would• prob- ably be a reduction in the rates, which, he said, wanted reducing. (Hear, hear.) Mr. G. WOODS, in supporting the resolution, referred to the traffic in and out of Warrington,and said that some few years ago he had occasion to collect some statisties in connection with the Ship Canal, which might be relied upon, because the manufacturers gave him all the infor- mation they possibly could. At that time—about five years ago—he calculated that the amount of cpal brought into Warrington was not less than 300,000 tons per annum. The amount of pig iron brought into the town for manufacturing purposes and-chiefly consumed by the Pearson and Knowles Company, and Monks, Hall, and Company, was about 170,000 tons a year;. bar iron 125,000 tons; wire 50,000 tons; wire rods 70,000, total- ling in all to about 700,000 tons per annum. Then he had got machinery at 90,000 tons, glass between 60,000'and 70,000 ; leather nearly 200,000, and altogether he was not far wrong when he said that the tree to and from Warrington amounted to over 1,000,000 tons. He had ,other interesting information, for he found that, leaving out babes and sucklings, and taking the population at 30,000, the amount of flour consumed in the year in • Warrington did not fall below 5,000 tons; provisions,. allowing half a pound of butter and half a pound of bacon and cheese—(a voice "And what about beer'')- 1,000 tons; potatoes 3,000 tons, and soon. (Hear, hear.) It would perhaps be said that the railway would never pay, but he should like to see the man who would- say so (a voice" There's Diggle on the platform" and laughter). He thought they should at least wait to see whether it paid. (Hear hear, and applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and car- ried unanimously. Mr. NicuoisoeT, one of the directors of the company, then gave an account of what had been done in Maccles- field in promotion of the scheme. He said that at Mac- clesfield they did not forget that unless they did some- I thing for its promotion it might not even come so far as their town. The railway was cut up into twenty or twenty-five sections, and the making of any one of those sections would depend upon circumstances, such as how capital might be found. The decisions of the directors would be largely influenced by the support given in the large centres on their railway. (Hear, hear.) He then moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presid- ing. Mr. J. L. TIINSTALL, in seconding this resolution, said it had been suggested that possibly the Ship Canal docks at Warrington might not be made, but it seemed to him that if this railway were laid, it would; at all events, be one more guarantee that the docks would be made, be- cause the railway company were not going to spend £s,ooo,oooand then find that they had no outlet at War- rington. (Applause.) At the same time he himself thokight the docks would be made whether the railway was-made or not. (Hear, hear.) The vote of thanks was then passed, and the MAYOR having responded, the meeting terminated.

div.head: SEIZURE OF A BRITISH STEAMER BY PORTUGUESE.
div.p: SEIZURE OF A BRITISH STEAMER BY PORTUGUESE.

Later advices say that confirmation has been received of the report concerning the capture of the steamer Countess of Carnarvon by Portuguese. While the vessel was ascending the Limpopo River she was captured by the Portuguese gunboat Marshal M'Mahon and taken to Delagoa Bay as a prize with her cargo. Messrs. Jameson, Boyle, Stevens, and Moodie, of Manicaland, were on board the steamer Countess of Car- narvon returning to Caketown to meet Mr. Rhodes whet. the vessel was fired upolf andcaptured by the Portuguese. The Countess of Carnarvon ascended the Limpopo at the express wish of Gungunhama, who has declared the river, which forms a splendid waterway leading to Matabeleland and the Tati goldfields, as open to British commerce. Gungunhama utterly repudiates the vassal- age to Portugal which the Portuguese allege him to have accepted.
• The Cardiff strikes are now over, and all the trades resumed work on Monday.

div.head: OFF GIBRALTAR.
div.p: OFF GIBRALTAR.
THE ANCHOR LINER UTOPIA IN COLLISION.

div.head: FOUNDERING OF THE STEAMER.
div.p: FOUNDERING OF THE STEAMER.
LOSS OF OVER 500 LIVES.

,A terrible disaster occurred on Tuesday evening off Gibraltar, resulting in the loss of upwards of 500 lives. The British steamer Utopia, belonging to the Anchor Line Company, whose head offices are at Glasgow, left ' taly a few days since for New 1 ork, with nearly 800 souls on board, consisting of the crew and Italian emigrants from Naples and Sicily. All went well, apparently, until dusk on Tuesday, when the Utopia, was putting into Gibraltar for coal, and when only about half a mile from shore, collided with H.M.S. Anson, and sank in about five minutes. From the accounts- to hand, the scene which followed the collision WM heartrending and appalling, and only a few more than 300 of those on board the Utopia succeeded in the terrible struggle for their lives. Fifty bodies have been recovered up to the present, and the survivors are being well looked after by the •authorities at Gibraltar. The captain of the Utopia, Mr. M'Keague, has been in the service of the Anchor Line for a number of years, but he made his first' voyage in the Utopia when she left the ClYde in November last. The officers and crew were all shipped at Glasgow. The officers' names, in addition •to that of the captain, are James Thompson, first officerr.Glasgow ; C. VV. Lees, second officer, Liverpool; T. H. Wadworth, third officer, Chesterfield ; Robert Cook, first engineer, Glasgow; -John M'Call,. second engineer, Glasgow; David Thompson, third engineer, Glasgow John • Adam, fourth engineer, Gihsgow ; and M. Hedderwick, finst steward, Glasgow. The ill-fated vessel was an iron screw steamer of 2,731 tens register, and was built at Port Glasgow in 1874. News was on Wednesday received by the Anchor Line firm stating that the following have been saved :—Captain MlCeague ; Dr. Seller, medical officer: Macfarlane, boatswain; Hedderwick, stew- ard; Taggart, carpenter; and the following deck hands—Barrie, Bdwie, Hossack, Miller, Paterson, Rowe, and Willcox: W. T. Colbron, New York, a saloon passenger, is also reported safe; but beyond this all is uncertain, and the greatest anxiety is manifested at Glasgow to obtain pews of friends and relatives who were known to be on the Utopia at the time she started on her fatal voyage. The Point where the Utopia sank is known as the Ragged Staff. She went down in seven fathoms of water, having been struck abaft the engine-room; and had it not been for the assistance from the boats which put off from vessels of the Channel Squadron and the Swedish man-of-war Freya, nearly all those on board would have perished. Alarm guns were fired immediately the Utopia sank, and six electric lights were kept playing round the spot, the masts and funnel of the vessel being just visible above water among the struggling mass .of humanity. Several sailors of the fleet are missing; and Lloyd's agent at Gibraltar telegraphs that a steam pinnace belonging to the British ironclad Immortalite has been lost, and two of her crew, named Crayton and Irayles, are missing. The difficulties of the rescuers were greatly increased by the fact that a strong gale was blowing at the time of the collision; but this did not discourage the British and Swedish sailors who displayed the utmost daring, and did their work at great personal risk. The sea, however, has now moderated, and the recovery of.bodies is rendered more easy. Lloyd's' agent telegraphing at midday stated that the number of the crew saved was twenty, and that a lads- saloon passenger was saved; while the second officer and Mr. Charles G. Davies, Boston, saloon • pas- senger, are missing. He further states that the Utopia got in ampng,st the ironclads and fouled the ram of the Anson. and was strqc_k amidships.

A later teleg,rare from Lloyd's agent, at Gibraltar, timed 2.55 p.m. on Wednesday, shows that the loss of life was oven more terrible than was at first reported,anu nearly equals the number drowned in the Thames when the Princess Alice went down. From this telegram, it appears that there were 830 passengers on the Utopia, and a crew of 50. Twenty-four of the crew were saved, and 292 passengers, making a total Of 564 drowned and 316 saved. Fifty bodies had been recovered, and the remainder were supposed to be in the-sunken ship, which was being examined by divers. The men Crayton and Hales, of the Immortalite, were both drowned, and the bodies had been recovered.

Upon inquiry at the Admiralty on Wednesday evening, it was learned that the First Lord had received no de- tails of the collision. It was stated, however, that the Anson was at her moorings at the time the vessels col- lided.

A Plymouth ,correspondent states that the Duke of Edinburgh has received the following trlegram from Sir M. Culme Seymour :—" Gibraltar, Wednesday morning. —From Sir Michael Culme Sevmour.—The Utopia, An- chor line, came ifito Gibraltar seven p.m.. after dark. Fowled Anson's bows, moorednff' New Mula. Utopia foundered almost immediately.: 8.50 Italian emigrants .on board. Fear great loss of life. Am doing everything possible. Particulars later. No damage to Anson."

div.head: LATER DETAILS.
div.p: LATER DETAILS.

The total number on board the Utopia when she left Naples was 880. Of these only 311 have been saved, leaving 569 drowned or missing. The Utopia last left the Clyde on November sth for the Adriatic, touching. at Niples on the 24th of the same month, and arriving at Fiume a few days afterwards. From that port the vessel sailed on November 30th for New York, which she reached on the 7th January last. Leaving for the Mediterranean, she reached Trieste on the 13th ult., and when lose was again on a voyage to New York. Previous to leaving the Clyde on the sth Nevember she was refitted at the cost of £30,000. [" TIMES."' SPECIAL IMAM ON TELEGRAM.] GIBRALTAR, WEDNESDAY, WA. M.—The British man-of- war with which the Anchor liner Utopia came in colli- sion last night was the Anson, and not the Rodney. The disaster occurred at seven o'clock. The ram of the Anson tore a hole thirty feet long in the side of the Utopia near the stern, and the vessel sank within ten minutes, going-down stern Rrst. Her funnel and masts are just above the water. There were 880 passengers all told on board. A heavy south-westerly gale was blow- ing at the time of the collision, and a tremendous sea washed everything on deck overboard. The boats of the Channel Squadron were on the scene almost itnmediatelv, and rendered valuable assistance. It is feared that quiie two.thirds of the passengers have been drowned. The launch of FLAT S: Themortalite was smashed to pieces, and several blnejackets were drowned. The electric. light on the fleet was thrown upon the scene of the wreck, and rendered the most vital service, enabling. many to be saved who would otherwise have been drowned in the darkness. The bodies of many men, women, and children have been washed ashore. The boats of the squadron were patrolling all night, piCklng. up bodies and saving lives. Captain M'Keague, corn-- ma,nder of the Utopia, and the doctor and steward are. saved'.

div.head: SURVIVORS OF THE CREWE.
div.p: THE SURVIVORS OF THE CREWE.

The Press Association Glasgow correspondent tele- graphs :—A telegram was received on Thursday at the head office of the Anchor Line at Glasgow from Gilaral- tar„ stating that two of the crew of the Utopia, ,who were reported missing, have been saved. They are Joha Flett, seamark, of Pitterweem, Fifeshire, and 3. Graves, donkeyman, of Glasgow. The survivors of the crew will be brought to Glasgow in the Anchor Liner•Dritan- nia, which left Marseilles on Wednesday, calling at Gib- raltar and reaching Glasgow on the 28th. ARREST OF TFIE CAPTAIN OF THE UTOFIA..

GIBRALTAR, TITURSPAY NIGHT..—NO little excitement has been created among the British garrison here-by the the arrest of Captain M'Keague, of the emigrant ship, Utopia, which sunk after collision with her Majesty's ship Anson, on Tuesday. Captain M'Keogue has been taken into custody by the British authorities, wthose alle- gations against him are briefly these :—" Wrongful acts improper conduct, negligence of duty, and raiSmanage- ment of his ship." Captain M`licague has becntadmkted to bail.

It is now known that the Utopia, which,foutuiered after collision with the Ansonbattleship (not the Rodney, as at first reported), took on board 813 entigrants at Naples, of whom 681 were men. Examination a the hull of the Utopia, which was made on Thursday,. b 7 divers trom the warships, revealed a frightful seen& The emi- grants who crowded the lower decks had been surprised, as we said, by the sudden inrush of the sea, and in their frantic haste to reach the deck they had bkcked the gangways, and there, fighting and struggling, they died in hundreds. The steamer appears to have been taken too close to the Anson It the first place,and in the second the offcers had forgotten the existence. of the terrible spur which projects for many feet in front of the stem, but under water. The survivors are being well cared for ashore.
