THE MURDER OF THE NEW ORLEANS CHIEF OF POLICE. ELEVEN PERSONS LYNCHED. The trial of the Italians charged with the assassination of Chief of Police Hennessy has been concluded at New Orleans. The jury acquitted six of the accused, and disagreed as regardsthe remaining three. A Reuter's telegram of Saturday from New Orleans says :—" A committee of fifty of the inhabitants met last night and called a meeting for to-day at the Clay • Statue, to consider the verdicts given by the jury in the case of the Sicilians charged with the assassination of the Chief of Police Hennessy. The meeting took place this morning, and thcrp present subsequently adjourned to the parish prison, which was soon surrounded by a howling mob of several thousand persons, who immedi- ately proceeded to attack the goal. The doors were forced open, and in a very short space of time six of the Sicilians were either shot or hanged by the infuriated crowd. A man named Incardonia Matrianga and the boy Marchesi are the only two that escaped. A later telegram says :—" According to the latest particulars obtainable, eleven of the prisoners in the parish gaol were either shot or hangel by the mob." A Reuter's telegram from Rome says :—" A despatch received here from Washington states that the Italian Minister in that city in calling Mr. Blaine's attention to the lynching of Italian prisoners in New Orleans, pro- tested against the inaction of the local authorities during the invasion of the prison by the mob. Arr. Blaine expressed sorrow at the acts committed by the populace, and assured the Minister that he would immediately take the orders of the President with regard to the measures to be adopted, information of which would be immediately communicated to the Italian Govern- ment. More men were killed than was intended. Baquetto had !moved an alibi, and was acquitted by the Court. The Jurymen are already suffering for the verdict they returned. Seligman, the foreman, besides being expelled by the Cotton and Stock Exchanges, has been advertised by his brother, who is a senior partner in his firm, as no longer connected with it. The Italian papers in New Orleans demand venge- ance, stating all the Italian citizens would force the, Minister at Washington to take action to punish the rioters who had taken part in the affray. Only two of the victims are reported to be Italian sub- jects. The Governor and the Mayor declare that they received no call for assistance in preserving order. Selig- man, the foreman of the jury, has been arrested and imprisoned, but the charge preferred against him is not known. The mob was no ordinary lynching mob, but included lawyers, editors, and leading and wealthy business , men.
THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The annual report of the Medical Officer of Health for 1890 has been prepared and presented to the Sanitary Committee. In the course of the re- port, Dr. Gornall estimates the population at mid- summer at 50,000, with an area of 1,442 acres, the density of population being 34 per acre, and the number of inhabited houses 9,245. There have been 1,926 births-994 males and 932 females; and 1,152 deaths —6lO males and 542 females. The birth- rate has, therefore, been 3852, and the death-rate 22.68.
BIRTHS. The births registered during 1890 were 1,926, of which 994 were males, and 932 females. The birth-rate of

borough were 3852 per 1,000 of the population, that of the Warrington registration sub-district 35•73, and Latchford 41.08 per 1,000. The birth-rate of England and Wales during 1890 was 29.7 per 1,000
DRATHS.
The total number of deaths recorded in . the borough,

during the year 1890, was 1,152, of which 610 were males and 542 females; 1,060 were registered in tbe Warrington and 92 in the Latchford registration district. This number included 16 that took place at the Fever Hospital, 10 at the Infirmary, and 86 at the Workhouse Hospital. From the total of 1,152 must be deducted 19,
'which occurred at the Workhouse, Infirmary, &c., of

, persons admitted from the several parts of the Warrington Union outside the municipal boundary, and from other towns. The remainder, 1,133, was the number of deaths debited to the borough, and on Which the death-rate was

calculated. The rate of mortality for the year was equivalent to 22-68 per 1,000, on an estimated population b of 50,000, to the middle of the year, being .56 higher than 1889 (22-12), and 1-27, the average (21:41) of the ten years (1880-1889.) The excess of births over deaths, representing the natural increase to the population, was 773, against 847 in 1889, and against 890, the average of the 10 years (1880-1889.) The death-rate of England and Wales during 1890 was 19-2 per 1,000. The number of deaths under one year was 351, that for the previous year 318, and in 1888 it was 277. Measured by the Proportion of deaths to births registered, infant mortality in Warrington was equal to 171 per 1,000 as compared tvith 163 in 1889, 147 in 1888. 170 in 1887, and 132 in 1886, and 152 the average of the previous five years. ZYMOTIC DISEASES.—DIPHTHERIA.

The seven principal zymotic diseases caused 194 deaths: scarlet fever, 18; measles, 33; whooping cough, ; diphtheria, 17; fevers, 15; diarrhcea, 57. The zymotic death-rate was 3-88 per 1,000 of the population, against 4.22 in 1889, and 3.54 the average of the ten years (1880-89). There was no. sensible decrease in the _ _ _ _ .

number of deaths from these diseases, though the total was slightly under that of the preceding year. Whoop- ing cough in the first and second quarters, and diarrhcea In the third, were mainly responsible for the high mor- tality. The deaths from scarlet fever and measles were much fewer than in 1889, but those from diphtheria and enteric fever had about doubled. In England and Wales the zymotic death-rate was 2.03 per 1,000, whilst in London it was 2.7, the lowest being 1.2 in Huddersfield, and the highest 4•3 in Preston. As in other towns, diphtheria had been more prevalent during 1890. Twenty-seven cases were notified, and the number of deaths was large in comparison, namely, 17, or 63.0 per cent. In 1889 the number of cases reported was ten, and in 1888 nine. Though the cause of the disease was sur- rounded with so much obscurity, yet, apart from the association of personal filth with many of the cases re- ported, a fair proportion occurred in perfectly sanitary houses. In several of the cases there was defective drainage, allowing the entrance of sewer gas into the dwellings. In others the only perceptible nuisance was noxious effluvia from the house drains and the sewers, pointing to the retention and deposit of offensive Matters In them. During the coming year the Corpora- tion would obtain possession of the Water Works, and it was to be hoped that steps would be taken to organize the periodical flushing and disinfection of every sewer in the town.
DIARRMEA AND ITS CAUSES.

This disease contributed 57 deaths, against 36 in 1889. and 47 the average of the ten years 1880-1889. At the risk of being importunate, the Medical Officer says that again he must mention some of the causes which influ- enced the production of diarrlicea, and over which a Sanitary Committee, being the conservators of public cleanliness, had control. Dr. Ballard, as a result of his recent enquiry, dwelt on the importance of preventing overcrowding and the fouiing of the soil and air, while he pointed to the necessity of promoting the free circula- tion of air about and within dwellings, of doing away With domestic darkness and general dirtiness and fusti- ness of houses, the free ventilation and cleansing of sewers and drains the removal of filthy accumulations. All these unsanitary conditions could be remedied by the Paving and cleansing of back passages,courts, and yards, as well as the front streets, thus drying the sub-soil, the re-arrangement of unhealthy areas, ' the prevention of erection of buildings in back yards, the demolition of houses unfit for human habitation, and the making of back-to-back houses into through ones.

div.head: EPIDEMIC INFLUENZA.
div.p: EPIDEMIC INFLUENZA.

This disease was prevalent in the early part of the year. On one occasion it was introduced by a nursif to the Fever Hospital, who had been staying in Edinburgh at a house where the disease existed. She communi- cated it to four others (servants and nurses),but none of the patients then in the hospital were affected. Eleven deaths are attributable to the disease.

THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. The total number of pvients admitted since the hos- Pital was opened on the 28th May, 1877, was 2,022; number admitted since the Improvement Act received the royal assent, 1,945, and during the year 1890, 135. Phone, £10; printing, £4; sundries, £7 17s. Bd. ; total, £1,106 19s. sd. The average cost of each patient in tha ~.hospital was £6 14s. 11d. Food cost per case. £1 18s. The average cost of fowl per person per week was ss.lid. Of the 135 patients admitted during the year 1890, five were attended by their own medical attendant, and 130 by the medical superintendent.

div.p: FLETT'S (3ELEBRATED MARMALADE. NOW READY.

and in other ways endeavour to buy off that remorse which. must of necessity afflict their thoughtful moments, but, sir, a shadow thick and dark overhangs all their "benevolence." The blasted lives of drink-sodden men, and the curses of ruined women and the tears of bereaved little ones by the scores of thousands daily accumulate and must sooner or later be atoned for—by whom? Will not the men whose present opulence, whose palatial resi- dences—always situate far away from the scenes of deso- lation which inevitably accompany their "pest houses" —whose dashing equipages and ever-increasing estates have been purchased at a cost to this pegple, greater than the accumulated evils of war, pestilence and famine— will these men go scot-free at the time of the "great account ?" I leave it to your readers to judge for them- selves, but suffice it for me to say,that all the generosity, church and school building, almsgivings, and accumu- lated benevolence of all the brewers and publicans com- bined, are but as a drop of pure water,which falling into the filthy cesspool of evil which their trade is daily in- flicting upon us, does no lasting good. If my friend is so vexed with the Rev. H. P. Hughes, let me commend to his notice the words in which John Wesley described "Pluto's" clients—he says :—" All who sell them (intoxicating liquors) in the common way to any that will buy are poisoners general. They murder His Majesty's subjects by wholesale, neither does their eye pity or spare. They drive them to hell like sheep; and what is their gain? Is it not the blood of these men? Who would envy their large estates and sumptuous palaces? A curse is in the midst of them. The curse of God cleaves to the stoles, the timber, the furniture of them. The curse of God is in their gardens, their walks, their groves, a fire that burns to the nethermost hell. Blood, blood is there; the foundation, the walls, the floor, the roof, are stained with blood! And can'st thou hope, 0 thou man of blood! tho' thou art clothed in scarlet and fine linen,and farest sumptuously every day, canst thou hope to deliver down thy fields of blood to the third generation? Not so,for there is a God in heaven, therefore thy name shall be rooted out. Like as those whom thou hast destroyed, both body and soul, thy memorial shall perish with thee.'" I repeat and endorse emphatically, the assertion of the Rev. H. P. Hughes, viz:, that "any professing Chris- tian who votes for a brewer or a publican is a Christian humbug," and I commend John Wesley's words to the serious consideration, not only of "Pluto," but of every Christian of every denomination,with a perfect confidence that, if they are carefully and seriously pondered, they will result in the ultimate casting out of the "Imelean thing" which at present so largely dominates every social, political, and religious effort. And now, sir, just another word in conclusion. " Pluto " says that we are constantly "hunting for stinks." Would to God it were necessary to hunt for these ill-savoured foulnesses! Instead of that being the case, they meet us at every street corner, and thrust their hideous excrescences upon our notice at every hour of the day and night. The duration of the present condi- tion of things depends upon the common-sense of our peoßle ; and those who can read the signs of the times are full of hope that in the near future we shall do much towards the removal of our national disgrace.—Yours, &c.,
FELIX.

div.head: Retttrs to tin Obttor.
div.p: Retttrs to tin Obttor.
PLUTO'S COMMON-SENSE.

Sir,—We have heard of "good honest beer (of which " Pluto " speaks so feelingly) sometimes getting into people's heads. Of course we would not for a moment imply that when" Pluto" penned his last letter he was not responsible for what he wrote ; but, to say the least of it, his state surely was a highly excited one. How vexed he must have been when, in more rational 'moments, he saw his wandering effusion in print I His letter does not merit a reply; but I should like .(fr his guidance in the future) to remind hin4, that such terms ,as "swipes "and " bunkum" are familiar only to a cer- tain class of society, and that respectable readers find it difficult to interpret them.—Truly yours, March 17, 1891.
VERITAS.
"GAS" V. COMMON-SENSE.

Sir,—A week or two ago you published a letter signed by "Pluto." I read that letter, also the replies sent by " M.A.," "Felix," and " Veritas." This week you pub- lish another letter signed by " Pluto." It suggests , several questions. Ist, the outrage it commiti against good literary taste leads one to ask where had " Pluto " been to before he wrote the letter? 2nd, why such fondness for the" Brewers" and the stuff they brew? 3rd, does his detestable slang reveal the company he keeps? If so, I feel sorry for " Pluto." Poor fellow! Is he to be pitied or despised? Judging from his letter, I should say the latter. Let me advise him before attemp- ting any more letters to think a little more, and so order his conversation as becometh a gentleman.—Yours, &c. ON-LOOKER.
Sir. —The best way to deal with the argumPnts of a " Pluto is to strip them of their amplificatory verbiage, and place them naked before the reader. They confute themselves.

" Pluto" argued that Parnell was the strongest man in the Irish party to-day by reason of the "moral smell" which he asserted had been raised around him by Messrs. Price Hughes and Stead. I asked him how a smell couldmake a man strong (except in the sense of malodourous) but he has attempted no reply. Of course no reply is possible. The argument is too absurd to secure a moment's credence when thus bladly stated. It might be illustrated thus :—A man, fresh from labour in the middens, comes into a meeting and offends the public nose. I demand his expulsion. "But, says "Pluto," "the offender is deserving of, and secures, the public support and sympathy by reason of his very smell ; and, further, you, the objector, are the cause of that smell !" Absurdity could go no further. " Pluto's " only escape is to abandon the argument as such and take refuge in opinion. In that case I should simply reply that facts do not bear out his opinion, but point in the opposite direction. When Parnell's life comes to be written, I think the task should be entrusted to "Pluto." After describing the career of his hero, he might, in the manner of biographers, conclude with an inquiry into the causes of that hero's greatness. He might sum up as followers :—" But none of the theories I have examined is sufficient to account for the stability of the mighty fabric of his fame. That gigantic edifice could rest on one, and only one, adequate foundation. What was that foundation? It was a MORAL. SMELL !"

Two other arguments of " Pluto's" need only be nakedly exposed to exhibit their fallacies. Argument 1. "Some Christians ask and receive mone- tary support from brewers. Mr. Price Hughes is a Christian, therefore he receives such support. 'Therefore he is a canting humbug for denouncing brewers." Argument 2. "All teetotallers drink non-intoxicating liquors. Mineral and aerated waters are non-intoxica- ting. Therefore all teetotallers drink them, and none but they do." It does not require a skilled logician to see the absurdi- ties contained in the above, and yet " Pluto's " denun- ciations and ridicule repose entirely. upon them. If Lam right in a conjecture as to the identity of your correspon- dent, he is possessed of far better sense than his present letters give evidence of ; and I would earnestly entreat him to try in future to be more true to himself, and hence to others, than he has been on this occasion.—Yours
MASTV OF ARTS.

COMMON-SENSE V. PLUTO'S GAS. Sir,—l really am sorry for my old friend. Talk about running" amuck "—he has done it with a vengance. I hardly like to tell you what I fear, but it is perhaps only fair to poor old " Pluto " that I should do so, because there certainly was a time when those of us who knew him best could not help but admit his p,bilities as a "reasoner," although we might not agree with his con- clusions. Hislast concoction, however, is such a shock- ingly forcible example of a serious decay of mental force and power of argument, and is at the same time so full of irritable nastiness and incoherent "blather," that 1 am:forced unwillingly to the supposition t hat my poor o'.d friend has a tendency to softening of the brain.

" Pluto's " attack on the Rev. 11. P. Hughes has most ignominiously failed, and his assertion that there are "brewers living to-day who have done more real good to their fellows by a scratch of the pen, than the Rev. H. P. Hughes will do if he lives to be as old as Methusaleh," is all moonshine. I challenge "Pluto "to give a single instance in support of such a wild and foolish assertion. True, there are brewers who build churches and endow them, assist to build church schools, erect alsmhousfss, contribute greatly to Art Institutions,

div.head: VIADUCT BRASS BAND.
div.p: THE VIADUCT BRASS BAND.
Sr,—You will certainly oblige by inserting the follow. ing in your next issue. _ . ..

_ The conceit and impudence of some persons really goes beyond bounds at times, and Earlestown is not free, it seems from intermeddlers, for we have in our town an individual who dubs himself "Watchman," who goes about pushin7 and poking into other people's affairs instead of minding his own business. Whatever need be said of the Viaduct Brass Band requires no " Watchman" to spread it abroad, for it is as conscientious and honourable a body of men, as any in the town, and the late services which were given by them in the St. John's Church, were heartily and honourably worked by each member, and fully earned the tribute that was accorded to them. If " Watchman" and all others would go in the same sincere andlonest spirit as the "Band" did, there would be no sneering and un- mannerly remarks passed about any person, the indul- gence of which exhibits ignorance and meanness. It would look far better of him to stay amongst his own denomination than go picking holes elsewhere. But perhaps he is thinking of self a little bit, and wishing a deputation of the St. Helens Bottle Blowers' Association would pay his clan a visit, and give them a lift with some of the money, wasted, as he has said, on a Brass Band. Does he want the Band to administer to their neces- sities ? I must say I feel a slight touch of pity for hin —Yours. Sze.. Earlestown, 17th March, 1891.
ANTI-WATCHMAN.

div.head: SUNDAY TRAINS FROM RUNCORN.
div.p: SUNDAY TRAINS FROM RUNCORN.

Sir,--Sir Edward Moon having retired from the chair- manship of th 3 London and North-Western Railway Company, I should like to suggest that -just now would be a suitable time to make a further effort to obtain a service of Sunday trains. At present we are shut out from the world, but if we had Sunday trains we should no longer be at a disadvantage compared with other civi- lized communities. We could:then take a run into the country, inflate our lungs with fresh air (an absolute im- possibility in Runcorn), and enjoy the beauties of nature. We could have the pleasure of exchanging visits with our friends and relatives, and, further, we could avail our- selves of a service in the ancient Cathedral of Chester, which I can assure you is a positive treat. This may appear a trivial matter to those who are able to leave their homes at will, and enjoy themselves till their heart is content, but it is not so to those who have to apply themselves at the desk, behind the counter, or at the bench from week end to week end. To them it is a serious affair, for they require change of air and enjoy- ment just as much as their more fortunate townspeople some of whom do rot object to use their own and hired carriages to take them to and from their respective places of worship whether the day be fine or wet. The new Chairman of the Company (Lord Stalbridge) is a man of broad and liberal views, and I feel sure if he were approached in a suitable manner, and a statement of our position laid before him, it would not be long ere the facilities so much needed would be accorded to us. Will our Commissioners take the matter up? I hope so. —Yours truly, Runcorn, March, 1891.
PRO BONO PUBLIC°.

homeless, stagger to and fro in our streets? Are the thousands of naked and famishing wives and children who silently pine in their misery because reckless hus- bands and fathers have given the money that should have supplied their wants to enrich the publicans? Or are the inmates of our prisons, workhouses, and lunatic asylums? Nay, verily. The responsibility lies at the doors and upon the souls of the drink traffickers, and the Legislature which sanctions and derives enormous I revenues from their nefarious trade. If Mr. Langham and his friends really desire to deliver their country from the horrors of drink, and earn the blessings of them that are ready to perish through it, they must adopt means more powerful and drastic than speech-making. As skilful physicians, and not quacks, they must apply the lance to the root of the evil, and not to its excrescences. 'rhey must attack the makers and sellers ot drink rather than the unfortunate consumers.

According to a Parliamentary return recently issued that good friend and ofnament of "the church," Sir Gilbert Greenall, Baronet. M.P., is not only a great brewer, but a mighty publican also, his firm (Messrs. Greenall. Whitley, and Co.), owning no less than five hundred and thirty-eight public-houses in Lancashire and Cheshire, no fewer than sixty-two of them being in the borough of Warrington t. Now here is a chance for Messrs. Langham and Company to earn distinction in the cause of temperance. Let them approach the pious and benevolent baronet, and, in their most glowing lan- guage, lay before him the wrongs his huge trade is inflicting upon his fellow creatures, and urge him, in the interests of poor suffering humanity, to dismantle his breweries and close up his grog shops. The man who is so generous when a church is to be built, or a priest endowed, could not surely turn a deaf ear to the eloquent pleadings of his spiritual guides in such a cause as this!

But even the pious baronet might object; for the passion for heaping up wealth is strong in some men even on theeborders of the grave. In that case the good men need not give way to despair. Could they not move the whole machinery of" the Church " against him, and have him turned out of Parliament to make room for some one who would pledge himself to use every effort in his power to reform the liquor laws by destroying the liquor trade.---Yours truly,
A VOICE FROM THE WILDERNESS.
THE WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL, MR. DIXON, AND THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS.

Sir,—l must say that I think there is one part of your eport of the proceedings of the Town Council with which he public can hardly be edified, that is, the part relating to the reading of the letter from the foreman at the Inter- cepting Depots communicating to the Sanitary Com- mittee an account of the demonstration made there by Mr. Dixon against the Council. It stikes me that it by no means conduces to the dignity of a civic corporation or tends to exalt it in the estimation of its constituents, ro emp:oy its workmen in the capacities of spies and informers as far as one of their employers is concerned, for the purpose of retailing to the rest every chance observation that he in a moment of excitement may choose to direct against them. It is demeaning and demoralising to the workmen; and it is not creditable to the Council.

I would suggest that if the Council are desirous to have an accurate record of the harangues of Mr. Dixon in future, and considering the deceitfulness of human memory and the decidedly ex parte character of the tes- timony of an employe, and the temptation he must have to be artistic at the expense of truth in order to please an anti-Dixon majority, a better plan might be adopted. The Council might purchase a phonograph on the latest and most improved principle, and, imitating the device of a recently dis-satisfied inmate of a New York boarding house, who by means of such a mach:l'le discovered all the impositions his landlady was practising on her boarders,have it placed in a convenient spot at the Incercepting Depots. Then when Mr. Dixon pays his next visit, the foreman might manage to coax him into the immediate proximity of the instrument, the tell-tale apparatus, so that his observations might be re- . corded with such minute precision, that there would be no possibility of exaggeration or deception. The phono- graph might subsequently, on the night of the Council meeting, be conveyed to their meeting room, and after a due preface from one of the anti-Dixon majority,it might be set in revolution, when, lo! Mr. Dixon's harangue would be re-produced with all the characteristic unction and accentuation with which he delivered it at the works. This would at once relieve the workmen from a very humiliating duty and be equivalent to the whole of ' the Town Council being present at the original deliver- ance, nay more than equivalent; for the diversity of the reports which a multitude of witnesses of the same occurrences will give is proverbial. But this I am inclined to think that if there could be a contrivance by which as exact a reproduction of the stinks of which Mr. Dixon. complains, as of his utterances at the works by the pho- nograph, could be presented in the Council Chamber, his strong expressions would be paralleled by those which would emanate from his brother Councillors.
MANLIUS

Certain members of the Corporation have recently, very forcibly, remarked that if some of the wealthier magnates of the Corporation could have the nuisanze in question brought close to their own habitations it would not be allowed to continue a week. By a curious irony of circumstances, certain of the better-to-do people have lately had the delicious aroma of this quintessence of perfumes which makes the atmosphere of Warrington so uniquely pleasurable to breathe, brought iminediately under their noses through the conveyance of the manure to the close vicinity of the Town -Hall. The farmers would thus, it was thought, be more conveniently pro- vided with a sample of the manure, but meantime the 'nasal organs of the would-be purveyors of this delight- ful stuff were furnished with a more than abundant sample of the stink it dispenses. rue result was that it was carted away, so that no more might it thus rudely assail the nostrils of the august smellers of it, by coming "twixt the wind and their nobility." lam only sorry it was not allowed to remain till the Council meeting: it might have done more than all Mr. Dixon's eloquence to bring converts to his side; and, assuredly, it would have been a most excusatory commentary on the some- what sensational description furnished to the Council of his proceedings at the depots. Already we are having a delicious earnest of what is in store for us next summer, in the shape of smells from those works, and I think it is coming to this, that a vigorous campaign will have to be entered upon against the intolerable nuisance at Warrington, just as there has been one commenced lately at Widnes, against the nuisance from the chemical works there, with apparently some satisfactory result, at any rate, for the present. The Corporation have been prosecuting people wholesale of late for having unsanitary outbuild- ings and the like ; and yet they are creating themselves a gigantic nuisance, which could hardly be outmatched, when at its height, if all the inhabitants of Warrington were to follow the example of those who have been thus dealt with. The nature of this obnoxious subject neces- sarily prevents one from speaking out in that plain, sledge-hammer, Saxon style which is so useful to drive comprehension of their duties into the heads of public men, and to bring about the reform of abuses, and we are so much the creatures of words, that euphonious terms seem to partly hide from ourselves the real na- ture of an evil. Otherwise lam certain that long ago such an impression would hasre been produced upon the public mina by the agitation against the Intercepting Depots that their abolition would have been demanded as an imperative necessity at all hazards, and no matter at what cost.—Yours truly,
THE LOCAL BOARD ELEcTtoN.—The members of the Lymm Local Board who retire at the end of the present month are Messrs. Daniel Rogers, David Forster, and James Gibbons.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—Mr. J. R. Taylor presided at the weekly meeting of the above Band of Hope Society, held on Monday evening. Recitations, songs, &c., were contributed by the members. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—Under the auspices of the above society, a lantern lecture was given in the Parochial Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. The Bev. R. Coward occupied the chair, and there was a moderate attendance.

LECTURE BY THE REV. J. YoNoE. —ln the Congregational Church on Tuesday evening, the Rev. John Yong,e, of 1 Warrington, delivered the last of a series of descriptive lectures on the history of Nonconformity. The period dealt with was from 1688 to 1888. There was again a large and appreciative audience. Tux POPT/LA ft CONCERTS.—The Rev. William Evans pre- sided at the popular concert, on Saturday evening,when a programme of an enjoyable and varied character was submitted to a large gathering. The Lymm string band, for the first time since the inauguration of these penny concerts, took part in the entertainment, and their selec- tions were highly appreciated by the audience. Miss Marion Thorpe sang "Dolly's Revenge" in a capable manner. Mr. Wilson was encored for his singing of "Home once more," and in response gave "The Old Arm chair." Mr. Hall contributed a reading, entitled "The tenth of January," Mr.Everton recited.and Messrs. Thomason and Owen were warmly applauded for their respective songs, "True till death" and " When other lips." Mr. Rogerson gave a Lancashire reading, which was amusing, and after Miss Tipping had sung, Messrs. Smith and Joinson were very successful in their render- ing of the vocal duet, "The Battle Eve." The Chairman delivered a suitable address. Mr. Smith and Miss Thorpe played the accompaniments duraig the evening.

A Select Committee of the House of Comtnans on Wed- uesdav passed the preamble of the Bill promoted by the Lancashire County Council for the establishment of a County Asylums Board. Miss Martha Roberts, milliner, Heckmondwike, was awarded £l,OOO damages at the Leeds Assizes,on Thurs- day, against Mr. Arthur Whitley,manufacturer, Golcar, near Huddersfield, for breach of promise.

div.head: WHY EAT FISH?
div.p: WHY EAT FISH?

Sir.—l wonder how many of the countless nnmber who will indulge themselves with fish on Friday next will consider whether the food they eat is wholesome and beneficial. Doubtless not many will reflect that in eating fish they are simply consuming the bodies of scavengers, for as the popular pig is the natural scavenger of the earth, so fish fulfils a similar mission in the sea. Divers testify to haying seen the dead bodies of shipwrecked people swarming with fish of every description, eagerly voraciously engaged in feasting upon the decomposing flesh, and thus fulfilling their natural functions in freeing the sea of its refuse. Ms we see that fish i 3 an undesirable and really unwholesome article of human food ; and in proof of this, I may point out that, when the "Eurydice "sank off the Isle of Wight some years ago, the inhabitants all along the coast were pro-. hibited for two years,:under heavy penalty, from buying or selling fish. There is nothing attractive abeut fish as an article of diet, nor is there any nutriment in it. But for the strong impregnation of salt, it would be tasteless, and, as it is, its saline quality is productive of nothing but thirst in those who partake of it. Ask yourselves it this is not so ; and if it be, why eat fish? Many persons take fish to follow some custom, of which they are in utter ignorance, and if this letter but causes such people to think it will not have been written in vain. If lovers of shrimps could only see them alive, especially when a dead body (with eyes, ears, mouth, &c., literally swarming with these industrious crusta- ceans), is taken from the water, they would doubtless not entertain so high an opinion of them. As to the in- jurious effects of eating mussels, which fatten in sewage we had a painful illustration not long ago when a whole family near Dublin, met their deaths through indulging in them. Depend upon it, the denizens of the sea are valueless and objectionable as articles of human con- sumption, and those personswho expunge fish from their dietary will be happiest and healthiest.—Yours &c., ANTI-FISH.

div.head: MR. LANGdAM AND THE DRINK BILL.
div.p: MR. LANGdAM AND THE DRINK BILL.

Sir,—l confess I have no heart either to admire or laugh at the impassioned utterances of the priest of Padgate regarding the horrors of the liquor traffic. Their sound and fury are soon lost in "the desert air," ,and when the explosion has died away there is nothing more substantial left behind than the well-deserved plaudits of appreciating friends. No amount of declamation, no "moral suasion," and no combination of teetotallers and moderate tipplers will ever free us from the eVil which Mr. Lanham so forcibly condemns. If the people are to be saved from the awful clutches of the British Moloch, they must pull down his temples and disband his priests. In spite of all the agencies and " isms " that are said to be doing battle against him, we have the authority of Mr. Lang,ham for the terrible statement that, alongside an increase of fifty per cent. in population, we have an incrPase of eighty per cent. in drunkenness!

SIR CHARLES RUSSELL.

Sir C. Russell, the most distinguished of living English barristers, is (if we may put it so) like so many other distinguished Englishmen, an Irishman. He is a nephew of the late Dr. Russell, President of May- nooth College, of whom Cardinal Newman spoke in his " Apologia " as the dear friend to whom,under Heaven, am indebted for my conver-

n 1833, in County Down, was educated at Trinity College. Dublin, and sat for Dundalk in the Parliament of 1880-85. He was called to the bar in 1859, and appointed Q.C. and elected Bendier of Lincoln's Inn in 1872. it is said of Sir Charles that " unlike many

leaders at the bar, he is not an exceptionally early riser, but he has an extraordinary faculty of getting to the root of things very quickly. He can do with remarkably little sleep,and find time both to ride and to go to Newmarket. So great, indeed, is his author- ity in turf matters that in the famous Ben d' Or case briefs for both plaintiff and defendant were sent for his acceptance. Sir C. Russell also plays a good hand at whist,and is one of the few thorough- going snuff-takets of his generation. He has an excellent House of Commons manner; his special forensic gift is that of 'carrying weight '—being just suited to that assembly. Sir Cnarles was returned to the House of Commons in 1885 by South Hackney, and again in 1886. Ile was Attorney- General in Mr. Gladstone's last administration and received the honour of knighthood. Sir Charles, it will be remembered, was engaged in the famous Maybrick murder case in Liverpool in August, 1889 and in the Parnell Commission, when he increased his reputation by the masterly oration he then I made.

div.head: DEATH OF MAJOR LITTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MAJOR LITTON.

It is with regret that we record that Major Litton, who has been ill for some weeks past, died about noon on Tuesday at his residence Hill Crest, Grappenhall. The deceased gentleman belonged to an old Warrington family, and in his time took a part of considerable prominence in sev- eral spheres of public life. He was the second son of the late Mr. Thomas Litton, of Sankey Hall, and was educated at Warrington Grammar School. He afterwards took part, in conjunction with an uncle, Mr. Wm. Litton, of Orford Hall, in the manage- ment of the corn mills of Bank Quay, and, on his uncle's retirement, Major Litton succeeded to the business, and carried it on till 1880, when the milts were purchased by Messrs. Fairclough and Sons. Major Litton's active connection with the Corporation began in 1879, when he was elected for the South-west Ward. He continued in the Council, and took a share in transacting the business of several committees till 1888, when, having sold his corn mill he lost his quali- fication and retired from the Town Council. He was appointed a magistrate of the borough in 1879, and con- tinued up to the time of his illness to give a regular attention to magisterial duties. For many years his name wao, perhaps, most prominently associated with the volunteer movement in Warrington. He joined the local corps,at is very beginning in 1850,as a private,and was successively raised to the positions of ensign, lieu- tenant, captain, and major. With one slight break,. he was continuously connected with the volunteers till 1886, and upon his retirement his past services were very suit- ably acknowledged by the commanding officer of the battalion. The deceased gentleman also gave much of his valuable aid in the management of the Infirmary,of which he was a life governor, and a member of the House, Visitors and Finance Committees. For the last two or three years he acted as treasurer to the institu- tion, and was, notwithstanding his illness, re-elected to this position at the meeting of governors a few weeks ago. Major Litton was a pronounced Conservative in politics, and was for a long time chairman of the North- west Ward Committee. He was likewise a director of the Conservative Club Buildings Company, and a member of the Finance Committee of the Association. At the time of his death, Nihich was due to heart disease, Major Litton was 59 years of age. He leaves a widow and seven children.

div.head: REFERENCE AT THE POLICE COURT
div.p: REFERENCE AT THE POLICE COURT

At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday morning, Alderman Sutton, the presiding magistrate, said before they proceeded with the business that morning, it was his painful duty to refer to the death of Major Litton which had taken place on the Tuesday previous. Major Litton had been a magistrate of that borough for up- wards of ten years, and so long as his health permitted always attended there to his duties very regularly. They all knew that Major Litton was always very straight- forward, and determined to do justice to everybody in his capacity of magistrate. He was identified with al- most all the charitable institutions in the town, and was officially connected with, and took a very active part in, the management of the Infirmary. He was also a trustee of the Blue Coat School ;in 'fact there was scarcely an institution in the town that he did not take some interest in. He (the Chairroan) considered therefore that the town had lost a very valuable citizen, and that it would feel his loss very materially. Mr. G. F. White, deputy magistrates' clerk, said he should like on behalf of the officers of the court to endorse what Mr. Sutton had said as regarded the attendance of the deceased gentleman at court. He had rarely if ever missed being present in his place, except through bad health or pressing business, and he was sure they would feel his loss a very great deal. Chief-Constable Hunt said it was his duty not only for himself but the whole force ,to say that they had always had very great pleasure in coming before Major Litton in any case they might have,knowing that he discharged his duties faithfully and conscientiously, and strictly according to law ; and if he erred at all he erred on the merciful side. He was sure they had all lost a very warm-hearted fnend,and nobody more than the borough police had.

div.head: FUNERAL
div.p: THE FUNERAL

The interment of the dece sed took place at Grappen- hall Churchyard, yesterday afternoon. The funeral pro- cession started from late the residence of the deceased, Hill Crest, Grappenhall, about half-past twelve. The procession was headed by a contingent of the War- rington Borough Police Force, which included Inspectors Cox and Spinks, and Sergeant Jones. Then followed the members of the Warrington Conservative Association with the Mayor of the Borough (Mr. Alderman R. W. Francomb) wearing the civic chain; Mr. Alderman Har- rison coming immediately after in Hs carriage. Lieut.- Colonel Bolton, and several other officers of the Warring- ton Volunteer Corps, all in uniform, and the Blue Coat School boys, under the charge of the head-master Mr. Edward Rose, also took part in the procession. The hearse, the coffin in which was almost hidden with flowers and wreaths, was followed by nineteen carriages. The first contained Mrs. Litton, the widow of the deceased, Mr. Litton, his son, Miss Litton, and Mrs. A. Reynold.. the second, Miss L. Litton, Miss G. Litton, Miss A. Litton, and Miss Jackson. In the third were Mr. Arthur Reynolds, Capt. Ridgeway, and Miss Barnes, and in the fourth Mr. Charles White, Mr. McKay, Mr. H. Geddes, and Mr. T. W. Geddes, in the fifth Major Pickmere, Mr. John White, and Mr. Mor- timer, and in the sixth, Mr. George Dakin, Mr. Edward Greenall, and Mr. H. Greenall. In addition to those we have mentioned there were present the following mem- bers of the Warrington Corporation :—Aldermen Sutton, Wright, Davies, and Burgess, and Councillors J. Taylor Muir, Mr. Whittle, (town clerk), Mr. G. P. White (deputy magistrates' clerk), Mr. K. Isherwood, the Revs. B. B. Prescott and C. E. Jackson, Drs. White, Smith, and Sherratt, Messrs. John Hampson (Con- servative registration agent), S. Higham (manager of the Warrington Conservative Club), Wallace, Harrison (Latchford stationmaster), and P.C.'s Mil- lington and Bennett of the county police force, were also present. The mourners were met at the gate of the churchyard by the Rev. Canon Greenall, rector of Grappenhall, and the surpliced choir, and preceeded by them to the church,the choir singing a hymn adapted to the occasion. The services were conducted by the Rev. Canon. At the graveside in addition to those we mention as joining in the procession we noticed the Rev. F. W• Willis, (rector of Warrington) and the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (vicar of Holy Trinity. Wreaths were contributed by a large number of persons the cards upon them being inscribed as follows —Mrs. Litton, "with the children's love," Mr. and Mrs. Geo. Litton, and Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Jessie Murray and Harriet Geddes, Mr. and Mrs. Edelsten, Infirmary nurses, Mr. James Hepherd. "With Edith's love," Mrs. Charles Broadbent, Mr. and Mrs. William Tinsley, Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Reynolds, The members of the Latchford mothers' meeting, Miss Andrew, "Servants at Hill Crest," Conservative Association and Club, "The Rector and Mrs. Willis," Mrs. Sylvanus Reynolds, Mr. and Mrs. Eclctard Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. John White, "Porter and Servants of the Infirmary," Mr. and Mrs. Greenall, Mrs. Hill, Mrs. Deacon, Mr. and Mrs. H. Woods, Mr. Tinsley, " Bruche Hall," Mr. P. H. and E. Litton. Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield, Mrs. Geddes and family, Captain and Mrs. Ridgeway, Matron and house surgeons of the Infirmary. The funeral arrange- ments were carried out entirely by Messrs. J. and W. Dutton.

MR. GOSCHEN.

The Right Hon. George Joachim Goschen is the son of the late William Henry Goschen, a London, merchant of German extrac- tion. He was born in Lon- don, on the 10th August, 1831, and was educated at Rugby :nd at Oriel College, Oxford, where he took a first class in lassics. After leaving college te entered the firm of Fruh- ing and Goschen, and became director of the Bank of Eng- ism, in 1856. He first entered Parliament in 1863, when at a

al, he was returned as a Liberal for the City of London. In 1865, he was re-elected at the. head of the poll, and in the same year he was appointed Vice-President of the Board of Trade, and in 1866 he became Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, with a seat in the Cabinet. His tenure of that office, however, was only of brief duration, as Lord John Russell's ministry retired in June of the same year. On Mr. Gladstone's acces- sion to power in 1868, Mr. Goschen joined the Cabinet as President of the Poor Law Board, and. in 1871 succeeded Mr. Childers as First Lord of the Admiralty. He was again returned for London in 1874, but only as the . minority member, and in 1880, he did not seek the suffrages of his old constituents, but accepted an invitation to stand for Ripon, which he represented till the General Election of 1885, when he was returned for the Eastern division of Edinburgh. Mr.. Goschen did not join Mr. Gladstone's govern- ment in 1880 because he was opposed to the exten- sion of the franchise, but he acted as a special Ambassador to the Porte in 1880-81. Mr. Goschen has fur many years been spoken of as a " shaky" Liberal, and in the Parliament of 1880 be opposed the government both on the extension of the franchise and on foreign policy. When Mr. Glad-I, stone launched his Home Rule Bill in 1886, Mr. Goschen was among the first to enrol himself in opposition, as a consequence of which he was beaten in his old constituency of East Edinburgh. He was again defeated in the Exchange division of Liver-. Pool, but afterwards found a seat in St. George's, Hanover Square. On the resignation of Lord R. Churchill in December 188 es Mr. Goschen accepted the Chancellorship of the Exchequer, which he has since held. It may be added that Mr. Goschen the author of several financial and political pamphlets, and of the well-known work on the "Theory of Foreign Exchanges."

OPEN CHURCH MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening a public meeting of the Open Church Association for tne dioceses rf Chester and Liverpool was held in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey- st., Warrington. The Rector. the Rev. F. W. Willis, presided, and there was a fair attendance. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, referred to some abuses in connection with churches arid which he earnestly hoped were ,things of the past—such, for instance, as the letting of pews for hire and gain. He had read of those things, which, he had been told, had been exaggerated, but which undoubtedly had taken place in the past. He had no knowledge of such things himself and he did not think anybody had now. There was another practice he remembered as a boy, and he did not know whether it was quite obsolete yet. That ' was the reservation. of pews for absentees. He could re- recollect that as a boy he was brought up always to think their pew was their right and their own property, and they should have resented very much the intrusion, as they should have thought it, if anybody had entered it when they were not there. That kind of thing had not yet, he believed, entirely gone. There was another abuse, that of favouring the rich and the great at the expense of the poor. He could remember that pews at the end of a church, in which people could with difficulty hear and see, were thought good enough for the poor, while large boxes were appropriated by the rich and the great. He believed that abuse was almost gone, and if there were still places reserved for the great and the rich he hoped it was not at the expense of the poor, but at places were, perhaps, the congregation was not very large, and where persons had from time immemorial had their seats. As a broad principle, they should upon the. Church as a House of God, in which there should be no distinction, no charges and no rights of proprietor- ship. People should not bring their own cushions and their own pieces af carpet, nor even put their books in the pews, because that was a kind of quasi ownership, while at the most their rights,if they had any,would only be for the year and no longer. Churchwardens had great duties and one of these was to find seats for the parish- ioners. There were some qualifications and modifica- tions to the broad principles he had laid down. They must not be generous at other people's expense, and when there were incumbents who had taken benefices is which a great part of thejr income came from pew rents, it would be very hard to take all this from them at a stroke, and leave a man to do the work was only half his means. (Hear. hear.) Mr. JOHN WHITE moved "That- all parishioners whether rich or poor, have an equal right to the free use of their parish or district church, and that the pew-rent system is opposed to Christian precept, the law of the Church, and the spiritual interest of the people." He remarked that the system of free and open churches was accepted everywhere, and though some did not see the advantage of putting it into force, the majority of people accepted the principle, and cierymen and wardens preferred to have a free and open church, except under circumstances over which they had no control. In Lan- cashire towns it had been proved that no other system could be adopted. and he was glad to say that the system was in force in the majority of the Warrington churches. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HERBERT WOOD seconded the resolution, and said that not onlyratepayers were classed as parishioners,but any person who had been confirmed had a right to com- municate at Easter at the church of the parish he might be in. By the system of pew-rents, a traveller was prac- tically kept out of church, and thus, in a mild sense, he was ex-communicated. (Arealause.) MT. HENRY CLARKE, Liverpool, supported the resolution, and remarked that the work of the association, was educational. It was simply to set before the world, and the church, certain principles which, if accepted, would lead at once to every church in the diocese being made free and open. , There was, he said, no single case of failure in a free and open church provided the clergyman did his duty and was backed up by earnest workers. One advant- age of an open church was that it enabled the clergy- man to go round his parish and invite everybody to church ; but he could not do that in a pew-rented church. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was adopted, and afterwards the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

The Conservatives are watching With much Interest the next move that may be made by Mr. Parnell upon Mr. Maurice Healy's acceptance of his challenge to vacate the two seats in the city of Cork. Should vacancies occur, the Conservatives will run a candidate in each division. They have already selected Mr. Wright, Q.C., as one of the can- didates. --- There is another Kipling in the field. John Lock- wood Kipling is his name, and he is the father of the clever young Anglo-Indian who took England by storm with his Plain Tales from the Hills." Pretty soon we shall be hearing of Kipling pire and Kipling fils. A book from the former is shortly to be issued by a London publisher, and London will be able to judge how much of his wit and origina- lity young Kipling derives from his father. Mr. John .Kipling is not unknown in India is an artist and writer, but he has yet to win his laurels in Eng- land. The success of a son tempting a father to the pursuit of fame is '1 spectacle unique in the annals of English literature.

SUMMONSES AGAINST MR. JACKSON WITHDRAWN. Yesterday summonses against mr.Jackson, Blackburn, for assaulting Mrs. Baldwin were at Clitheroe withdrawn. THE ASTON CONTEST. Pblling opened at Aston yesterday morning, both Mr. Beale (the Liberal) and Captain Hutchinson (the Con- servative candidate) • being early in the field. At eleven o'clock the voting had proceeded slowly all morning. ThaConservatives had plenty of vehicles,aud the Liberals no so many. RESULT. Hutchinson (U). 5310 Beale (G) Majority 2978 The'Conservative majority in 1886 was 782 THE GREAT LICENSING CASE MAGISTRATES' AUTHORITY CONFIRMED. APPEAL DISMISSED WITH COSTS. The House of Lords, yesterday, gave judgment in an important licensing appeal,. Sharpe v. Wakefield. It raised the question of the right of the justices to refuse, their discretion, the renewal of a license. The court, I however, decided, in favour of the justices having this right. The Lord Chancellor, Lord Herschell, Lord Bracnaughton,Lord Bramwell ,and Lord Hannen, unanim- ously upheld the decisicns of the Courts below, so that the magistrates' discretion remains unaltered. The ap- peal was accordingly dismissed with costs. YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarterpast four. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Consolidated Funds (No. 1) Bill and the Army Annual Bill were read a third time, and passed. The Fishery Board (Scotland) Bill, the Clergy Discipline Bill; and Technical Instruction Bill were read a third time, and the sitting was suspended for the ar- • rival of the Tithes Bill from the abuse of Commons. THE TITHES BlLL.—Discussion was resumed on the Lords Amendments to the Tithe Bill, the particular clause discussed being one which provides that where a receiver satisfies the County Courtthat the rent reserved is insufficient to par the tithe, the court may, after cal- ling on the occupier to appear,. adjudge him to pay the amount,. the tenant deducting the sum from any moneys due from him to the landlord. The clause was strongly opposed from Opposition benches. The Lords re-assembled •at ten minutes past seven, when the consideration of the Commons amendments to the Lords amendments to the. Tithes Bill was post- poned until Monday. The House adjourned at aquarter-past seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair shortly after two o'clock. THE NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERIE%—Mr. STAVELEY HILL asked whether the Government were prepared to accede to the request chmtained in a telegram from the Speaker of the House of Representatives which he received, to the effect that both branches of the Legislature desired the Britiilalouse of Commons to delay legislation on the subject- of a treaty with France in respect of the New- foundland fisheries until the Legislature of Newfound- land had an opportunity of presenting their views. Mr. W. H. SMITH was cheered by both sides of the House when he replied that he could not be expected to give a hasty answer to a question of such grave importance. If the question was repeated on Monday he would be able to answer it. A committee was appointed to, draw up reasons for disagreements with some of the Lords' amendments. The sitting' was then suspended.

SIGNS AND, RHYMES. Mr. R. E. Egerton-Warburton, of Arley Hall, Cheshire, has a, happy knack of rhyming, which has found its way to the finger-posts and signs on his extensive estate. Three of the finger-posts are as, follows : Trespassers-this notice heed;: Onward you may not proceed, Unless to Arley Hall you speed. No cartway, save on sufferance, here; For horse and foot the road is clear To Lymm, High. Legh,,Hough Green, and Mere. This. road iaforbidden to all, Unless they wend them way to call At Mill, or Green, or Arley Hall. Perhaps the most interesting of the verses is that which is. on the sign over the door of the inn at Appreton Thorn : You may safely, while sober, . Sit under the thorn, But if drunk over-night It will prick you next morn.
